docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
In another terminal, ask for the product twice:

$ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json
etag: W/"d5c916899a1291fccfef605e3d4ede40"
cache-status: Alcazaba; fwd=miss; stored
cache-control: max-age=60
vary: Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key

{"name":"Olive oil","price":9.5}

$ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json
etag: W/"d5c916899a1291fccfef605e3d4ede40"
cache-status: Alcazaba; hit; ttl=60
cache-control: max-age=60
vary: Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key

{"name":"Olive oil","price":9.5}

The first request ran read_product and stored its response: fwd=miss; stored. The second one came from the cache, hit, with the seconds the entry has left. A product that isn't there gets its 404, which is never cached:

$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/2
{"detail":"No such product"}

docs.title: Interactive API docs
docs.text: Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. FastAPI's interactive docs show the endpoint as usual: @cache keeps its parameters and its response model. Try it out twice, and look at the cache-status header of each response.

docs.title: Recap, step by step
docs.text:
FastAPICache.init(), in the lifespan, says where the entries live:

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    FastAPICache.init(InMemoryBackend(), prefix="shop")
    yield

InMemoryBackend keeps them in the process, which is enough to try things out. In production, Redis or Valkey keeps them for every process at once.

@cache(expire=60) keeps each response for 60 seconds:

@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
@cache(expire=60)
async def read_product(product_id: int) -> Product:
    if product_id not in PRODUCTS:
        raise HTTPException(404, "No such product")
    return PRODUCTS[product_id]

Under the route's decorator

@cache goes between @app.get(...) and the function. FastAPI registers the function below its decorator: with @cache above @app.get, the route would serve the uncached function.

Technical details

Each user gets entries of their own: requests with an Authorization, Cookie or X-API-Key header have their own keys, and their responses are sent as Cache-Control: private. That's what vary: Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key tells browsers and proxies. Cache-Status is the header of RFC 9211, and the ETag lets clients revalidate with If-None-Match and get a 304 Not Modified. The response cache page has the rest: shared entries, keys, signed entries.

docs.title: Step 2: limit the rate
docs.text:
Reading a product is cheap now, but nothing stops a single client from taking all the server's time. Give each client five requests a minute:

main.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPICache, FastAPIRateLimiter
from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.inmemory import InMemoryBackend
from fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache import cache


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    FastAPICache.init(InMemoryBackend(), prefix="shop")
    yield


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float


PRODUCTS = {1: Product(name="Olive oil", price=9.5)}


@app.get(
    "/products/{product_id}",
    dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=5, minutes=1))],
)
@cache(expire=60)
async def read_product(product_id: int) -> Product:
    if product_id not in PRODUCTS:
        raise HTTPException(404, "No such product")
    return PRODUCTS[product_id]

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
fastapi dev has reloaded the app. Make six requests:

$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1; done; echo
200 200 200 200 200 429

$ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
ratelimit: "5/60s";r=0;t=15
ratelimit-policy: "5/60s";q=5;w=60
retry-after: 15
content-type: application/json

{"detail":"Too Many Requests"}

The sixth request and those after it get a 429 Too Many Requests, with Retry-After: the seconds to wait. Every response carries the RateLimit header, so that clients can slow down before they get there: r is what's left, t the seconds until there's more.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
FastAPIRateLimiter is a FastAPI dependency: put it in dependencies=[...] of a route, of a router, or of the whole app. Dependencies run before the endpoint, so cached responses count too.

Behind a proxy

The limiter counts per client address, the one the ASGI server reports. Behind a proxy or a load balancer, tell uvicorn to take it from the proxy's headers (--forwarded-allow-ips); Rate limiting tells how, and how to count per user or per API key instead.

docs.title: Step 3: authorize with Casbin
docs.text:
Anybody may read the products, but only the staff may change their prices. Who's staff isn't written in the code: it's in a Casbin policy. Create these two files next to main.py:

model.confpolicy.csv model.conf
[request_definition]
r = sub, obj, act

[policy_definition]
p = sub, obj, act

[role_definition]
g = _, _

[policy_effect]
e = some(where (p.eft == allow))

[matchers]
m = g(r.sub, p.sub) && keyMatch2(r.obj, p.obj) && r.act == p.act
policy.csv
p, staff, /products/:id, PUT
g, ana, staff

The model says what a request is, (user, object, action), and when the policy allows it: when one of the user's roles (g) has a rule (p) whose path pattern matches the request's (keyMatch2, which takes :id for any value) and whose action is the request's. The policy says that the staff may PUT any product, and that Ana is staff.

Then use it in main.py:

main.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Annotated

import casbin
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer
from pydantic import BaseModel

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIAuthz, FastAPICache, FastAPIRateLimiter
from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.inmemory import InMemoryBackend
from fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache import cache


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    FastAPICache.init(InMemoryBackend(), prefix="shop")
    yield


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float


PRODUCTS = {1: Product(name="Olive oil", price=9.5)}
TOKENS = {"ana-token": "ana", "ben-token": "ben"}  # stands in for your authentication


def current_user(
    credentials: Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())],
) -> str:
    if credentials.credentials not in TOKENS:
        raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid token", headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    return TOKENS[credentials.credentials]


here = Path(__file__).parent
enforcer = casbin.Enforcer(str(here / "model.conf"), str(here / "policy.csv"))
authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_user)


@app.get(
    "/products/{product_id}",
    dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=5, minutes=1))],
)
@cache(expire=60, tags=lambda product_id, **_: [f"product:{product_id}"])
async def read_product(product_id: int) -> Product:
    if product_id not in PRODUCTS:
        raise HTTPException(404, "No such product")
    return PRODUCTS[product_id]


@app.put("/products/{product_id}", dependencies=[Depends(authz)])
async def update_product(product_id: int, product: Product) -> Product:
    if product_id not in PRODUCTS:
        raise HTTPException(404, "No such product")
    PRODUCTS[product_id] = product
    await FastAPICache.invalidate_tags(f"product:{product_id}")
    return product

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Read the product, which caches it:

$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1
{"name":"Olive oil","price":9.5}

Then change its price without a token, as Ben, and as Ana:

$ curl -i -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"name": "Olive oil", "price": 8.0}'
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
www-authenticate: Bearer

{"detail":"Not authenticated"}

$ curl -i -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer ben-token" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name": "Olive oil", "price": 8.0}'
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

{"detail":"Forbidden"}

$ curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer ana-token" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name": "Olive oil", "price": 8.0}'
{"name":"Olive oil","price":8.0}

And the product has its new price at once, although its old one was cached:

$ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/products/1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json
ratelimit: "5/60s";r=3;t=2
ratelimit-policy: "5/60s";q=5;w=60
etag: W/"615d43a0044f76d19c5f354c5be3a495"
cache-status: Alcazaba; fwd=miss; stored
cache-control: max-age=60
vary: Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key

{"name":"Olive oil","price":8.0}

In the interactive docs, the PUT endpoint now has a lock: click Authorize, give ana-token, and try it out.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
FastAPIAuthz takes the enforcer, which reads the model and the policy, and subject: a dependency that says who makes the request. current_user stands in for your authentication here; with yours, it decodes a JWT or reads a session.

here = Path(__file__).parent
enforcer = casbin.Enforcer(str(here / "model.conf"), str(here / "policy.csv"))
authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_user)

Depends(authz) asks the policy about the request: may ana PUT /products/1? A request without a token gets a 401 before the policy is asked; one that the policy refuses, a 403.

Tags drop cached entries when the data changes: tags= names the product's entry, and FastAPICache.invalidate_tags() drops it after the update.

Your own actions

The path and the method aren't the only things to ask about: authz.require("prices", "change") asks whether the user may change prices, whatever the route. Casbin tells how, and how to open routes to visitors without an account.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
You have an app whose product pages are cached and refreshed when they change, whose clients can't flood it, and whose prices only the staff can change:

  • FastAPICache.init() in the lifespan, and @cache(...) under the route's decorator.
  • FastAPIRateLimiter(...) in a route's dependencies.
  • FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=...) in a route's dependencies, with a Casbin model and policy.

In production

So far everything lives in the process: each process has its own cache and counters. With Redis or Valkey every process shares them, and a signing key keeps whoever can write to the backend from planting entries: see the production setup.

docs.title: Accounting
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

FastAPIAccounting meters what each subject uses: a user, an API key, a tenant. It counts each meter (requests, tokens, rows, bytes…) per period, holds it to a quota, and sends a usage record for each charge, which is what billing adds up. Authentication tells who makes the request, authorization whether they may; accounting, how much they have used.

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIAccounting
from fastapi_alcazaba.accounting import Metering, Quota


async def tokens_of(tenant: str) -> int:
    return (await plans.of(tenant)).tokens_a_month  # from your database


accounting = FastAPIAccounting(
    subject=current_tenant,  # your dependency: the tenant's ID, None without one
    quotas=[
        Quota("searches", limit=1_000, period="day"),
        Quota("tokens", limit=tokens_of, status=402),  # a month by default
    ],
)


@app.get("/search", dependencies=[Depends(accounting.meter("searches"))])
async def search(q: str) -> list[Result]: ...


@app.post("/summaries")
async def summarize(
    text: Text,
    usage: Annotated[Metering, Depends(accounting.meter("tokens", amount=None))],
) -> Summary:
    summary = await model.summarize(text)
    usage.add(summary.tokens)  # charged when the endpoint ends
    return summary
  • Two ways to charge: meter("searches") charges 1 unit before the endpoint runs (amount=5 for more), checked against the quota and counted in one atomic operation, so concurrent requests never go past it. meter("tokens", amount=None) gives the endpoint a Metering for what is only known as it goes (tokens, bytes, seconds), charged when it ends. Its quota is checked when the request starts: the requests running then may together go past it, by what each one uses.
  • Over the quota: a 429 with Retry-After, the seconds until the period ends, or a 402 (status=402: a plan to upgrade); a WebSocket is closed with 1008. The request isn't counted. Every response carries the IETF draft's RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers, named after the meter ("searches";r=997;t=48600), and problem details carry them too.
  • Plans: limit is a number, or a function (plain or async) of the subject's ID that gives its plan's; None from it is no limit. Meters without a quota are counted, not bounded, per period= (a month by default).
  • Periods: calendar hours, days or months, in UTC: a monthly quota starts again on the 1st at 00:00 UTC. period_of("month", at) gives a period's label (2026-11) and its bounds.
  • What's charged: a client error (a 4xx, a validation error) was served, and stays charged: otherwise invalid requests would be free. A server error (an exception, a 5xx) or a client that went away is refunded, without a record. What an endpoint added to its Metering is charged whatever happens next: it was used.
  • Who: subject is a dependency that returns an ID (a str, an int or a UUID), from your authentication: a user's, an API key's, a tenant's to share one quota among its users. Without one, a 401 (WWW-Authenticate: <challenge>). The counters' keys are SHA-256 digests: the IDs never reach the backend in clear.

docs.title: Usage and records
docs.text:
@app.get("/usage")
async def read_usage(
    request: Request,
    tenant: Annotated[str, Depends(signed_in_tenant)],
) -> Usage:
    report = await accounting.usage(tenant, "tokens", request=request)
    return Usage(used=report.used, remaining=report.remaining, resets=report.resets)
  • Counters: in the cache's backend (the app's, get_cache, or cache=), shared by every process, per subject, meter and period. usage(subject, meter) reads one: used, limit, remaining, period and when it resets; at= reads the period before, which they keep through the next one. request= takes the cache installed on the app.
  • Records: each charge is a UsageRecord (a random id, time, subject, meter, amount, period, and the request's ID, trace, method and route template), sent to the fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.usage logger at INFO, one line of JSON, by default. That is what billing adds up, deduplicated by id: give the logger a handler and ship its lines, or pass sinks= of your own (any object with async def write(record), such as one inserting into a table), MemoryUsageSink for tests, () for none. A sink that fails or takes longer than timeout is logged with the record, so that it isn't lost, and the others still get it.
  • Outside requests: await accounting.record(tenant, "tokens", 1200) charges what a job or a webhook used, without checking the quota (it's been used), and sends its record.

docs.title: When the backend fails
docs.text:
The counters go through the cache's timeout and circuit breaker. When the backend fails, the requests go through uncounted (fail_open=True, the default) and the quotas aren't checked, but the records still have every charge: billing doesn't lose them. fail_open=False refuses them with a 503 (a WebSocket, 1013) instead, for quotas that cost money to go past. usage() raises BackendUnavailable.

  • Counted: the requests in fastapi_alcazaba.accounting, by meter and outcome (allowed, exceeded, unauthenticated, unchecked, refunded), the units in fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.usage by meter, and the records not written in fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.undelivered.
  • And the rate limits: a quota bounds what a subject uses in a calendar period, to bill or to share a resource; a rate limit bounds how fast, in a sliding window, to protect the service. An API usually has both: Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(10, seconds=1)) before Depends(accounting.meter("requests")), so that a burst is refused before it's charged.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

FastAPIAudit records the sensitive actions: who did what to which resource, whether it worked, and the request it came from. As a dependency, it writes the event when the endpoint ends:

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIAudit
from fastapi_alcazaba.audit import AuditEntry

audit = FastAPIAudit(signing_key=settings.audit_signing_key)
deleting = audit.action("invoice.delete", resource="invoice:{invoice_id}")


@app.delete("/invoices/{invoice_id}", status_code=204)
async def delete_invoice(
    invoice_id: int,
    entry: Annotated[AuditEntry, Depends(deleting)],  # first: it records refusals too
    user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)],
) -> None:
    entry.actor = user.id
    entry.details["amount"] = await invoices.delete(invoice_id, owner=user.id)
  • How it ended: success when the endpoint returns, denied when it raises a 401 or a 403 (1008 for WebSockets), failure otherwise, with the exception's type and status, never its message: messages carry data. Declared before the dependency that authenticates, the audit dependency also records the requests that one refuses, with the resource from the path. An endpoint that answers an error without raising sets entry.outcome; entry.reason says why.
  • Outside endpoints: await audit.log("user.login", outcome="failure", reason="wrong password", request=request) writes one event, and async with audit.record("backup.restore", actor="cron") one for a block of code (a job, a task), which fails when it raises or is cancelled.
  • Correlation: each event has the request ID (with RequestIDMiddleware), the OpenTelemetry trace, the method, the route template (/invoices/{invoice_id}, never the path, which may carry tokens) and the client's address as the server reports it (see client_ip behind a proxy).
  • No secrets: in details, the values under keys that name one (password, newPassword, X-Api-Key, refresh_token, session_id, cookie, card_number…: SENSITIVE_WORDS, plus yours with redact=["iban"]) and the strings that look like credentials (Bearer …, JWTs, private keys) are recorded as [redacted]. Objects and bytes are recorded by their type, not their content; strings are cut at 500 characters, lists and dicts at 50 items and 4 levels. Give actor and resource IDs, not e-mail addresses.
  • Where they go: to the logger fastapi_alcazaba.audit.events, at INFO, one line of JSON per event, ASCII only so that nothing in it splits a line: give it a handler of its own and let the log pipeline ship it to storage that can't be rewritten. If that logger outputs nothing (no handler, the root logger at WARNING), it says so once. sinks= takes others: any object with async def write(event), such as one inserting into a table, and MemoryAuditSink for tests.
  • Signed and chained: with a signing_key (the same in every process), each event is signed and carries the signature of the previous one of its stream (one per process), numbered. verify_audit_trail(events, keys) lists the events altered, forged, missing or out of their chain, from AuditEvents or the JSON lines read back. The signature is <algorithm>:<kid>:<value> of fastapi_alcazaba/audit3, a NUL byte and the event's RFC 8785 canonical JSON without its signature (fastapi_alcazaba.core.canonical_json): any language with a JCS library checks it the same way, a SIEM or an auditor's script included. For that, details keep to I-JSON: integers beyond 2⁵³ are recorded as text, lone surrogates as U+FFFD. See "Verifying it" below for the keys and the newest events.
  • Authentication and authorization: FastAPIAuth(audit=audit) records failed authentications, OAuth2, OpenID Connect and SAML logins, and missing scopes (In the audit trail); FastAPIAuthz(audit=audit) and AuthzMiddleware(audit=audit) the requests their policy refuses (Authorization).
  • Delivery: a sink that fails or takes longer than timeout (5 s) is logged at ERROR with the event, so that it isn't lost, and counted; the other sinks still get it, and an event is written even when its request is cancelled meanwhile. The action isn't undone or refused for it: when an action mustn't happen unrecorded, write the record in the action's own database transaction.

docs.title: Verifying it
docs.text:
An HMAC secret signs and verifies alike: whoever checks the trail could rewrite it. An Ed25519 key pair separates both: the app signs with the private key, the auditor verifies with the public one, which can't sign.

fastapi-alcazaba audit keygen audit-private.pem audit-public.pem  # the private one: 0600

audit = FastAPIAudit(
    signing_key=settings.audit_private_key,  # PEM; or [new, old] while it's rotated
    checkpoint_interval=300,  # a checkpoint every five minutes, through the cache's backend
)

fastapi-alcazaba audit verify audit-2026-11-*.log --key audit-public.pem --key audit-public-2025.pem
# events: 18342 in 6 streams
# last checkpoint: 2026-11-03T17:55:02+00:00
# ok
  • Keys: signing_key is an Ed25519 private key (PEM, or cryptography's object; generate_audit_key_pair()) or an HMAC secret of 32 bytes or more. Each signature names its algorithm and key (ed25519:<kid>:…, hs256:<kid>:…), so verify_audit_trail(events, keys) takes every key the events span (public keys, or the secrets) and checks each event with its own. Rotating: sign with the new key ([new, old]), keep giving the verifier the old public key for the events it signed; HMAC to Ed25519 the same way.
  • Checkpoints: every checkpoint_interval seconds (with the next event), a process writes an audit.checkpoint event listing the newest event (its number and signature) of every stream of the trail, as each process last published it in the cache's backend (under its lock; cache=, FastAPICache's by default; without one, its own stream only). A stream whose newest events were removed then ends before what a later checkpoint saw, and the verifier says so; so it does when a whole stream is missing, or an event was replaced by one signed again. What came after the last checkpoint can still be removed unnoticed: last_checkpoint(events) (and the command) says when that was. Send the checkpoints also somewhere the app can't rewrite (a second sink), and the window shrinks to checkpoint_interval.
  • The command: fastapi-alcazaba audit verify FILE… reads the events from JSON lines (after a log line's prefix too; other lines are skipped), - for stdin; --key PEM for public keys, --hmac-env NAME for a secret in an environment variable (never on the command line); --json for scripts. It exits with 1 when something's wrong.
  • From Python:
import json

from fastapi_alcazaba.audit import last_checkpoint, verify_audit_trail

with open("audit.log") as lines:
    events = [json.loads(line) for line in lines]
problems = verify_audit_trail(events, [public_key_pem, old_public_key_pem])

docs.title: API keys, tokens and codes
docs.text:
Credentials kept only as digests: API keys with scopes and expiry, revoked tokens and one-time codes. The codes of an authenticator app, as a second factor: Second factor.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
FastAPIAPIKeys authenticates machine clients by an API key. It generates the keys and checks them; your database keeps a record of each, never the key itself:

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import FastAPIAPIKeys


async def load_key(key_id: str) -> ApiKeyRow | None:  # any object with digest, scopes, expires_at
    return await db.get(ApiKeyRow, key_id)


keys = FastAPIAPIKeys(load_key, pepper=settings.api_key_pepper, bearer=True)


@app.post("/api-keys")
async def create_key(user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)]) -> dict[str, str]:
    new = keys.generate(scopes=["orders:read"], expires_at=datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(days=90))
    await db.add(ApiKeyRow(owner=user.id, **dataclasses.asdict(new.record)))
    return {"key": new.key}  # shown once: only its digest is stored


@app.get("/orders")
async def orders(key: Annotated[ApiKeyRow, Depends(keys.require("orders:read"))]) -> list[Order]:
    return await db.orders(owner=key.owner)
  • Key format: ak_<id>_<secret>_<checksum> (prefix changes ak; sk_live works too): an 80-bit id that finds the record, a 256-bit secret, and the CRC-32 of the rest, in lowercase base32. A distinctive prefix lets secret scanners (GitHub's, GitLab's) spot leaked keys, and the checksum lets them tell a key from a string that looks like one without asking anybody (as GitHub's own tokens do). It isn't a secret: a key with the wrong one is refused as malformed, without a lookup.
  • Stored as a digest: the record holds a SHA-256 digest of the secret, bound to the key's id. Random 256-bit secrets don't need a slow password hash. With a pepper (a server secret of at least 32 bytes, kept out of the database) the digest is an HMAC, so a copy of the database alone can't even test a guess. A list of peppers rotates them: the first one makes new keys, all of them are accepted.
  • Your database: lookup(key_id) returns your row, async or not (a plain function runs in a thread, like FastAPI's sync dependencies), and the dependency returns that same row. Any object with digest, scopes (a collection, or a space-separated string) and expires_at works; APIKeyRecord is what generate() gives.
  • Where the key comes from: the X-API-Key header (header=...) and, with bearer=True, Authorization: Bearer <key>. Both appear in the OpenAPI schema, for the docs' Authorize button.
  • One answer: a missing, malformed, unknown, wrong or expired key gets the same 401, with WWW-Authenticate; the secret is compared in constant time, and malformed keys don't reach lookup. keys.require("a", "b") adds a 403 for a valid key without all those scopes (with an RFC 6750 insufficient_scope challenge in bearer mode). Keys and secrets are never logged.
  • Revocation: delete the record, or set its expires_at in the past (naive datetimes are taken as UTC). cache_ttl keeps looked-up records in each process for that many seconds to spare the database, so a revocation then takes up to cache_ttl to reach every process; keys.forget(key_id) drops one from this process at once. Unknown ids are never cached.
  • Floods: each request with a well-formed key costs a lookup: put a FastAPIRateLimiter in front.
  • Without a dependency: await keys.authenticate(key) for keys that come some other way (a WebSocket message).

docs.title: Revoked tokens and one-time codes
docs.text:
A JWT can't be taken back once issued. TokenBlocklist keeps the revoked ones in the cache's backend, shared by every process, until they would have expired anyway:

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import OneTimeCodes, TokenBlocklist

blocklist = TokenBlocklist()  # FastAPICache's backend; or TokenBlocklist(cache)


async def current_user(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(decode_jwt)]) -> str:
    sub, iat = claims["sub"], claims["iat"]
    if await blocklist.is_revoked(claims["jti"], subject=sub, issued_at=iat):
        raise HTTPException(401)
    return sub


@app.post("/logout")
async def logout(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(decode_jwt)]) -> None:
    await blocklist.revoke(claims["jti"], expires_at=claims["exp"])


@app.post("/password")
async def change_password(user: Annotated[str, Depends(current_user)]) -> Token:
    ...
    await blocklist.revoke_subject(user, ttl=TOKEN_LIFETIME)  # log out everywhere
    return issue_token(user)  # issued now: still valid

OneTimeCodes are the codes you send by e-mail or SMS:

codes = OneTimeCodes(secret=settings.otp_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.post("/login/code", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=3, minutes=15))])
async def send_code(email: str) -> None:
    await send_email(email, await codes.issue(email, purpose="login"))


@app.post("/login")
async def login(email: str, code: str) -> Token:
    if not await codes.verify(email, code, purpose="login"):
        raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid or expired code")
    ...
  • Nothing in clear: token ids and subjects are stored as SHA-256 digests. Codes are stored as an HMAC with secret, bound to their subject and purpose: a plain digest of a 6-digit code is brute-forced in milliseconds by whoever reads the backend. A list of secrets rotates them.
  • Expiry: each revocation lasts while the token could still be accepted (exp, plus leeway, 60 s by default, for what your JWT library tolerates). Codes last ttl seconds (300).
  • Log out everywhere: revoke_subject refuses the tokens issued before the current second. iat has whole seconds, so the token you issue right after for the current session stays valid.
  • One login: revoke_session(sid, ttl=...) refuses every token whose sid claim is sid: JWTStrategy checks it, and RefreshTokens revokes a login's access tokens this way (see refresh tokens).
  • Guesses and single use: every guess counts, malformed ones included, and a code is lost after max_attempts (5). Of several requests with the right code at the same time, only one succeeds. The guesses are counted for the subject and purpose, not for each code: issuing a new one replaces the previous one but doesn't give them back, so asking for code after code never adds up to more than max_attempts guesses each ttl. Once they're used, new codes fail too until the window ends (up to ttl, 5 minutes); the right code starts the count again. Rate-limit the route that issues them anyway: each code is an e-mail or an SMS.
  • Every process sees them at once: they're read from the shared backend, never from TieredBackend's copies in each process. On DynamoDB, whose reads are eventually consistent, a revocation or a new code can take about a second to reach every process.
  • Failures: if the backend fails, is_revoked refuses tokens (fail_open=True accepts them), verify returns False, and revoke, revoke_subject and issue raise BackendUnavailable. With a signing_key or encryption_key, revocations are sealed and planted ones are ignored. Whoever can delete keys in the backend can still un-revoke tokens.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
Where the cache and every other tool keep their entries and their state.

Every class and function: the API reference.

  • InMemoryBackend(max_size=10_000): per process; for development, tests and single-process apps. Up to max_size cached responses, and as many keys of state (counters, revoked tokens…) in a store of their own.
  • RedisBackend(redis): redis-py client, standalone or cluster, created without decode_responses=True. Works with any server that speaks the Redis protocol (Valkey, KeyDB, Dragonfly).
  • ValkeyBackend(valkey): the same with valkey-py (valkey.asyncio, not the sync client).
  • GlideBackend(client): Valkey GLIDE, the official Valkey client with a Rust core (await GlideClient.create(...) or GlideClusterClient).
  • TieredBackend(remote, local_ttl=5): a per-process memory level in front of any of these (see "Two-level cache").
  • MemcachedBackend(client): aiomcache.
  • DynamoBackend(table_name, region, endpoint_url=None): aiobotocore; await backend.init() first. Enable TTL on the ttl attribute of the table. endpoint_url for DynamoDB Local or LocalStack.
Backend Clear a namespace or a tag Locks Rate limiter InMemory yes (one process) (one process) Redis, Valkey, GLIDE yes (SCAN + UNLINK; tag sets) yes yes, one Lua script Memcached yes (generations) yes (add, gets + cas) yes, adding and taking back what doesn't fit DynamoDB yes (generations) yes (conditional writes) yes, a conditional write Tiered like its shared backend like its shared backend in its shared backend

Every backend tells a hit how long its entry has left, for max-age and early_refresh.

Generations. memcached and DynamoDB can't list keys, so they don't delete a namespace's or a tag's entries: each namespace or tag that was cleared has a generation, a random token under a key of its own, and each cached response records the generations it was stored under. A clear writes a new token, and the entries stored before it are no longer served; they expire in their own time. So clear(namespace=...) and invalidate_tags return 0 there: what they hid can't be counted.

  • A hit reads the entry and its namespaces' generations at once (one round trip; two for a tagged entry). An entry computed while a clear ran isn't served either.
  • Only namespaces with fewer than 8 : can be cleared (the default keys have two); a deeper one raises ValueError.
  • memcached may evict a generation: its entries are then recomputed, never served stale. DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent: a clear may take a moment to be seen.
  • State (locks, counters, sessions, revoked tokens…) isn't in any namespace, as with every backend: no clear touches it.

memcached's locks last whole seconds: up to two more than their ttl, never less.

A backend of your own may lack locks or tags (supports_locks, supports_tags): Lock, the concurrency limiter, IdempotencyMiddleware and the second factor (FastAPITOTP) refuse it when they're set up, distributed_lock is skipped with a warning, and @cache(tags=...) stores untagged entries with a warning.

Valkey example with valkey-py:

import valkey.asyncio

from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.valkey import ValkeyBackend

client = valkey.asyncio.from_url("valkey://localhost:6379/0")
FastAPICache.init(ValkeyBackend(client), prefix="myapp", signing_key=settings.cache_signing_key)

docs.title: Two-level cache
docs.text:
from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.tiered import TieredBackend

FastAPICache.init(TieredBackend(ValkeyBackend(client), local_ttl=5), prefix="myapp")

TieredBackend keeps a small copy of each entry in the memory of every process, in front of the shared backend: hits served from there skip the network (131 µs → 56 µs per hit against a Valkey on the same machine; more across a real network). A local copy lives at most local_ttl seconds and never longer than the shared entry.

With Redis or Valkey through redis-py/valkey-py, writes, clears and tag invalidations are also announced on a pub/sub channel (invalidation_channel), so every process drops its copy at once: a tag invalidation names the keys it deleted, also the copies of processes that only read those entries (beyond 1000 keys, every process drops all its copies). A value read while an invalidation arrives isn't kept, since it may be the old one. Copies are only kept while the process is subscribed: if the subscription drops, or the client reconnects by itself, the local level is emptied, and bypassed until it's back. The channel is read with its own timeout, so a client socket_timeout doesn't end the subscription, and pinged after 5 quiet seconds: a connection that died silently is given up within 10. With the other backends (memcached, DynamoDB, GLIDE, a valkey-py cluster) staleness is bounded by local_ttl. If the shared backend goes down, the local copies keep being served until they expire.

docs.title: Background work
docs.text:
Work outside requests, shared by every process: jobs at given times, a task queue, a leader, locks, messages to every process, and an outbox for the messages a change announces.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs
docs.text:
FastAPIScheduler runs jobs every N seconds or by a cron expression, in every process of the app, and each tick once across them all:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIScheduler

scheduler = FastAPIScheduler()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIScheduler(cache)


@scheduler.every(minutes=5)
async def refresh_catalog() -> None: ...


@scheduler.cron("0 3 * * *", tz="Europe/Madrid")
def nightly_report() -> None: ...  # sync jobs run in a thread


@scheduler.every(seconds=30, exclusive=False)
async def reload_settings() -> None: ...  # in every process: what each keeps in memory


app = FastAPI(lifespan=scheduler.lifespan)  # or `async with scheduler:` in your lifespan
  • Once per tick: at each tick, the processes claim it in the backend, with an atomic counter named after the job and the tick, and only the first runs it. A lock held while the job runs keeps a run that outlasts its interval from overlapping the next tick in another process (on a backend of your own without locks, each tick still runs once, but long runs may overlap). The ticks are the same in every process: every(minutes=5) runs at :00, :05… (UTC), so keep the servers' clocks in sync (NTP). exclusive=False runs a job in every process.
  • Cron: five fields (minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week, Sunday being 0 or 7) with *, lists, ranges, steps and names (*/15 9-17 * * mon-fri), or @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly and @yearly, in the time zone tz (UTC by default). When the clocks change it does what cronie does: a job at a fixed time runs an hour later on the day its hour is skipped and once on the day it repeats; a job with * in its minute or hour follows real time. No dependency: the parser is Alcazaba's.
  • No drift, no bursts: the next run is the next tick after the clock, not a delay after the last run ended; ticks missed while a run took longer than its interval are skipped, not run in a row afterwards.
  • Failures: an exception is logged with its traceback, counted, and the job keeps its schedule. If the backend fails, the tick is skipped (fail_open=True runs it anyway, maybe in every process).
  • Start and stop: the jobs start with the app and never hold up its startup. At shutdown, jobs waiting for their next run stop at once and running ones get grace seconds (10) before they're cancelled; a sync job's thread runs to its end. scheduler.next_run(name) says when a job runs next. A job is named after its module and function (name= for another), the name that its ticks have in the backend.

docs.title: Task queue
docs.text:
FastAPITaskQueue hands work over from an endpoint to run in the background, in this process or in any other that shares the cache's Redis or Valkey:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPITaskQueue

queue = FastAPITaskQueue()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPITaskQueue(cache)


@queue.task(retries=5)
async def send_welcome_email(user_id: int) -> None: ...


app = FastAPI(lifespan=queue.lifespan)  # this process runs tasks too


@app.post("/users")
async def create_user(user: NewUser) -> None:
    ...
    await queue.enqueue(send_welcome_email, user.id)  # delay=60 or a timedelta to wait first
  • At least once: tasks live in a Redis stream read by a consumer group, and leave it only once they've finished. A process that dies while running one, or can't reach the backend to say it finished, means that it runs again elsewhere: write tasks so that running one twice does no harm (check first whether the e-mail went out). A worker that stops answering has its tasks taken over after visibility_timeout (60 s); running tasks are kept from that by heartbeats, however long they run. A task handed out more than max_deliveries times (5) goes to the dead letters instead: it may be what kills the workers.
  • Only registered tasks run, with JSON arguments, never pickle. enqueue checks that the arguments fit the function and serialise (TypeError otherwise), up to max_payload_size bytes (64 KiB); they arrive as JSON gives them back (tuples as lists).
  • Sealed: with a signing_key or encryption_key on the cache, every task is signed or encrypted and bound to its queue. A task that someone planted in the backend or altered is refused, logged and sent to the dead letters, never run, and so is a copy of a sealed task written back to the queue: each delivery has a run id that only one entry may claim, until replay_window (7 days) after it was due, when it's refused as stale. Without a key a warning is logged at start: whoever can write to the backend can run your tasks with arguments of their choosing.
  • Retries: a task that raises is tried again retries times (3), backoff seconds after the first failure (1), twice that after the second… up to max_backoff (600), each with jitter so that tasks that failed together (a service down) don't all retry at once. Then it goes to the dead letters with the type of its error, never the message, which may hold personal data. dead_letters() lists them, requeue_dead_letters() puts them back with their attempts reset, and discard_dead_letters(ids) deletes them.
  • Delayed tasks and retries wait in a sorted set, and move to the stream when they're due in a Lua script: two processes never both move one.
  • Bounded: the queue holds at most max_length tasks (100,000: waiting, running or delayed), and enqueue raises QueueFull beyond, instead of dropping any; about max_dead_letters (10,000) are kept. pending() counts the tasks that haven't finished.
  • Workers: start() and stop(), lifespan or async with, running concurrency tasks at a time (10) in each process; sync functions run in a thread. stop() takes no more tasks and gives the running ones grace seconds (10); those still running then are cancelled and go back to the queue at once (a sync task's thread can't be stopped: it runs to its end, so that task may run twice). A process that only runs tasks: async with queue: await asyncio.Event().wait().
  • Backends: Redis 6.2+ or Valkey through RedisBackend or ValkeyBackend (or a TieredBackend in front of one), clusters included: a queue's keys share a hash tag. Other backends raise NotImplementedError. Its keys are state keys, which clear() never deletes.
  • Small on purpose: no results, priorities or workflows. Each run is the root of a trace of its own, linked to the span of the request that enqueued it.

docs.title: Keeping it healthy
docs.text:
@queue.task(
    retries=5,
    timeout=30,  # seconds a run may take
    retry_on=(httpx.TransportError,),  # only these are retried
    give_up_on=(ValueError,),  # these go to the dead letters at once
)
async def send_invoice(invoice_id: int) -> None: ...


task_id = await queue.enqueue(send_invoice, 42, unique_key="invoice-42")
await queue.status(task_id)  # TaskStatus(state="pending", attempts=0, ...)
await queue.cancel(task_id)  # True: it hadn't started
  • Timeouts: a run that takes longer than timeout is cancelled and fails with TimeoutError: retried, or to the dead letters, and its worker takes other tasks. Without one, a task that hangs holds one of the concurrency slots for good: heartbeats keep it from being taken over. A sync task's thread can't be stopped: it's left to finish, outside the count.
  • Which errors retry: retry_on lists those that are (all by default), give_up_on those that never are; either way the task goes to the dead letters at once, reason failed.
  • Unique tasks: with unique_key, while a task enqueued with it waits, runs or waits for a retry, enqueue returns its ID and adds nothing: a message the outbox delivers twice, a request the client retries, run once. Once it succeeds, goes to the dead letters or is cancelled, the key is free (a requeued dead letter doesn't take it again). Many processes enqueuing with one key at once add one task. The backend keeps a digest of the key, not the key.
  • Status: status(task_id) says where a task is: pending (waiting, delayed, requeued), running, retrying (waiting for its next attempt), succeeded, dead (with its reason) or cancelled, with its attempts, the type of its last error and when it was enqueued and last changed; never its arguments. Each task's record is written by the scripts that move the task, and kept status_ttl (a day) after it ends; then status() gives None.
  • Cancelling: cancel(task_id) makes sure a task that hasn't started (pending, delayed or waiting for a retry) never runs, and frees its unique_key; a running or finished one isn't cancelled (False). A worker about to start it and cancel have one winner. The task counts in pending() until a worker drops it.
  • Inside a task: current_task() gives its id, name, this run's attempt (1, 2…) and how many it may have, e.g. to record "the last attempt failed" without counting on your own.
  • Dead letters: dead_letter_count() besides dead_letters(), requeue_dead_letters() and discard_dead_letters().

docs.title: From a shell
docs.text:
fastapi-alcazaba tasks does the same from a shell, where the app's settings are. Point it at the queue (module:attribute), or at a function that sets up what it needs and returns it: a queue on FastAPICache has no backend until the app's lifespan runs, which the command doesn't (it would start workers).

# myapp/worker.py
async def queue_for_cli() -> FastAPITaskQueue:
    FastAPICache.init(
        RedisBackend(redis.from_url(settings.redis_url)),
        prefix="myapp",
        signing_key=settings.cache_signing_key,
    )
    return queue

fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker queues                     # every queue of the module
fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker:queue_for_cli pending
fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker:queue_for_cli dead-letters -n 20
fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker:queue_for_cli requeue --all  # or their IDs
fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker:queue_for_cli discard 1730000000000-0
fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker:queue_for_cli status 3f2a…
fastapi-alcazaba tasks myapp.worker:queue_for_cli cancel 3f2a…

--json (before the command) prints JSON. It exits with 1 when a task isn't found or wasn't cancelled, and 2 for a wrong target or arguments. The current directory is importable, as with uvicorn; queues needs the module's queues to have their cache (FastAPITaskQueue(cache)).

docs.title: Leader election
docs.text:
FastAPILeader elects one process among all those sharing the backend, for work that must run in exactly one of them all the time (a queue consumer, an outbox relay, a watcher) rather than at given times (that's the scheduler):

from fastapi_alcazaba.background import FastAPILeader

leader = FastAPILeader("outbox")  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPILeader("outbox", cache=cache)


@leader.run
async def relay_outbox() -> None:
    while True:
        await relay_pending()
        await asyncio.sleep(1)


app = FastAPI(lifespan=leader.lifespan)  # or `async with leader:` in your lifespan

...
if leader.is_leader:  # anywhere, sync code included
    ...
  • Election: every process campaigns for a lock named after the leader, renewed every ttl / 3 seconds (ttl is 15 by default). The one that takes it leads and runs the functions given to run; the others try again every ttl / 3 seconds or so, with jitter.
  • Hand-over: a leader that stops releases the lock, and another process takes over within ttl / 3 seconds; one that dies, within ttl and a third. A leader that loses the lock (its renewals couldn't keep up) cancels its functions within a second and campaigns again; at the next election they run again.
  • Functions: async, without arguments, added before start(). They're cancelled when the leadership ends and must let the cancellation through. An exception is logged with its traceback; the process keeps leading.
  • Failures: while the backend is down nobody is elected, and a leader that can't renew steps down when its lock expires: no leader is better than two.
  • Limits: a leader that stalls for longer than ttl (a long pause, a network partition) can overlap the next one for a moment. Check is_leader between the steps of long work, and keep that work idempotent.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
A lock shared by every process and container, for work that only one of them must do at a time:

from fastapi_alcazaba.background import LockNotAcquired


async def nightly_report() -> None:  # every instance runs it; one builds the report
    try:
        async with FastAPICache.lock("nightly-report", ttl=60):  # or cache.lock(...)
            await build_report()
    except LockNotAcquired:
        pass  # another instance is on it
  • Expiry and renewal: a lock expires after ttl seconds, so a holder that dies doesn't keep it forever; while it's held, a background task renews it every ttl / 3.
  • Only the holder releases or renews it: each acquisition has a random token, checked by a Lua script on Redis, Valkey and GLIDE, by conditional writes on DynamoDB and by gets + cas on memcached (in memory, within one process). memcached counts whole seconds: a lock there lasts up to two seconds more than its ttl, never less. On DynamoDB, expiry compares the clocks of the app's servers: keep them in sync (NTP). A custom backend written for 0.1 has no extend_lock: use renew=False there, with a ttl longer than the work.
  • Waiting: wait=0 (the default) tries once, wait=5 keeps trying for 5 seconds, wait=None as long as it takes. acquire() and release() work without async with.
  • Failures: if the backend fails, acquire() raises BackendUnavailable: without it nobody can tell who holds the lock.
  • Limits: a holder that stalls for longer than ttl (a long pause, a network partition) loses the lock while it still runs. lock.held turns False when the renewals couldn't keep up: check it between the steps of long jobs, and make work that must never overlap idempotent too.

docs.title: Broadcast
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.7: its API may still change in any release.

What one process must tell the WebSockets of the others (a chat, a live board, notifications), or the other processes themselves (a setting changed): FastAPIBroadcast, over Redis or Valkey's pub/sub.

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIBroadcast

broadcast = FastAPIBroadcast(redis_client, signing_key=settings.broadcast_key)


@app.post("/rooms/{room}/messages")
async def say(room: int, form: Say, user: CurrentUser) -> None:
    await broadcast.publish(f"room:{room}", {"from": user.name, "text": form.text})


@app.websocket("/rooms/{room}")
async def listen(websocket: WebSocket, room: int) -> None:
    await websocket.accept()
    async with broadcast.subscribe(f"room:{room}") as messages:
        async for message in messages:
            if message.gap:
                await websocket.send_json(await room_state(room))  # some may have been missed
            else:
                await websocket.send_json(message.data)
  • At most once: a message reaches those subscribed when it's published. One that a subscriber missed (its connection to Redis dropped, or it fell queue_size messages behind) doesn't come back: the subscriber gets a gap instead, and sends the state again. Work that must happen goes to the task queue or the outbox.
  • One subscription per process, whatever its number of subscribers, which reconnects by itself, with a backoff.
  • Signed: with signing_key (32 bytes or more, the same in every process; a list rotates it), each message carries an HMAC of its channel and data, and those without it, planted by whoever can write to Redis, are dropped.
  • Bounded: a message is JSON, 64 KiB at most; channels are letters, digits and _.:-.
  • Without a client, messages stay in the process: for tests, and apps of one process.
  • At shutdown, await broadcast.close() in the lifespan.

docs.title: Outbox
docs.text:
A change saved and the message that announces it (to the task queue, a webhook, another service) go together or not at all: the message is written in the same database transaction as the change, and a relay delivers it afterwards, at least once. With the sqlalchemy extra.

from fastapi_alcazaba.background import FastAPILeader
from fastapi_alcazaba.background.outbox import (
    OutboxMessage,
    OutboxRelay,
    SQLAlchemyOutbox,
    outbox_table,
)

outbox = SQLAlchemyOutbox(outbox_table(Base.metadata), sessions=async_session)


@app.post("/orders")
async def place(form: Order) -> dict[str, int]:
    async with async_session() as session, session.begin():
        order = Order(**form.model_dump())
        session.add(order)
        await session.flush()
        await outbox.add(session, "order.placed", {"order_id": order.id})  # same transaction
    return {"id": order.id}


async def deliver(message: OutboxMessage) -> None:
    # Delivered twice (the relay stopped before marking it sent): enqueued once.
    await queue.enqueue(order_placed, message.payload, unique_key=message.id)


relay = OutboxRelay(outbox, deliver)
leader = FastAPILeader("outbox")  # one process relays


@leader.run
async def relay_outbox() -> None:
    await relay.run()
  • The table is yours, in your migrations: outbox_table(metadata) defines it (outbox by default). sessions makes the relay's sessions, a sessionmaker or an async_sessionmaker.
  • At least once: deliver(message) is awaited, and the message marked as sent when it returns. A process that stops in between delivers it again: each message has an id, and consumers keep the ones they've seen.
  • Retries: when deliver raises, the message is tried again 1, 2, 4… seconds later, up to max_delay, and given up on after max_attempts: kept in the table with its last error, never sent, for someone to look at.
  • In order, by one relay: the oldest due messages first, batch at a time. Run the relay in one process (leader election).
  • Payloads are JSON, 256 KiB at most: ids and what changed, not files.
  • The table doesn't grow without bound: run() deletes the messages sent more than retention seconds ago (7 days), every purge_interval (an hour), purge_batch (1000) at a time, each batch in a short transaction of its own. Those given up on stay. retention=None keeps everything; outbox.purge(older_than) purges on demand.
  • Messages given up on are listed by outbox.given_up() (id, topic, attempts, when written and given up, last error; not the payload), and outbox.requeue(ids) (all of them without ids) sends them again with their attempts reset, or outbox.discard(ids) deletes them.
  • Traced end to end: a message keeps the trace context of where it was written (its traceparent column), and each delivery is a span of its own (fastapi_alcazaba.outbox <topic>) linked to it: from the request to the delivery, and on to the task the delivery enqueues, which links to the delivery. Failures are recorded on the span.
  • Counted: fastapi_alcazaba.outbox (delivered, retried, given_up; by outbox and topic) and fastapi_alcazaba.outbox.purged; a BacklogMonitor measures how many wait and since when. Metrics and traces go to FastAPICache's providers when it's set up, to the global ones otherwise.
  • Indexes: ix_<table>_due on (sent, next_try), which serves the relay, the backlog and the purge, and ix_<table>_failed. Async sessions (async_sessionmaker, asyncpg) and plain ones (in a thread) work alike; the tests run on SQLite and PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Sessions, CSRF and security headers
docs.text:
What an app that browsers use needs: sessions it can revoke, requests from other sites refused, and the headers and limits every response should carry.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Server-side sessions
docs.text:
Starlette's SessionMiddleware keeps the whole session in a signed cookie: the client can read it (it's only base64), it can't be revoked (a copied cookie keeps working after logout, until it expires) and it can't hold much more than 4 KB. ServerSessionMiddleware keeps the data in the cache's backend instead, and the cookie only carries a random id; request.session works the same:

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import ServerSessionMiddleware, clear_session, rotate_session

app.add_middleware(ServerSessionMiddleware, max_age=8 * 3600, idle_timeout=1800)


@app.post("/login")
async def login(request: Request, form: Annotated[Login, Form()]) -> RedirectResponse:
    user = await authenticate(form)
    request.session["user_id"] = user.id
    rotate_session(request)  # a new id: one planted in the browser before is now worthless
    return RedirectResponse("/", status_code=303)


@app.post("/logout")
async def logout(request: Request) -> RedirectResponse:
    clear_session(request)  # deleted from the backend: a copied cookie is worth nothing now
    return RedirectResponse("/", status_code=303)
  • The cookie holds 256 random bits (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)), HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax by default, with Max-Age = max_age, named __Host-session so that a sibling subdomain can't plant one (cookie tossing). Plain HTTP in development needs secure=False and another cookie_name.
  • The backend keeps the data under a SHA-256 digest of the id (whoever reads the keys can't use them as cookies), sealed with the cache's signing_key or encryption_key (use the latter when sessions hold personal data). Without either, whoever can write to the backend can forge a session, and a warning is logged. With a TieredBackend only the shared tier is used, so a logout is seen by every process at once.
  • Saved only when it changed, nested changes included (request.session["cart"].append(...)), when the response starts. Empty sessions aren't stored and get no cookie; a session the app empties is deleted and its cookie expired. Responses that read it get Vary: Cookie, and those that set the cookie Cache-Control: no-store unless they set their own.
  • New ids are always the server's: a cookie whose session doesn't exist (expired, made up) never becomes the id of a new session. rotate_session gives a new id with the same data (and a fresh max_age) at login, against session fixation; clear_session deletes the session and expires the cookie at logout, and data stored afterwards goes to a new session.
  • Expiry: max_age seconds after creation or rotation, and idle_timeout seconds without requests (refreshed in the backend at most every tenth of it, not on every request). Both are checked when the session is read, and the backend drops it then as well.
  • JSON only, up to max_size bytes (16 KiB): more, or a value that isn't JSON, raises when the response starts.
  • Backend failures: if the session can't be read, the request goes on with an empty one (anonymous, which fails closed) and a warning. Changing it then, or failing to save, rotate or clear it, replaces the response with a 503 and leaves the cookie alone: the response would claim a login or a logout that didn't happen. Concurrent requests of one session: the last save wins.
  • WebSockets get websocket.session too, read-only (rotate_session and clear_session raise there). A plain ASGI middleware: streaming responses still stream.

docs.title: Each user's sessions
docs.text:
Experimental

UserSessions is new in 0.6: its API may still change in any release.

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import ServerSessionMiddleware, UserSessions

user_sessions = UserSessions()  # the sessions whose data has "user_id", as SessionStrategy's
app.add_middleware(ServerSessionMiddleware, users=user_sessions)


@app.get("/devices")
async def devices(request: Request, user: CurrentUser) -> list[SessionInfo]:
    return await user_sessions.list(user.id, request=request)


@app.post("/password")
async def change_password(request: Request, form: NewPassword, user: CurrentUser) -> None:
    await db.users.set_password(user.id, form.password)
    await user_sessions.end_all(user.id, request=request, keep_current=True)
  • Listed: list(user_id) gives the user's live sessions, the newest first: when each started and was last seen, the browser's User-Agent and the client's address when it started (record_client=False for neither), and which is the request's (current). Its ref names it to end(user_id, ref), which only ends the user's own; it isn't the session's id, which only its cookie holds.
  • Ending all of them ("log out everywhere", a new password, a stolen phone): end_all(user_id) ends every session in the index, and refuses, from then on, every session of the user that started before, those the index missed too. keep_current=True keeps the request's, with a new id. It costs one more read for each request with a user.
  • Kept with the sessions: the middleware keeps an index of each user's sessions in the backend, sealed like them, when they start, rotate and end, holding a lock (where the backend has locks) so that two logins at once don't leave one out. At most max_sessions (50): a login past it ends the oldest.
  • When the backend fails to tell whether a session was ended, the session is refused: fail closed.
  • Logins at an OpenID Connect provider: a session whose data has oidc_sid (sid_key=), the provider's session id of the login, is ended by end_sid(sid): what the provider's back-channel logout calls.

docs.title: CSRF protection
docs.text:
A page on another site can make the user's browser send a form, or a fetch, to your app, and the browser adds the user's cookies by itself. CSRFMiddleware refuses those requests with a 403, from the headers browsers send to say where a request comes from:

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import CSRFMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CSRFMiddleware,
    trusted_origins=["https://admin.example.com"],  # other origins whose pages may post here
    exempt_paths=["/webhooks"],  # signed in their own way
)
  • Fetch metadata first: every current browser sends Sec-Fetch-Site. same-origin (and none, a request the user typed) goes through; same-site and cross-site are refused unless their Origin is in trusted_origins. Sibling subdomains are other origins too.
  • Older browsers: without Sec-Fetch-Site, the Origin header (or else the Referer) must be the app's own origin or a trusted one. Origin: null (sandboxed frames, redirects) is refused, and so is a request with neither header.
  • Only what the browser adds by itself is protected: requests without cookies or remembered HTTP authentication (Basic, Digest, Negotiate, NTLM) go through, so APIs that take a bearer token in a header keep working from anywhere (a page on another site can't set the header). Except form submissions from other sites (Sec-Fetch-Mode other than cors): before the user has a cookie they would log the browser into the attacker's account (login CSRF). check_all=True checks every request, for apps that trust TLS client certificates or the network.
  • Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) always go through: they mustn't change anything.
  • The app's own origin is the scheme and the Host header as the server sees them. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, let the server trust it (uvicorn --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy address>) and have the proxy pass Host on; otherwise every request looks cross-site, so list the public origin in trusted_origins.
  • Double-submit token for single-page apps, as defence in depth: with require_token=True every response to a request without a valid token sets a random one (256 bits) in the __Host-csrftoken cookie (readable by JavaScript, Secure, SameSite=Lax, the __Host- prefix keeps sibling subdomains from planting one), also in request.state.csrf_token. Requests with cookies must send it back in X-CSRF-Token; it's compared in constant time. A browser that sends neither Origin nor Referer passes with a valid token. HTML forms can't set headers, so with require_token=True every form that changes something must be sent by JavaScript (fetch with the header), the login form included; apps with plain HTML forms leave it off and rely on the origin checks, which protect them on their own.
  • WebSockets: browsers don't apply CORS to WebSocket handshakes, so any site could open one with the user's cookies and talk to it (cross-site WebSocket hijacking). Handshakes with cookies get the same checks and are closed with 1008 before they're accepted (the server answers 403); handshakes without Origin aren't from a browser and go through.
  • Refusals are logged at INFO with the method and the reason (never cookies or tokens), and counted in fastapi_alcazaba.csrf.refused. A plain ASGI middleware: streaming responses still stream.

docs.title: Security headers and body size
docs.text:
Two ASGI middlewares for what FastAPI leaves to the deployment:

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import BodySizeLimitMiddleware, SecurityHeadersMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    BodySizeLimitMiddleware,
    max_size=1_048_576,  # 1 MiB
    paths={"/uploads": 50 * 1_048_576, "/internal/stream": None},
)
app.add_middleware(SecurityHeadersMiddleware)  # last: the outermost
  • Security headers: the OWASP REST ones: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin; and a Permissions-Policy that turns off the camera, the microphone, geolocation, payments, USB, screen capture and the motion sensors, which no API response (nor the Swagger UI) needs. Headers the app sets itself are never overwritten; headers= adds others or changes the defaults (None removes one). Add it last, the outermost, so that the answers of the middlewares inside it (BodySizeLimitMiddleware's 400 and 413) get them too. Starlette's 500 for an unhandled exception never does: ServerErrorMiddleware wraps every middleware you add.
  • HSTS only on HTTPS requests: browsers ignore it over plain HTTP, and on a development localhost it would stick. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, let the server trust it (uvicorn --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy address>).
  • Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none' for everything that isn't HTML (nothing in a JSON response should load anything). HTML responses get html_csp, None by default, so that the Swagger UI and ReDoc, which load scripts from a CDN, keep working.
  • Body size: FastAPI has no limit of its own; a client could send an endless body that the app reads into memory. A Content-Length over the limit gets a 413 before the app runs, a malformed or ambiguous one a 400. Bodies without one (chunked) are counted while the app reads them and refused once they pass the limit, also when FastAPI parses them into a model. paths sets other limits by path prefix (the longest wins, None for no limit), matched like the routes, without the root_path.
  • Both are plain ASGI middlewares, not BaseHTTPMiddleware: streaming responses still stream, and WebSockets go through untouched.

docs.title: Response cache
docs.text:
@cache for endpoints and functions, and Cache behind it: what each entry is stored under, for how long, and how it's kept safe. The quick start sets one up.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: FastAPICache.init()
docs.text:
Call it once, at startup (in the lifespan).

Parameter Default Description backend InMemoryBackend, RedisBackend, ValkeyBackend, GlideBackend, MemcachedBackend or DynamoBackend prefix "" prefix of every key expire None default time to live, in seconds coder JsonCoder how values are stored key_builder default_key_builder builds keys from the function and its arguments cache_status "Alcazaba" this cache's name in the Cache-Status header (RFC 9211); None to leave it out enable True False turns the cache off signing_key None secret of 32+ bytes to sign entries; a list rotates keys (the first signs) encryption_key None secret of 32+ bytes to sign and encrypt entries (crypto extra); instead of signing_key compression None "zstd" or "zlib": store large entries compressed compression_min_size 1024 bytes; smaller entries aren't compressed compression_level codec's default vary_headers ("authorization", "cookie", "x-api-key") request headers that give each value its own entry. The header FastAPIAPIKeys or UnkeyStrategy read a key from counts too, whatever its name; add any other header the app reads credentials from itself respect_cache_control False let clients skip the cache with no-cache/no-store single_flight True concurrent misses for one key compute once, per process backend_timeout 1.0 seconds a backend call may take before the request goes on without cache circuit_breaker_failures 5 consecutive failures that stop the backend calls; None disables the breaker circuit_breaker_reset 30.0 seconds before trying the backend again max_value_size None bytes; larger values aren't stored distributed_lock False one process computes a missing value while the others wait for it lock_timeout 10.0 seconds before a lock expires (if its holder dies) lock_wait 5.0 seconds a process waits for another one's value before computing it early_refresh None fraction of the lifetime, at its end, in which hits may refresh the entry metrics True OpenTelemetry metrics, with the otel extra meter_provider global OpenTelemetry meter provider tracing True OpenTelemetry spans, with the otel extra tracer_provider global OpenTelemetry tracer provider

docs.title: @cache()
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description expire from init time to live, in seconds coder from init key_builder from init namespace "" group of entries, for FastAPICache.clear(namespace=...) injected_dependency_namespace "__fastapi_alcazaba" prefix of the Request/Response parameters added to the endpoint exclude_params None arguments left out of the key (a nonce, a database session…) vary_headers from init () for responses that are the same for everybody respect_cache_control from init stale_while_revalidate None seconds past expire an entry is served at once and refreshed in the background (see below); also that Cache-Control directive stale_if_error None seconds past expire an entry is served when computing a new one fails refresh_timeout None seconds computing may take while stale_if_error can serve: past them, the stale entry cache_control None the Cache-Control directives to send (see below) single_flight from init max_value_size from init distributed_lock from init early_refresh from init tags None names to invalidate the entry by: a list, or a function of the arguments

Only 200 responses are stored, and never one that says no-store, sets a cookie (its hits would hand that cookie, a session, to everyone else), streams or sends a file.

docs.title: What a hit returns
docs.text:
The response the endpoint gave, whatever its type and whatever the coder:

  • A Response it returned (JSON, HTML, CSV, an image…) comes back with its status, its headers and its body, byte for byte. Its background tasks run when the endpoint does, not on hits.
  • A value, with the headers the endpoint set on the injected response (response.headers["X-Total-Count"] = "2"). Those its dependencies set first, before the endpoint ran (a remaining quota, a request ID), belong to each request: they're never stored.
  • With a response model, only what the model has is stored: a field the endpoint returns and the model leaves out (a password hash) never reaches the backend. The route's response_model_include, exclude and exclude_none apply to each response, hit or miss.

Set-Cookie, the connection's own headers (Connection, Transfer-Encoding…) and the cache's own (ETag, Cache-Status) are never stored, whoever writes the entry.

docs.title: Cache-Control
docs.text:
What each response is sent with, miss or hit:

  1. cache_control="public, s-maxage=600" on @cache: those directives, with max-age the time the entry has left, unless they give one (stale-while-revalidate too, if set).
  2. Else the endpoint's own Cache-Control, as it set it.
  3. Else max-age, the time the entry has left (and stale-while-revalidate).

An entry of one user (a request with Authorization, Cookie or X-API-Key, see vary_headers) is private whatever these say. A 304 repeats the response's Cache-Control, Expires, Vary and Content-Location. no-store isn't a directive to configure: set on the response, it keeps it out of the cache.

@app.get("/logo.png")
@cache(expire=86_400, cache_control="public, immutable")
async def logo() -> Response:
    return Response(LOGO, media_type="image/png")

Delete entries with await FastAPICache.clear(namespace="products"), one entry with await FastAPICache.clear(key=...), or by tag with await FastAPICache.invalidate_tags(...). clear() without arguments deletes every cached response under the prefix. memcached and DynamoDB can't list their keys: there, a clear or an invalidation hides the entries instead (they expire in their own time) and returns 0, since it can't count them. Locks, rate-limit counters, revoked tokens, one-time codes and idempotency records are kept apart, under {prefix}! instead of {prefix}:, so no clear() frees a held lock, resets a limit or takes a revocation back; InMemoryBackend keeps them apart too, so caching many responses never evicts them.

docs.title: Serving stale entries
docs.text:
When a fresh value is slow or can't be had, an expired one is often better than waiting or an error:

@app.get("/prices")
@cache(expire=60, stale_while_revalidate=300, stale_if_error=3600, refresh_timeout=2)
async def prices(db: Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(session)]) -> list[Price]: ...
  • stale-while-revalidate: up to 300 seconds after it expires, the entry is served at once (Cache-Status: Alcazaba; hit; ttl=-12; detail=stale-while-revalidate), and the endpoint runs again after the response, to store a fresh one. One process does it (a lock in the backend, tried once), once (the other requests meanwhile get the stale entry too). In an endpoint, the refresh is a background task of the response: it runs once the response is sent, before the request's dependencies are closed, so the database session above is still open. A refresh that fails is logged; the next request tries again.
  • stale-if-error: up to an hour after it expires, a request computes a fresh value as on a miss, but when the endpoint raises, or takes longer than refresh_timeout (it's cancelled then), the expired entry is served instead (Cache-Status: Alcazaba; hit; ttl=-1800; detail=stale-if-error). Past the window, the error goes through.
  • How: entries are stored for expire plus the longest of both windows, and a read tells a fresh entry from a stale one by the time it has left. Signed, encrypted and compressed entries, tags, invalidation, single flight and the distributed lock work as for any entry: an invalidated entry isn't served stale.
  • Counted in fastapi_alcazaba.lookups as stale and stale_if_error. Stale responses get no max-age: browsers and CDNs don't keep them as fresh.
  • Without an expire (entries that never expire), nothing is ever stale.

docs.title: Several caches, dependency injection and get_or_set
docs.text:
FastAPICache is one global cache. For one cache per app, or several with different settings, create Cache instances (same arguments as FastAPICache.init()) and decorate with their cached():

from fastapi_alcazaba import Cache, get_cache

public_cache = Cache(RedisBackend(redis), prefix="public", vary_headers=())
private_cache = Cache(
    RedisBackend(redis), prefix="private", encryption_key=settings.cache_encryption_key
)
private_cache.install(app)  # what get_cache returns


@app.get("/catalog")
@public_cache.cached(expire=600)
async def catalog() -> list[Product]: ...


@app.get("/me/orders")
async def orders(
    user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)], cache: Annotated[Cache, Depends(get_cache)]
) -> list[Order]:
    # Anything worth caching that doesn't fit a decorator; the key is hashed before storing.
    return await cache.get_or_set(f"orders:{user.id}", lambda: load_orders(user.id), expire=60)

get_or_set goes through the same pipeline as the decorator (signing or encryption, compression, single flight, locks, tags). Close the backend at shutdown with await cache.close().

docs.title: Invalidating by tag
docs.text:
Tag entries when they're cached and delete them all when the data changes, without knowing their keys:

@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
@cache(expire=600, tags=lambda product_id, **_: [f"product:{product_id}", "catalog"])
async def product(product_id: int) -> Product: ...


@app.put("/products/{product_id}")
async def update_product(product_id: int, data: Product) -> Product:
    saved = save(product_id, data)
    await FastAPICache.invalidate_tags(f"product:{product_id}")
    return saved

The function receives the same arguments as the endpoint. Tags work with the in-memory, Redis, Valkey and GLIDE backends; in Redis-like servers each tag is a set that lives as long as its longest-lived entry.

docs.title: Responses in several languages
docs.text: If an endpoint translates its response according to a request header, such as Accept-Language, add that header to vary_headers (@cache(vary_headers=["accept-language"])), or a user would get the cached response in another user's language.

docs.title: Encrypted entries
docs.text:
FastAPICache.init(
    RedisBackend(redis),
    prefix="myapp",
    encryption_key=settings.cache_encryption_key,  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
)

Each entry is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived (HKDF-SHA256) from the secret and a random salt, with the cache key as associated data: an entry only decrypts under its own key, and any change to it is detected. A list of secrets rotates them: the first encrypts, all of them decrypt. Encryption also authenticates the entries, so it replaces signing_key rather than adding to it. It costs a few microseconds per entry.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
FastAPICache.init(RedisBackend(redis), compression="zstd")  # or "zlib", no dependencies

Entries of at least compression_min_size bytes (1 KiB) are compressed when that makes them smaller; JSON lists shrink about 10-15 times with zstd, which means less memory in Redis/Valkey and less network. zstd is in the standard library from Python 3.14 (zstd extra before). Compressed entries are recognised when they're read whatever the setting, so it can be turned on or off at any time; decompression is bounded by max_value_size (64 MiB if unset), so a compressed bomb planted in the backend is rejected.

Compression happens before signing or encryption. With encryption, the size of an entry still says how compressible it was: if an attacker can both read the backend and put chosen text into a response next to a secret, that can leak information about the secret (the CRIME/BREACH family). Leave compression off for such responses.

docs.title: Coders
docs.text:
JsonCoder (the default) stores anything FastAPI can turn into JSON, through pydantic-core (Rust) when it can: about 8 times faster than jsonable_encoder() for a list of models. Annotate the return type and cache hits come back as that type (Pydantic models, dataclasses, lists of models…), validated straight from the stored bytes:

@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=60)
async def products() -> list[Product]: ...

PickleCoder stores any picklable object. Unpickling runs code chosen by whoever wrote the bytes: it needs a signing_key or an encryption_key, and without one FastAPICache.init (or the first call of an endpoint that asks for it) raises UnsignedEntriesError.

A custom coder subclasses fastapi_alcazaba.Coder:

import orjson
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder

from fastapi_alcazaba import Coder


class ORJsonCoder(Coder):
    @classmethod
    def encode(cls, value: Any) -> bytes:
        return orjson.dumps(value, default=jsonable_encoder)

    @classmethod
    def decode(cls, value: bytes) -> Any:
        return orjson.loads(value)

docs.title: Key builders
docs.text:
