The default key is the SHA-256 of the function's module and qualified name and the repr() of its arguments, under <prefix>:<namespace>:. Arguments whose repr() changes on every call (a database session or a service injected with Depends, whose repr() shows a memory address) make every call a miss: Alcazaba warns about them (UnstableCacheKeyWarning) on the first call. Leave them out with exclude_params:

@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=30, exclude_params=["session"])
def products(session: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)], page: int = 1) -> list[Product]: ...

A custom key builder receives the function, the namespace and the request:

from typing import Any

from starlette.requests import Request
from starlette.responses import Response


def request_key_builder(
    func: Any,
    namespace: str = "",
    *,
    request: Request | None = None,
    response: Response | None = None,
    args: tuple[Any, ...],
    kwargs: dict[str, Any],
) -> str:
    assert request is not None
    return ":".join(
        [
            namespace,
            request.method.lower(),
            request.url.path,
            repr(sorted(request.query_params.items())),
        ]
    )


@app.get("/")
@cache(expire=60, key_builder=request_key_builder)
async def index() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"hello": "world"}

Whatever the key builder, Alcazaba appends a digest of the vary_headers.

docs.title: Idempotency keys
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

A client that retries a POST after a timeout or a dropped connection gets the first response again, instead of creating a second order or paying twice (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header):

from fastapi_alcazaba.idempotency import IdempotencyMiddleware, require_idempotency_key

app.add_middleware(IdempotencyMiddleware)  # the app's cache (Cache.install) or FastAPICache's


@app.post("/payments", status_code=201, dependencies=[Depends(require_idempotency_key)])
async def pay(payment: Payment) -> Receipt: ...

The client sends a fresh key with each new request, and the same one when it retries it: Idempotency-Key: "8e03978e-40d5-43e8-bc93-6894a57f9324".

  • Retries get the first response (status, headers and body, but no Set-Cookie) with Idempotent-Replayed: true; the endpoint runs once.
  • One at a time: a retry that arrives while the first request still runs gets a 409 with Retry-After: 1. A lock in the backend, renewed while the request runs, sees to it across processes.
  • The same key for another request (method, path, query or body) gets a 422. The body is compared byte for byte: a retry sends the same bytes, not the same JSON written another way (keys in another order, other spacing).
  • Per client: keys are looked up among the requests with the same credentials (hashed): the Authorization header, or the cookies when there's none (a cookie session), so one user never gets another's response, nor someone without the victim's cookie who learned their key. With access tokens that get refreshed, or cookies that change between a request and its retry (either way the retry would run again), pass identifier= returning the user's id. Requests without credentials share one space of keys, safe as long as clients make their keys random (UUIDs).
  • Replays come before authentication: the route's dependencies don't run for a retry, so a copy of the request (token, key and body, from a log) gets the response again until it expires, even once the token is revoked. An async identifier= that checks the credentials, returning the user's id or raising a 401, closes that; a shorter expire narrows it.
  • What's kept, and for how long: responses below 500 for expire seconds (24 hours), except those worth retrying (408, 409, 425, 429) and those about the request itself, given before the endpoint did anything (401, 403, 404, 405, 413, 415, 422 and the like): a retry gets them afresh, and nobody can fill the backend with them (FastAPI's 422 echoes the request body). Request bodies are read whole to fingerprint them, up to max_body_size (a 413 beyond); a client that goes away before sending all of it doesn't reach the endpoint. Responses above max_response_size aren't kept, so a retry runs again. The stored responses go through the cache's signing or encryption: use an encryption_key when they carry personal data.
  • Failures: if the backend fails the request gets a 503: running a payment twice is worse than refusing it. fail_open=True runs it without idempotency instead. Errors of the endpoint itself, BackendUnavailable included, are left to the app.
  • Requests without the header go through untouched. It applies to POST and PATCH (methods=), and needs a backend with locks.

docs.title: Rate and concurrency limits
docs.text:
How many requests a client may make in a window, and how many may run at the same time, across every process.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
FastAPIRateLimiter is a FastAPI dependency that lets each client make times requests per window to a route; the next ones get a 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After. Its counters live in the cache's backend, so every process and container shares them:

from functools import partial

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from starlette.requests import HTTPConnection

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import FastAPIRateLimiter


@app.get("/search", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=10, minutes=1))])
async def search(q: str) -> list[Product]: ...


def user_id(connection: HTTPConnection) -> str:  # a Request, or a WebSocket
    return connection.state.user_id  # set by your authentication middleware


# 1000 requests per hour and user, for all the routes of the router together.
api = APIRouter(
    dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(1000, hours=1, name="api", identifier=user_id))]
)

# One budget across routes, of which each export takes 50.
partner_budget = partial(FastAPIRateLimiter, 1000, hours=1, name="partners", identifier=user_id)
partners = APIRouter()
partners.get("/orders", dependencies=[Depends(partner_budget())])(list_orders)
partners.get("/export", dependencies=[Depends(partner_budget(cost=50))])(export_orders)
  • Who: by default, the client's address as the ASGI server reports it (client_ip), IPv6 addresses by their /64 network: each customer gets at least a whole /64, and one budget per address would give a client 2⁶⁴ of them. Many ISPs delegate a /56 or a /48, and tunnel brokers hand out /48s for free: client_network(24, 48) groups wider networks. Behind a proxy, let the server take the address from the proxy's headers: uvicorn reads them, but only from the addresses in --forwarded-allow-ips (127.0.0.1 by default), so give it your proxy's. The limiter never reads X-Forwarded-For itself, which any client can set. identifier= counts per user, API key… Identities are hashed before they reach the backend.
  • Where: each route has its own budget, whatever its path parameters (those of a Mount too): /items/1 and /items/2 share one, and so does an endpoint mounted twice. Limiters with the same name and rate share one budget across routes, and cost= makes a route take more of it.
  • How: a sliding window. The count of the previous window is added in proportion to how much of it is still less than a window ago, so nobody doubles the limit around the boundary between two windows. Requests over the limit don't count: checking and counting is one atomic operation (a Lua script on Redis, Valkey and GLIDE, a conditional write on DynamoDB). A client with nothing left is then refused by each process without asking the backend, until something fits again: a flood doesn't reach the backend. limiter.forget() drops that memory (between tests; a new cache drops it too). Windows follow the clocks of the app's servers: keep them in sync (NTP).
  • What clients see: responses carry the RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers of the IETF draft: RateLimit: "api";r=998;t=3540 means 998 requests left, at least for the next 3540 seconds. Clients can slow down before they get a 429. headers=False leaves them out. An endpoint that returns a Response object itself gets none: FastAPI only adds the headers that dependencies set to the responses it builds from a return value. Nor do the errors it builds from an exception (a 422, an HTTPException raised after the limiter), unless FastAPIProblemDetails is installed: it adds them back. An invalid request counts too: FastAPI runs the dependencies before it answers 422.
  • Which backend: the cache= given, else the app's (Cache.install) or FastAPICache's. Every backend can keep counters; TieredBackend keeps them only in its shared backend, and FastAPICache.clear() never resets them. They go through the cache's timeout and circuit breaker: if the backend fails, requests go through (fail_open=False answers 503 instead).
  • What happens over the limit: callback(request, seconds_to_wait), by default too_many_requests (the 429). If the callback returns, the request goes on.

On a WebSocket route, the dependency limits connections (closing with 1008). Call await limiter.hit(connection, key=..., cost=...) yourself to limit anything else: it counts and returns None within the limit, else the seconds to wait. For example, the messages of a WebSocket, or the login attempts to an account:

import unicodedata

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import FastAPIRateLimiter, too_many_requests

login_attempts = FastAPIRateLimiter(times=5, minutes=15, identifier=lambda _: "")
login_attempts_per_client = FastAPIRateLimiter(times=20, minutes=15)  # per IP


@app.post("/login", dependencies=[Depends(login_attempts_per_client)])
async def login(request: Request, form: Annotated[LoginForm, Form()]) -> Token:
    # Five attempts per account every 15 minutes, wherever they come from. The key is the
    # account as the app finds it, or "Alice@x.com", "alice@x.com " and the like would each get
    # five more.
    account = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", form.username).strip().casefold()
    if (wait := await login_attempts.hit(request, key=account)) is not None:
        too_many_requests(request, wait)
    user = await check_password(account, form.password)
    if user is None:
        raise HTTPException(401, "Wrong username or password")
    # The right password: the failed attempts before it don't count against the next login.
    await login_attempts.reset(request, key=account)
    ...

Normalise the key exactly as the login looks the account up. A limit per account also lets anyone lock that account out for the window with five wrong passwords: pair it with the limit per IP, and keep the window short.

docs.title: Adjusting limits at run time
docs.text:
PLANS = {"free": 100, "pro": 5_000}


async def requests_per_hour(request: Request) -> int:
    return PLANS[(await current_account(request)).plan]


api = FastAPIRateLimiter(
    times=requests_per_hour,  # each request's client gets its plan's limit
    hours=1,
    identifier=api_key_id,
    exempt={"monitoring"},  # or a predicate of the request
    name="api",
)

status = await api.status(request)  # RateLimitStatus(limit=5000, remaining=4210, reset=1800)
await api.reset(identity="key_123", cache=app_cache)  # from an admin page, without its request
  • Limits per request: times may be a function of the request (sync or async), e.g. by plan or API key tier. The RateLimit headers carry each request's limit (q=); a client whose plan changes keeps what it spent in the window. Without a name, the policy is per-<window>.
  • Exemptions: exempt takes identities (what identifier returns) or a predicate. Their requests aren't counted and get no headers; each is counted as exempt in fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit, and logged (INFO) the first time a process sees the identity.
  • Reading a budget: status(request) gives the limit, what fits now and for how long no more is sure to, without spending any (an account page, a GET /quota).
  • Resetting: reset(request, key=...) forgets what a client spent, in the backend, for every process. Other processes that refuse it without asking the backend (it had nothing left) do so until its budget would have refilled.
  • Without the request: status and reset take identity= (and cache=) when the limiter has a name; without one, its budget is the route's, which only a request names.

docs.title: Concurrency limits
docs.text:
FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter limits how many requests run at the same time, across every process and container, for endpoints whose cost is how long they run (AI, OCR, PDF rendering). The rate limiter counts requests per window; this counts the ones in flight:

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter
from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import client_ip

ocr = FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter(4, name="ocr", wait=2)  # FastAPICache's backend, or cache=...


@app.post("/invoices/scan", dependencies=[Depends(ocr)])
async def scan(file: UploadFile) -> Invoice: ...


@app.post("/summaries", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter(1, identifier=client_ip))])
async def summarise(text: str) -> Summary: ...  # one at a time per client


async def scan_pending() -> None:  # outside requests: a job, a queue consumer
    async with ocr.slot():
        ...
  • Slots in the backend: limit locks (up to 100), tried in random order so that the processes don't all queue on the first; a request holds one while it runs, renewed every ttl / 3 seconds, and the slots of a process that dies expire after ttl (60). Keys are SHA-256 digests: client identities never reach the backend in clear.
  • When it's full: a request waits up to wait seconds (0: tries once), polling with jittered backoff, then gets a 503 with Retry-After (retry_after, 1 s by default); a 429 when the limit is per client (identifier). There's no queue and no order among the waiters. WebSockets are closed with 1013 (1008 per client) and hold their slot while connected.
  • Sharing: by default each route (methods and path template) has its own slots; limiters with the same name and limit share them. slot(key=...) gives each key its own slots outside requests (it needs a name), and slot(connection=request) takes one around just the expensive part of an endpoint.
  • Streaming: the slot is released when FastAPI runs the dependency's exit code. Since FastAPI 0.118 that's after the response is sent, so a StreamingResponse keeps its slot until its last byte; Depends(limiter, scope="function") (FastAPI 0.121) releases it when the endpoint returns, before the body. FastAPI 0.115 to 0.117 release it before the response is sent: take a slot() inside the stream there.
  • Failures: if the backend fails, each process counts the slots on its own (fail_open=True, the default: at most limit per process run); fail_open=False refuses with a 503 instead (slot() raises BackendUnavailable).
  • Limits: like any lock on a cache-like store, a holder that stalls for longer than ttl loses its slot while it still runs, and someone else may take it. Taking a slot when most are busy costs a round trip per busy slot tried.

docs.title: E-mail
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.7: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

The messages an app sends by itself: a password reset, a sign-in code, a receipt with its invoice. FastAPIMail builds them so that nothing in them can add a header or a recipient, attachments included, and SMTPSender sends them over SMTP, which every provider speaks (Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, your own server), always encrypted. Nothing to install. SESSender sends them through Amazon SES's API instead.

Every class and function: the API reference.

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIMail
from fastapi_alcazaba.mail import SMTPSender

mail = FastAPIMail(
    SMTPSender(
        "email-smtp.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com",
        username=settings.smtp_user,
        password=settings.smtp_password,  # a SecretStr
    ),
    from_address="Example <no-reply@example.com>",
)

message_id = await mail.send(
    user.email,
    "Reset your password",
    f"Open {link} within an hour.",
    html=f'<p>Open <a href="{link}">this link</a> within an hour.</p>',
)

docs.title: The messages
docs.text:
• One address per recipient, name <user@domain> or user@domain, 50 at most: a string with a comma, a line break or two @ is refused, so a form field can't add recipients.
  • Headers that can't be forged: the subject is one line; headers= adds others (List-Unsubscribe...) but never From, To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, Date, Message-ID, Reply-To nor Sender, and nothing with a line break.
  • What FastAPIMail adds: Date, a Message-ID on the sender's domain (send returns it), Reply-To when given, and Auto-Submitted: auto-generated (RFC 3834), so that out-of-office replies don't answer it.
  • Text, and HTML as its alternative: mail clients show the one they can. Escape what goes into the HTML as you would in a page.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
from fastapi_alcazaba.mail import Attachment

await mail.send(
    user.email,
    "Your invoice",
    "Your invoice for October is attached.",
    attachments=[Attachment(pdf, f"Invoice {invoice.number}.pdf")],
)
  • The name the recipient sees goes through safe_filename: without a path, line breaks nor control characters (no header can come in through it), nor the right-to-left override that disguises an .exe; "attachment" when nothing is left. Names with accents or in other alphabets are encoded as RFC 2231 says.
  • The content type is type/subtype without parameters (application/pdf, text/csv); guessed from the name when not given, application/octet-stream when the name doesn't tell. multipart/* and message/* are refused: they'd change the message's structure.
  • Limits: 10 attachments a message (MAX_ATTACHMENTS), and 10 MiB of them together (FastAPIMail(max_attachments_size=...)), counted before base64, which adds a third: the providers count after it (SES up to 40 MB, most others 10 to 25 MB). Over the limits, or with a content that isn't bytes, message and send raise before anything is sent.
  • After the text and the HTML, in a multipart/mixed. Images inside the HTML (cid:) are out of scope: link them.

docs.title: Sending
docs.text:
• Encrypted: STARTTLS on port 587 by default, or tls="implicit" on port 465, with the server's certificate checked against the system's authorities (ssl_context for one of your own). Plain SMTP, tls="none", is only for localhost: a development server such as Mailpit.
  • A connection per message, with timeout seconds for each step, in threads of the sender's own: smtplib blocks, and Starlette's threadpool (40 threads) is the one the app's sync endpoints and dependencies share, so a slow server would hold them. connections messages go at once (4 by default); the others wait for a thread. await sender.aclose() at shutdown lets them go.
  • When it isn't sent (the server refuses every recipient, doesn't answer, the TLS or the login fails), send raises MailNotSent and logs who it was for, never the body: it holds the links and codes that open doors. When the server takes some recipients and refuses others, the message is sent: the refused ones are logged, and nothing is raised, so a retry doesn't send it to the others twice. Send from a task, which tries again:
@queue.task(retries=5)
async def send_reset(email: str, link: str) -> None:
    await mail.send(email, "Reset your password", f"Open {link} within an hour.")
  • The metric fastapi_alcazaba.mail counts the messages by outcome: sent or failed.

docs.title: Through a provider's API
docs.text:
SESSender sends through Amazon SES's API (SESv2 SendEmail) instead of SMTP, with aiobotocore (pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[ses]"):

from fastapi_alcazaba.mail import SESSender

sender = SESSender("eu-west-1", configuration_set="transactional")
mail = FastAPIMail(sender, from_address="Example <no-reply@example.com>")


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    await sender.connect()
    yield
    await sender.aclose()
  • The message goes whole, as FastAPIMail built it (Content.Raw): its headers, its alternatives and its attachments, the same as over SMTP.
  • The credentials come from AWS's chain: the task's role on ECS or Lambda, the instance's, the environment, a profile. No SMTP user to create and rotate, nor a port 587 to open from the app's network. Give the role ses:SendEmail and ses:SendRawEmail on the From's identity: AWS's guide doesn't say which of them a raw message checks.
  • When SES refuses it (an identity not verified, the account paused, too many messages) or can't be reached, send raises MailNotSent with SES's error code and message. SES sends to all the recipients or none.
  • One client, opened on the first message or by connect() and closed by aclose(); endpoint_url= and the rest of create_client's options go through (a VPC endpoint, an emulator).
  • Another provider: a sender is any class with async def send(self, message: EmailMessage) that raises MailNotSent when the message isn't sent (MailSender). message.as_bytes() is the raw message, for APIs that take it (Mailgun's messages.mime); for those that take fields, message.get_body(("plain",)), get_body(("html",)) and iter_attachments() give them.

docs.title: In tests
docs.text:
MemoryMailSender sends nothing, and keeps the messages, attachments included (message.iter_attachments()):

sender = MemoryMailSender()
mail = FastAPIMail(sender, from_address="no-reply@example.com")
...
(message,) = sender.messages
assert "reset?token=" in message.get_body(("plain",)).get_content()

docs.title: Errors and observability
docs.text:
Errors that say what went wrong without leaking internals, and what tells you how the app is doing: request IDs, deadlines, health checks, metrics and traces, and logs as JSON.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Problem details
docs.text:
FastAPIProblemDetails answers errors with RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) instead of FastAPI's {"detail": ...}, and without telling clients what they shouldn't know:

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import FastAPIProblemDetails, Problem

problems = FastAPIProblemDetails()
problems.install(app)


@app.post("/orders")
async def order(item: Item) -> Order:
    if stock[item.id] < item.quantity:
        raise Problem(
            409,
            f"Only {stock[item.id]} left",
            type="https://example.com/problems/out-of-stock",
            title="Out of stock",
            extensions={"available": stock[item.id]},
        )
    ...

{"type": "https://example.com/problems/out-of-stock", "title": "Out of stock", "status": 409,
 "detail": "Only 3 left", "instance": "/orders", "available": 3, "request_id": "4bf92f35…"}
  • Members: type (about:blank unless a Problem says otherwise), title (the RFC 9110 status phrase), status, detail when there's something to tell, instance (the request's path, percent-encoded) and request_id when RequestIDMiddleware gave the request one.
  • HTTPExceptions: FastAPI's, Starlette's and their subclasses (BreakerOpen, the rate limiter's 429…) keep their headers: Retry-After, WWW-Authenticate, Allow. A 4xx's detail is sent, since it's written for clients (expose_detail=False keeps it); a 5xx's never is: an HTTPException(500, str(error)) becomes a bare 500, and the hidden detail is logged as a warning. A detail that isn't a string goes in an errors member. Codes under 400 (a redirect raised as an exception) keep FastAPI's answer.
  • Validation errors: a 422 whose errors list each error's loc, msg and type, never its input (FastAPI echoes what was sent, passwords included) nor its ctx. At most max_errors=100, so that a huge invalid body doesn't get a huge answer.
  • Unhandled exceptions: a 500 that says nothing about them. Starlette raises the exception again after the response, so the server logs it with its traceback (uvicorn's "Exception in ASGI application", with the request ID when you use RequestIDLogFilter) and TestClient raises it in tests; it isn't logged a second time. With debug=True Starlette shows its traceback page instead.
  • Problem: an HTTPException with a type URI, a title and extension members, whose names are checked (three or more letters, digits or _, starting with a letter; never a standard member) and whose values are encoded when it's raised. Its detail is always sent, also with a 5xx: you wrote it for the client. problems.response(request, Problem(...)) answers one from your own exception handlers.
  • Alcazaba's middlewares too: what they answer themselves (the 504 of a timeout, the 413 of a body too large, the 503 of maintenance, the 403 of CSRF, the idempotency errors) is a problem as well, headers such as Retry-After kept, once it's installed on the app.
  • Handlers you register for a status code or an exception subclass still win; install it before the app starts.

docs.title: Request IDs
docs.text:
RequestIDMiddleware gives every request an ID, to find all the log lines of one request and to let a client quote it when it reports an error:

import logging

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import RequestIDLogFilter, RequestIDMiddleware, request_id

app.add_middleware(RequestIDMiddleware)  # last: the outermost

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.addFilter(RequestIDLogFilter())
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s [%(request_id)s] %(name)s: %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger().addHandler(handler)


@app.post("/jobs")
async def create_job() -> dict[str, str | None]:
    return {"ticket": request_id()}

With uvicorn, add the filter to its handlers too ("filters": {"request_id": {"()": "fastapi_alcazaba.observability.RequestIDLogFilter"}} in its log_config), and its access and error lines carry the ID.

  • Incoming IDs: the request's X-Request-ID (header= for another) is reused when a proxy or the client set one that's safe to log: a single value matching [A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,128}. Anything else (line breaks that would forge log lines, an endless value, several values) gets a new random one, 128 bits in hex. trust_incoming=False always makes a new one.
  • Everywhere in the request: request_id() returns it in endpoints, dependencies, sync endpoints' threads and WebSockets; None outside a request. The response carries it in the same header (unless the app set that header itself), and so do WebSocket handshakes.
  • In errors: after an unhandled exception the ID stays set for the rest of the request's task, so Starlette's 500 handler and the server's error log, which run outside every middleware, still know which request failed. FastAPIProblemDetails puts it in every problem, 500s included, and in their header.
  • In logs: RequestIDLogFilter sets record.request_id (default="-" outside a request; a request_id passed in extra= is kept). Add it to handlers: a logger's filters don't see the records of its child loggers.
  • Add it last, the outermost, so that the answers of the other middlewares (a 413, a 504) carry the ID too.

docs.title: Request timeouts
docs.text:
RequestTimeoutMiddleware gives every request a deadline, so that a hung dependency or a client that trickles its body doesn't hold a request (and its database connection, its memory…) forever:

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import RequestTimeoutMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    RequestTimeoutMiddleware,
    timeout=30,
    paths={"/reports": 120, "/events": None},  # Server-Sent Events: no deadline
)
  • Before the response starts: at the deadline the app is cancelled, its finally blocks and the exit of its yield dependencies run, and the client gets a 504 ({"detail": "Request timed out"}, or a problem with FastAPIProblemDetails). Reading the request body counts: a client that sends it a byte at a time runs out of time too.
  • While a response streams: it's too late for a 504. The app is cancelled all the same and the TimeoutError raised again, so the server closes the connection: the client sees an incomplete body (an unfinished chunked read), never a short one that looks complete. Give streaming endpoints their own deadline in paths, or None.
  • After the response: once its last byte is sent the deadline is off, so background tasks run as long as they need.
  • Sync endpoints run in a thread that can't be interrupted: the client gets its 504 on time, but the thread runs to its end, after the exit of its yield dependencies has run. Endpoints that may hit the deadline are better async.
  • Paths: paths sets other deadlines by path prefix (the longest wins, None for none), matched like the routes, without the root_path; timeout=None leaves the other paths without one. The app's own TimeoutErrors go through untouched, and WebSockets and lifespan events too.
  • Both cases are logged as warnings with the method and the route template. A plain ASGI middleware: streaming responses still stream.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
health_router() adds the two endpoints that load balancers and orchestrators probe:

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import HealthCheck, health_router


async def database() -> None:
    async with engine.connect() as connection:
        await connection.execute(text("SELECT 1"))


app.include_router(
    health_router({"database": database, "search": HealthCheck(ping_search, critical=False)})
)

Point the liveness probe at /health/live and the readiness probe (or the load balancer's health check, e.g. the target group of an ECS service) at /health/ready.

  • Live vs ready: /health/live only says that the process answers. /health/ready runs the checks concurrently, each with a timeout (timeout=2.0, or the check's own), and answers 200 (ok, or degraded when only non-critical checks fail) or 503 (fail) with each check's status and duration. Keep dependencies out of liveness: a probe that checks the database gets healthy containers restarted every time it blips. A check passes when it returns anything but False without raising. Sync checks run in a daemon thread of their own, off the event loop, so one that hangs holds up neither the shutdown nor the threads of the loop's default executor; it isn't started again, under the same name in the same router, until its thread finishes.
  • The cache is checked, but isn't critical: the cache's backend (cache=, else the app's or FastAPICache's) is asked for a key under its prefix, straight, not through the circuit breaker. The cache fails open, so its outage makes the app degraded, not unready: taking every instance out of the load balancer would turn a Redis outage into a full one. include_cache=False leaves it out.
  • No leaked errors: failures are logged with their traceback and never returned: a public probe mustn't tell the world the database's hostname or connection string.
  • Probes don't pile up: concurrent /ready requests share one run of the checks, and its result answers the next ones for reuse_for=1.0 seconds, so a flood of probes doesn't flood the database. A probe that goes away doesn't cancel the run the others are waiting for.
  • The endpoints are left out of the OpenAPI schema unless include_in_schema=True; responses carry Cache-Control: no-store.

docs.title: Checks of Alcazaba's components
docs.text:
Ready-made checks for what Alcazaba runs, to add to the router. Each is a HealthCheck that isn't critical by default (a backlog or a mail server that's down make the app degraded, not unready); critical=True and timeout= change that.

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import (
    broadcast_check,
    health_router,
    leader_check,
    object_storage_check,
    smtp_check,
    task_queue_check,
)

app.include_router(
    health_router(
        {
            "database": database,
            "tasks": task_queue_check(queue, max_backlog=10_000, max_dead_letters=0),
            "broadcast": broadcast_check(broadcast),
            "outbox_leader": leader_check(leader),
            "smtp": smtp_check(smtp_sender),
            "storage": object_storage_check(presigner, "health/probe"),
        },
        reuse_for=10,  # the SMTP and storage checks open a connection each time
    )
)
  • task_queue_check: the queue's backend answers, the tasks that haven't finished are at most max_backlog, and the dead letters at most max_dead_letters (0: any fails).
  • broadcast_check: Redis answers a PING, and the subscription isn't reconnecting (FastAPIBroadcast.connected).
  • leader_check: this process takes part in the election (FastAPILeader.campaigning). Whether anyone leads can't be seen from one process: alert on the sum of fastapi_alcazaba.leader.is_leader across them.
  • smtp_check: connects, starts TLS, logs in and says NOOP (SMTPSender.check()), sending nothing.
  • object_storage_check: reads the first byte of key with a URL the S3Presigner signs: the service, the credentials and the bucket at once. Upload a small object for it; the presigner's user only needs to read it.
  • Their errors are logged, never returned, as for every check.

docs.title: Backlog gauges
docs.text:
The work piling up is measured by a BacklogMonitor, every interval seconds, and by nothing without one: each measure costs a call to the backend or the database.

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import BacklogMonitor

monitor = BacklogMonitor(queue, outbox, interval=30, timeout=5)
app = FastAPI(lifespan=monitor.lifespan)  # or start() and stop() in your lifespan

It sets fastapi_alcazaba.tasks.backlog (by queue and state: queued, delayed), fastapi_alcazaba.tasks.dead_letters, fastapi_alcazaba.outbox.backlog and fastapi_alcazaba.outbox.oldest_age (seconds since the oldest message not sent was written). A source that fails or takes longer than timeout is logged, and the others are measured all the same. Every process may run one: the values are the same, alert on their maximum. Without metrics (no OpenTelemetry SDK) there's no reason to start one. queue.counts() and outbox.backlog() give the same numbers to your own code.

Two gauges need no monitor, as the process knows them: fastapi_alcazaba.breaker.open (1 while a FastAPIBreaker is open) and fastapi_alcazaba.leader.is_leader (1 in the process that leads).

docs.title: Metrics and traces
docs.text:
Alcazaba logs under fastapi_alcazaba.* with a NullHandler, as libraries do: its warnings (a breaker that opens, maintenance turned on, a backend that fails) show once the app configures logging, e.g. logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO). uvicorn alone only configures its own loggers.

Alcazaba only uses the OpenTelemetry API (the otel extra): it records nothing until the app configures an SDK, and never configures one itself. The simplest way is OpenTelemetry's own zero-code instrumentation, with the standard variables:

pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install  # instrumentations for FastAPI, httpx2, redis, SQLAlchemy…

OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=shop-api \
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=deployment.environment.name=production \
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://collector.internal:4317 \
OTEL_PYTHON_LOG_CORRELATION=true \
OTEL_PYTHON_FASTAPI_EXCLUDED_URLS="health/live,health/ready" \
opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn app:app

Give the collector's endpoint explicitly, over TLS: traces and logs carry what your app does. Then Alcazaba adds to them:

  • Spans: one per cached call (fastapi_alcazaba <function>, with fastapi_alcazaba.result: hit, miss, refresh or bypass) and, inside it, one per backend call (fastapi_alcazaba.backend get, set, lock…, with failures recorded); instrumented Redis/Valkey clients nest their own inside. Each run of a scheduled job is the root of a trace of its own (fastapi_alcazaba.scheduler <job>, failures recorded), so what the job does (queries, calls) is grouped under it instead of scattered. So is each run of a task (fastapi_alcazaba.task <task>, with its queue, ID and attempt), linked to the span that enqueued it, and each delivery of the outbox (fastapi_alcazaba.outbox <topic>, with its outbox, message ID and attempt), linked to the span that wrote the message.
  • On the request's span: the events fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit (a request limited or unchecked), fastapi_alcazaba.breaker.refused, .opened and .closed, fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.refused (an outbound call to an origin whose breaker is open) and fastapi_alcazaba.csrf.refused, and the attribute fastapi_alcazaba.idempotency with the outcome of an Idempotency-Key.
  • Never: keys, tokens, identities, codes or request bodies. Attributes are names, routes and outcomes, few enough to keep the cardinality of the metrics low.

docs.title: Structured logs
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.7: its API may still change in any release.

One line of JSON per record, for the log pipeline to search (CloudWatch, Loki, Elasticsearch, a SIEM): logging_config sends every record, Uvicorn's included, to standard output through JSONFormatter.

import uvicorn

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import logging_config

uvicorn.run("app:app", log_config=logging_config(static={"service": "shop"}))
# or logging.config.dictConfig(logging_config(...)) at start, with uvicorn's --log-config

logger.info("Order placed", extra={"order_id": 42, "card_token": token})

{"time":"2026-11-02T09:14:03.512+00:00","level":"INFO","logger":"shop.orders","service":"shop","message":"Order placed","request_id":"5f0c…","trace_id":"4bf9…","span_id":"00f0…","extra":{"order_id":42,"card_token":"[redacted]"}}
  • What each line has: the time (UTC, to the millisecond), level, logger and message; the static fields; the ID of the request being handled (request IDs) and its OpenTelemetry trace and span, so a line leads to its request and its trace; the exception's type, message and the last 30 frames of its stack.
  • extra= is redacted as the audit trail redacts details: the values of keys that name a secret (token, password, secret, authorization...; redact adds words) and strings that look like credentials become [redacted], and every value is bounded.
  • Uvicorn's access lines have the method, the status, the client and the path without its query, which may carry tokens, codes or e-mail addresses. access_log=False drops them, when the proxy in front logs requests already.
  • One line per record, whatever the message holds: line breaks in it are escaped, so nobody can forge a line by putting one in a field that ends up logged.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Switches every process sees at once: circuit breakers, maintenance mode and feature flags.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Circuit breakers
docs.text:
FastAPIBreaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing (a database, an SDK, a service reached without httpx), so that requests fail at once instead of waiting for it, and it gets room to recover:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIBreaker

payments = FastAPIBreaker("payments", failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30, timeout=10)


@payments
async def charge(order: Order) -> Receipt:
    return await payments_sdk.charge(order.id, order.total)


async def refund(order: Order) -> None:
    async with payments.attempt():  # or around a block
        await payments_sdk.refund(order.id)
  • States: after failure_threshold consecutive failures it opens, and for reset_timeout seconds calls fail with BreakerOpen without reaching the dependency. Then a single trial call goes through: its success closes the breaker, its failure opens it again.
  • In FastAPI: BreakerOpen is an HTTPException: an endpoint that hits an open breaker answers 503 with Retry-After (the seconds until the trial), without naming the dependency.
  • What counts: exceptions in failures (any Exception by default) are failures; those in exclude mean the dependency answered (a "not found" from its SDK) and are successes; others, and a cancelled call, give no verdict. timeout bounds async calls: a slower call is cancelled, raises TimeoutError and counts as a failure. Sync code can't be interrupted, so a breaker with a timeout refuses to guard it.
  • Per process: each process keeps its own state, with no round trip on every call. Sync functions work too, also from the threads of FastAPI's pool.
  • Closed by hand: payments.reset() closes it at once and forgets the failures, when you know the dependency is back (from an admin endpoint) or between tests; failure_threshold and reset_timeout can be read back.
  • Observability: opening is logged as a warning and closing again as info, and both are counted with the calls (fastapi_alcazaba.breaker.* metrics). breaker.state says "closed", "open" or "half-open", handy in a health check: HealthCheck(lambda: payments.state != "open", critical=False).

docs.title: Maintenance mode
docs.text:
FastAPIMaintenance is a switch shared by every process; while it's on, MaintenanceMiddleware answers 503 with Retry-After to every request but the allowed ones:

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import client_ip
from fastapi_alcazaba.operations import FastAPIMaintenance, MaintenanceMiddleware

maintenance = FastAPIMaintenance()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIMaintenance(cache)
app.add_middleware(
    MaintenanceMiddleware,
    maintenance=maintenance,
    allow_paths=("/health", "/admin"),  # always served
    allow=lambda request: client_ip(request) in OFFICE,  # the team keeps working
)

await maintenance.enable("Back at 10:30", retry_after=900)  # from an admin route, a script...
await (
    maintenance.status()
)  # MaintenanceStatus(enabled=True, message=..., retry_after=900, since=...)
await maintenance.disable()
  • Shared, but not asked on every request: the state lives in the backend, and each process keeps a copy refreshed at most every refresh seconds (1 by default), so a change reaches every process within about that. status() reads the backend now; forget() drops the copy, and a new cache drops it by itself (each test's lifespan sets one up).
  • Responses: a 503 whose detail is the message ("Service Unavailable" without one), with Retry-After when given and Cache-Control: no-store. WebSockets are closed with 1013 (try again later). Lifespan events go through. A pure ASGI middleware: streaming isn't affected.
  • Exceptions: allow_paths are prefixes (/health covers /health/live, not /healthz), matched without the root_path of a proxy or a mount, and are served without reading the state. allow (sync or async) receives the request: use the address the server reports (client_ip), never X-Forwarded-For.
  • Failures: when the backend fails, each process keeps the last state it read (maintenance often means work on the backend itself: its failure mustn't reopen an app closed on purpose) and serves normally if it never read one. enable() and disable() raise BackendUnavailable: nothing changes then.
  • Integrity: with a signing_key or encryption_key on the cache the state is sealed, and a state planted in the backend by someone else is ignored; the message is capped at 1000 characters.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
FastAPIFeatureFlags keeps flags in the backend: turn features on and off for everybody, for some users or tenants, or for a percentage of them, from any process and without a deploy:

from fastapi_alcazaba.operations import FastAPIFeatureFlags

flags = FastAPIFeatureFlags()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIFeatureFlags(cache, refresh=5)

await flags.set("new-checkout", enabled=True, percentage=10, allow=["user-42"], deny=["user-7"])

if await flags.enabled("new-checkout", subject=str(user.id)):
    ...


async def user_id(user: Annotated[User | None, Depends(optional_user)]) -> str | None:
    return str(user.id) if user is not None else None  # who the request proved to be


@app.get("/beta/report", dependencies=[Depends(flags.require("beta-report", subject=user_id))])
async def beta_report() -> Report: ...  # 404 while the flag is off for the user
  • Rules: a flag is on for a subject when it's enabled, the subject isn't in deny, and it's in allow or falls within percentage. No percentage means everybody, but only allow when there's an allow list: a flag for a few never goes to everyone by mistake. enabled=False turns it off for everyone, allow included. Without a subject, a partial rollout counts as off, and so does a flag with a deny list. An undefined flag gives default (False).
  • The subject is who the request proved to be (the user of your authentication), never a header or a parameter the client writes: whoever sends x-user-id: user-42 would get the allow list's features, and could pick a value inside any rollout.
  • Sticky rollouts: a subject's place comes from a hash of the flag's name and the subject, so it keeps its answer while the percentage stays, raising the percentage only adds subjects, and each flag picks different subjects.
  • Hidden when off: require() answers FastAPI's own 404 Not Found, so the flag isn't revealed, and closes WebSockets with 1008. For subjects that need other dependencies (the current user), call enabled() from your own dependency.
  • Local copies: each process keeps the definitions it reads for refresh seconds (5), so a change reaches every process within that, and a flag costs at most one round trip per refresh. When the backend fails, the last definition read is used, or the default. get(name) reads the backend now; delete(name) removes a flag; forget() drops the copies, and a new cache drops them by itself.
  • Privacy and integrity: subjects are stored as SHA-256 digests salted with the flag's name, never in clear (at most 10,000 per list). Whoever reads the backend can still confirm a guess of a guessable subject (an e-mail address): prefer opaque ids, or give the cache an encryption_key, which encrypts the definitions. With a signing_key or encryption_key, definitions planted by someone else are ignored. Names are up to 100 letters, digits, ., _ and -.

docs.title: Passkeys
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

Logins without a password (Touch ID, Windows Hello, a phone, a security key), which a phishing page can't relay, and a second factor that resists it: WebAuthn, by FastAPIWebAuthn, with the crypto extra.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIWebAuthn

webauthn = FastAPIWebAuthn(rp_id="example.com", rp_name="Example", origins=["https://example.com"])
  • rp_id is the site's domain (or one it's under: example.com for https://login.example.com); the passkeys only work there. origins are where the answers come from: https://…, or http://localhost:8000 in development.
  • In the browser, each ceremony is two requests: the options, which the page gives to navigator.credentials.create() (or get()) after PublicKeyCredential.parseCreationOptionsFromJSON() (or parseRequestOptionsFromJSON()), then credential.toJSON(), which the server verifies.

docs.title: Registering a passkey
docs.text:
@app.post("/passkeys/options")
async def options(user: CurrentUser) -> dict[str, Any]:
    existing = [Passkey.from_dict(p) for p in user.passkeys]
    return await webauthn.registration_options(
        user.id, user.email, user_handle=user.handle, exclude=existing
    )


@app.post("/passkeys")
async def register(request: Request, credential: dict[str, Any], user: CurrentUser) -> None:
    try:
        passkey = await webauthn.verify_registration(user.id, credential, request=request)
    except WebAuthnRefused:
        raise HTTPException(400, "That passkey wasn't accepted") from None
    await db.passkeys.add(user.id, passkey.to_dict())  # its id must be no one else's
  • The user handle is what the authenticator keeps for the user: random, not their email, and the same for all their passkeys. Without user_handle, the options have a new one (options["user"]["id"]); store it with the user. exclude keeps an authenticator from registering twice.
  • A passkey (residentKey: "required", the default) logs in without a username; the user is verified by the authenticator (user_verification="required": a PIN, a fingerprint, the phone's lock), so a passkey is both factors.
  • What to store: passkey.to_dict(), JSON: its id, its COSE public key, its algorithm (ES256, EdDSA or RS256), the user handle, its counter, and whether it's synced (backup_eligible, backed_up). Nothing in it opens a door: it's a public key.
  • Attestation isn't checked: attestation: "none" is asked, so the app doesn't learn the authenticator's make. A login's security doesn't rest on it.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
@app.post("/login/options")
async def login_options() -> dict[str, Any]:
    return await webauthn.authentication_options()  # any passkey of this site


@app.post("/login")
async def login(request: Request, credential: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, str]:
    stored = await db.passkeys.get(credential_id(credential))  # and its user
    try:
        passkey = await webauthn.verify_authentication(
            credential, Passkey.from_dict(stored.passkey), user_id=stored.user_id, request=request
        )
    except WebAuthnRefused:
        raise HTTPException(401, "That passkey wasn't accepted") from None
    await db.passkeys.update(passkey.to_dict())  # its new counter
    sessions.login(request, stored.user_id)
    webauthn.mark(request, stored.user_id)  # a recent second factor: step-up
    ...
  • Without a username: authentication_options() lets any passkey of the site answer, and the browser asks which (or offers them in the username field, with autocomplete="webauthn"). The answer's user handle must be the passkey's. With user_id and allow=[...], only theirs: a second factor after a password.
  • What's checked (WebAuthn Level 2, 7.1 and 7.2): the challenge (random, kept for timeout seconds, for this ceremony and this user, used once); the origin (one of origins, not in a cross-origin iframe); the RP ID's hash, which the authenticator signs, so a phishing site's answer is refused; the user present and verified; the signature, with the stored public key; and the counter.
  • A cloned authenticator: a counter that goes back, or doesn't move for one that counts, is refused. Synced passkeys count 0 and aren't checked; their backup eligibility mustn't change.
  • Refused answers raise WebAuthnRefused, whose reason (challenge, origin, rp_id, user_verification, signature, counter…) goes to the logs and the metrics, not to the user.
  • When the backend fails, no answer is checked: the challenges can't be used once.
  • Step-up: webauthn.mark(request, user_id) and webauthn.require_recent(current_user_id, max_age=300) are those of the second factor: a passkey or a TOTP code of the last minutes, in this session.

docs.title: Implemented here
docs.text:
The CBOR of attestation objects and COSE keys is read by the library itself, strictly: definite lengths only, no tags nor floats, no duplicate keys, nothing after the item. The keys are checked for their algorithm (P-256 for ES256, Ed25519 for EdDSA, RSA of 2048 bits or more for RS256) and the signatures verified with cryptography. The tests run the answers of real browsers and authenticators, besides a software authenticator that breaks each rule in turn.

With audit=, each passkey registered is an auth.passkey.register event and each login an auth.passkey one, with the outcome; counted in fastapi_alcazaba.webauthn, by ceremony and outcome.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.7: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

Passwords from sign-up to reset: kept as slow hashes, checked against those known to be leaked, guessed at most a few times per account, and reset by a link that works once. FastAPIPasswords, with nothing to install: the hashes are scrypt's, from the standard library. The leak check needs the passwords extra.

Every class and function: the API reference.

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIPasswords
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import PwnedPasswords

passwords = FastAPIPasswords(
    pepper=settings.password_pepper,  # a SecretStr of 32 bytes or more
    pwned=PwnedPasswords(),
    audit=audit,
)

docs.title: Signing up
docs.text:
@app.post("/signup")
async def signup(form: SignUp) -> dict[str, str]:
    problems = await passwords.check(form.password, user_inputs=[form.email, form.name])
    if problems:
        raise HTTPException(422, {"password": problems})
    user = await db.users.create(email=form.email, password=await passwords.hash(form.password))
    ...
  • What check refuses, as NIST SP 800-63B says: fewer than min_length characters (15 by default, the length for a password that is the only factor; 8 with a second factor), more than 1024, the e-mail address or the name in it, and a password among those leaked. No rules on its characters (a digit, a capital, a symbol): length is what makes a password strong.
  • Leaked passwords are the first that attackers try. PwnedPasswords asks Have I Been Pwned without sending the password: only the first five characters of its SHA-1 go out, and the answer is padded, so that its size doesn't tell them either. When the API doesn't answer, the password is taken as not leaked and a warning logged (fail_open=False raises instead).
  • The hash: scrypt (RFC 7914) with OWASP's parameters (128 MiB, a fifth of a second), a random salt each, in a thread, in PHC's format: $scrypt$ln=17,r=8,p=1$<salt>$<hash>.
  • The pepper: the password is first an HMAC with it, so that a stolen database without the pepper gives nothing to guess against. Keep it out of the database, in your settings: it can't be rotated without the passwords.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
@app.post("/login")
async def login(request: Request, form: Login) -> dict[str, str]:
    user = await db.users.by_email(form.email)
    user_id, stored = (user.id, user.password) if user else (None, None)
    if not await passwords.verify(user_id, form.password, stored, request=request):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Wrong e-mail or password")
    if passwords.needs_rehash(user.password):
        await db.users.update(user.id, password=await passwords.hash(form.password))
    log_in(request, user)
    ...
  • Guesses per account: after max_attempts wrong passwords (10), the account's logins are refused for lockout seconds (900), the right password too, in every process. Other accounts aren't affected. One client trying many accounts is a rate limit's: one per IP on the login route.
  • Unknown accounts take as long: with stored=None, verify hashes against a made-up hash, so the time of an answer doesn't tell which e-mail addresses have an account. Answer both cases with the same message.
  • Stronger parameters later: needs_rehash is true for a hash made with others than parameters; hash the password again while you have it.
  • When the backend fails, the attempts can't be counted, and the password is refused.

docs.title: Resetting
docs.text:
@app.post("/password/forgot")
async def forgot(form: Forgot) -> None:
    user = await db.users.by_email(form.email)
    if user is not None:
        token = await passwords.reset_token(user.id)
        await mail.send(user.email, "Reset your password", f"{settings.url}/reset?token={token}")
    # the same answer either way


@app.post("/password/reset")
async def reset(request: Request, form: Reset) -> None:
    if problems := await passwords.check(form.password):
        raise HTTPException(422, {"password": problems})
    user_id = await passwords.use_reset_token(form.token, request=request)
    if user_id is None:
        raise HTTPException(400, "The link expired or was used: ask for another")
    await db.users.update(user_id, password=await passwords.hash(form.password))
    await user_sessions.end_all(user_id)  # whoever knew the old password is logged out
  • A token, once: 256 random bits, kept as a digest for reset_ttl seconds (an hour). Of two requests with it, one gets the user; a newer token replaces the user's last one.
  • The user ID comes back as a string, as the backend keeps it.
  • Send it by e-mail (FastAPIMail), in the path or the body of the reset page's form, never in a page's links to other sites: the Referer would carry it.

docs.title: What's recorded
docs.text: With audit, each password checked is an auth.password event, and each reset an auth.password_reset, with the outcome as reason when it failed (wrong, locked, unknown, replaced...). The metric fastapi_alcazaba.passwords counts the same by outcome: a burst of wrong or locked is someone guessing. Neither ever has the password, nor the token.

docs.title: Production setup
docs.text: The quick start keeps everything in the process: each process has its own cache, counters and revoked tokens. In production, several processes or containers serve the app, and they share that state through a backend: Redis, Valkey, memcached or DynamoDB.

docs.title: Install the extras
docs.text:
Each backend and integration needs a library of its own, which an extra installs:

pip install fastapi-alcazaba            # in-memory backend only
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[redis]"   # or [valkey], [glide], [memcache], [dynamodb], [all]
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[otel]"    # OpenTelemetry metrics
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[crypto]"  # encrypted entries
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[zstd]"    # zstd compression before Python 3.14
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[casbin]"  # authorization with Casbin
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[cedar]"   # authorization with Cedar
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[opa]"     # authorization by Open Policy Agent
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-jwt]"     # JWTStrategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oauth2]"  # OAuth2Strategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oidc]"    # OIDCStrategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-saml]"    # SAMLStrategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-unkey]"   # UnkeyStrategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[sqlalchemy]"            # pagination queries for SQLAlchemy

Python 3.11+, FastAPI 0.115+ and Pydantic v2.

docs.title: The app
docs.text:
An app as it runs in production: its configuration from the environment, the cache in Redis, shared by every process, and its entries signed.

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
from redis import asyncio as aioredis

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPICache
from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.redis import RedisBackend
from fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache import cache


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """From environment variables (REDIS_URL...) or a .env file."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", env_file_encoding="utf-8")

    redis_url: str
    cache_signing_key: SecretStr  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


settings = Settings()


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    redis = aioredis.from_url(settings.redis_url)
    FastAPICache.init(RedisBackend(redis), prefix="myapp", signing_key=settings.cache_signing_key)
    yield
    await redis.aclose()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float


def current_user(authorization: str = Header()) -> str:
    return authorization  # validate the token here


@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
@cache(expire=60, vary_headers=())  # same response for everybody: one shared entry
async def product(product_id: int) -> Product:
    return Product(name="Olive oil", price=9.5)


@app.get("/me")
@cache(expire=30)  # one entry per Authorization/Cookie value, sent as private
async def me(user: str = Depends(current_user)) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"user": user}

@cache goes between the route decorator and the function. It also caches plain functions, sync or async (sync ones run in the thread pool, like FastAPI does).

The configuration comes from pydantic-settings (pip install pydantic-settings). Every parameter that takes a key or a secret also takes pydantic's SecretStr (or SecretBytes) as it is, so the value stays out of the settings' repr and of tracebacks until Alcazaba uses it. The other snippets read theirs from the same settings.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
With the metrics exported (see Metrics and traces) and a BacklogMonitor running, these catch what piles up silently. In Prometheus' terms, as the OpenTelemetry Collector's Prometheus exporter names them by default (dots become underscores; seconds get _seconds, and the 0-or-1 gauges, of unit 1, _ratio); the thresholds are a start:

groups:
  - name: fastapi-alcazaba
    rules:
      - alert: TasksDeadLettered  # a task gave up: look at it, requeue or discard it
        expr: max by (fastapi_alcazaba_queue) (fastapi_alcazaba_tasks_dead_letters) > 0
        for: 10m
      - alert: TasksPilingUp  # the workers aren't keeping up
        expr: max by (fastapi_alcazaba_queue) (fastapi_alcazaba_tasks_backlog{fastapi_alcazaba_state="queued"}) > 1000
        for: 15m
      - alert: OutboxStuck  # messages that should have gone out minutes ago
        expr: max by (fastapi_alcazaba_outbox) (fastapi_alcazaba_outbox_oldest_age_seconds) > 300
        for: 5m
      - alert: NobodyLeads  # the outbox relay (or what the leader runs) isn't running anywhere
        expr: sum by (fastapi_alcazaba_leader) (fastapi_alcazaba_leader_is_leader_ratio) == 0
        for: 2m
      - alert: BreakerOpen  # a dependency is failing
        expr: max by (fastapi_alcazaba_breaker) (fastapi_alcazaba_breaker_open_ratio) == 1
        for: 5m

Add the checks of Alcazaba's components to /health/ready too: they show in each probe what's degraded.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Backends: Redis, Valkey, GLIDE, memcached, DynamoDB, and a copy in each process in front of them.
  • Security model and resilience: what gets cached and for whom, what the backend is trusted with, and what happens when it fails.
  • Metrics and traces: what Alcazaba records with OpenTelemetry, and the logs to configure.

docs.title: Security model and resilience
docs.text:
What each tool protects against and what it trusts the backend with, and what happens when the backend fails.

Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: What each tool protects against, what it doesn't, and what it needs from your app. Report vulnerabilities as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: What every tool assumes
docs.text:
• The backend is trusted for availability, not for integrity: without a signing_key or an encryption_key on the cache, whoever can write to it decides what your endpoints return, forges sessions and runs your tasks. Give the cache one whenever the backend is shared or reachable by others; encryption_key when entries hold personal data, since signed ones are readable in the backend, its dumps and its backups. Keys are SHA-256 digests: arguments, ids and tokens never appear in it in clear.
  • What a key doesn't stop: someone who can write to the backend can still delete entries (a revocation, a rate-limit counter) and write back a genuine entry captured earlier: a cached response that changed since, a feature flag or maintenance state turned off since. The task queue refuses copies of its tasks (each run is claimed once); the other entries don't carry a version.
  • Secrets (the cache's keys, cursor and session secrets, JWT keys, API key peppers) are at least 32 bytes, the same in every process, kept in SecretStr, and rotate as lists: the first signs, all of them verify.
  • The client's address is the one the ASGI server gives: configure it to trust your proxy, and only it. Nothing reads X-Forwarded-For itself.
  • Failing: the security tools fail closed when the backend does: revoked tokens, one-time codes, idempotency, webhooks, sessions and the task queue answer 401, 503 or refuse. The cache, the rate limiters and the concurrency limiters let requests through by default (fail_open=False refuses them instead). InMemoryBackend never evicts live state: a kind of state (sessions, revocations, idempotency records...) that holds max_size live entries refuses new ones, as Redis with noeviction does, so a flood of one kind never makes room by forgetting another.

docs.title: Per tool
docs.text: Tool Protects against Doesn't, or needs from you Response cache One user's response served to another: requests are told apart by the endpoint's arguments and the vary_headers (Authorization, Cookie, X-API-Key), and per-user entries are sent private. Only 200s without no-store are kept, and none that sets a cookie; with a response model, only what it has. A response that depends on anything else (request.state, a header the app reads credentials from by itself, the client IP) needs it in vary_headers or the key builder; a shared entry otherwise. The headers Alcazaba's API key strategies read count already. Rate and concurrency limits Floods and brute force from one client: the check and the count are atomic, each route has one budget whatever its path parameters (those of a Mount too). Many clients (a botnet) get a budget each. A limit per account must use the account as the login finds it (normalised), and lets anyone lock the account out for the window: pair it with a limit per IP. Idempotency keys A retried POST running twice; another client getting a response by guessing a key (keys are per Authorization, or per cookies without one). Replays never carry Set-Cookie. A replay is answered before the route's dependencies: a copy of the request gets the response until it expires, even with a revoked token. An async identifier that checks the credentials closes that. JWTs alg: none, a public key used as an HMAC secret or a token verified with another algorithm than its key's (each key is pinned to one), HMAC keys in a JWKS, a JWKS over plain HTTP, short HMAC secrets, tokens meant for other services (an aud without audience is refused; a JWKS needs audience and issuer), tokens of a retired key, revoked tokens within the leeway; a provider that's slow or down (a deadline, a circuit breaker, at most one fetch every 30 s). Tokens read from a cookie need CSRFMiddleware. Sessions Fixation (rotate_session at login), cookie tossing (__Host-session), a copied cookie after logout, sessions left open elsewhere (UserSessions.end_all refuses those the index missed too), also from a request still running with it. Ids are 256-bit and stored as digests. rotate_session at login and clear_session at logout are yours to call; CSRFMiddleware with cookie sessions. OAuth2, OpenID Connect and SAML logins Login CSRF and code interception (state and PKCE in a __Host- cookie); ID tokens forged, for another app, from another login or another issuer (signature with the provider's JWKS, iss, aud, azp, nonce, at_hash; the discovery document's issuer checked); signature wrapping, replayed or unsolicited assertions, assertions for another audience or recipient. Redirecting after login is the app's: never to a URL from the request. RelayState comes back as the client sent it. Passkeys (WebAuthn) Phishing (the answer is for the site's RP ID and origin, which the browser enforces), replayed answers (each challenge once), cloned authenticators (the counter), answers for another user or ceremony, a stolen database (public keys only). Attestation isn't checked (attestation: "none"): the authenticator's make isn't known. Synced passkeys are as safe as the account they sync with. Second factor (TOTP) Codes replayed (each once, in every process), guessed (a lockout after max_attempts, recovery codes included), secrets read from the database (sealed with AES-256-GCM for their user), a recovery code used twice, a step-up inherited by another user of the browser. TOTP doesn't resist a phishing page that relays the code within its 30 seconds: WebAuthn does. The app keeps the user halfway in between the password and the code. Passwords Hashes cracked from a stolen database (scrypt with OWASP's cost, and a pepper kept outside it), guesses at an account (a lockout after max_attempts, in every process), accounts found by timing (unknown ones hash too), leaked passwords (refused, without sending them), reset tokens used twice, guessed or kept after a newer one (256 bits, digests, once). A lockout lets anyone lock an account out for lockout seconds: pair it with a rate limit per IP. Ending the user's sessions after a reset is yours (UserSessions.end_all). Revocations, codes, API keys Revoked tokens accepted while the backend is down (refused unless fail_open); brute force of codes (attempts counted atomically, kept past the code); API keys read from the backend (only HMAC digests with a pepper). Unkey's API keys Keys deleted, disabled or expired (verified on every request, nothing cached), over their credits or rate limit; Unkey down (a 503, never let through); malformed keys (not sent). Unkey takes up to 30 s to spread a deletion, and every request waits for its answer: a root key that may only verify for UnkeyStrategy, another to make keys. Authorization Requests the policy doesn't allow, with no way around it through the path: paths with control characters get a 400, HEAD is checked as GET, the subject is the user's identity. A broken policy refuses; with Cedar, so does a policy that can't be evaluated, which Cedar alone would skip (a failing forbid would let the request through). A policy service that doesn't answer (Open Policy Agent) refuses with a 503, and only a result of true allows. An anonymous subject must be a name no user can have (*anonymous). In keyMatch2, :name is a parameter: name objects without colons. Other processes see a policy change when they reload it (a Casbin watcher). CSRF, headers, body size Cross-site requests sent with the browser's cookies, clickjacking and the like, endless bodies (a 413). Webhooks and outbound calls Forged, altered, stale and replayed webhooks; outbound calls to internal addresses (every form of private IP, DNS rebinding, redirects checked again). Uploads Files whose name or type lies about what they are, decompression bombs (the canvas of a GIF counts its frames' extents), file names that traverse paths or hide extensions. Macro-enabled Office documents are told by their content types, read without an XML parser: don't take that as the only check before serving one back. Archives may expand far beyond their size. Object storage Uploads larger or of another declared type than the form allows (refused by the service), keys that escape their prefix, uploaded HTML or SVG run on the bucket's origin (filename downloads it). The form bounds the declared type, not the file's: check it before using it. A URL works for anyone who has it until it expires: keep expires short. E-mail Headers and recipients added through a field (line breaks, commas, reserved headers refused), mail read on the way (STARTTLS or TLS, certificates checked; plain only to localhost), bodies with links and codes in logs. SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the sender's domain are your provider's and your DNS's. Escape what goes into the HTML. Pagination Cursors made up, changed, or used with other filters (signed and bound to the query); limits past the maximum (a 422). Keyset keys are in plain sight and writable: sort by what clients may see. Task queue Tasks planted or altered in the backend (sealed, bound to the queue), copies of a sealed task written back (each run is claimed once, until replay_window), pickle (arguments travel as JSON). Delivery is at least once: tasks must be idempotent. Without a key, whoever writes to the backend runs your tasks. With one, the run claims and status records that refuse copies are state in the backend: whoever can also delete keys there can run a copy again until its sealed deadline (replay_window); restrict the app's backend user (Redis ACLs) to the commands it needs, and keep replay_window as short as your outages allow. Broadcast Messages planted by whoever can write to Redis (signed with signing_key), floods that exhaust memory (64 KiB a message, queue_size per subscriber). Delivery is at most once: a subscriber gets a gap for what it missed, and must send the state again. Without a key, a planted message reaches the subscribers. Outbox A change saved without its message, or a message sent for a change rolled back (both in one transaction). Delivery is at least once: consumers keep the ids they've seen. Run one relay. Feature flags, maintenance, breakers Flags and maintenance state planted in the backend (sealed); a deny-listed user getting a flag by not saying who they are (off without a subject). The subject of a flag is who the request proved to be, never a header. A breaker counts every exception by default: list in exclude the errors a client can cause (a 404 for its own input), or anyone can open it. Maintenance's allow_paths are prefixes: /health also lets /health/orders through, which a route /{tenant}/orders would serve. Accounting Going past a quota with concurrent requests (charging is an atomic check-and-add), subjects in clear in the backend (digests), billing that loses charges while the backend is down (the records still have them). With meter(..., amount=None), the quota is checked when a request starts: the requests running then may together go past it. With fail_open (the default), a backend that's down lets requests through unbounded. Audit trail Events altered, forged, reordered or removed from the middle of a stream (signed and chained). Removing the newest events of a stream, the oldest ones with everything before them, or a whole stream goes unnoticed: ship events off the host as they're written.

docs.title: Resilience
docs.text:
The cache never makes a request fail. Every backend call has a timeout (backend_timeout, 1 s by default): if it runs out, or the backend fails, the request goes on without cache. After circuit_breaker_failures consecutive failures the backend isn't called at all for circuit_breaker_reset seconds, so that requests don't each wait for the timeout; then one call tries again.

Concurrent misses for the same key compute once per process (single_flight). With several processes or containers, distributed_lock=True makes the first one take a lock in Redis/Valkey while the others wait for its value (up to lock_wait seconds). And early_refresh=0.1 lets callers refresh an entry, with growing probability, during the last 10 % of its lifetime: popular entries are renewed before they expire, instead of every caller missing at once. If that refresh fails, the cached value is served.

docs.title: Object storage
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.7: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

Files in S3, or anything that speaks its API (MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Google Cloud Storage's interoperability...), without passing through the app: S3Presigner signs URLs and upload forms with AWS's Signature Version 4, and the browser uses them directly. Nothing to install, and no SDK.

Every class and function: the API reference.

from fastapi_alcazaba.uploads import S3Presigner

s3 = S3Presigner(
    bucket="uploads",
    region="eu-west-1",
    access_key=settings.s3_access_key,
    secret_key=settings.s3_secret_key,  # a SecretStr
)

The bucket stays private: each URL is for one object, one method, and a few minutes (expires, 300 seconds by default, 7 days at most). Give the access key a user that may only do what the URLs need on this bucket.

docs.title: Uploads
docs.text:
@app.post("/avatar/upload")
async def avatar_upload(user: CurrentUser) -> UploadForm:
    return s3.upload_form(
        f"avatars/{user.id}/{uuid4()}",
        max_size=2_000_000,
        content_type_prefix="image/",
    )

The browser posts the file to url, with fields first and the file last, as file:

const body = new FormData();
for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(form.fields)) body.append(name, value);
body.append("Content-Type", file.type);
body.append("file", file);
await fetch(form.url, { method: "POST", body });
  • Bounded by the service: a file smaller than min_size (1 byte) or larger than max_size is refused by S3, as is one that declares another type than content_type, or one not starting with content_type_prefix.
  • A key of its own for each upload: a form overwrites what's under its key.

For a client that PUTs (an app, a script), upload_url signs a PUT of exactly the size the client declared, and of its SHA-256 when it gives one:

@app.post("/scans")
async def new_scan(body: NewScan, user: CurrentUser) -> PresignedUpload:
    if body.size > 50_000_000:
        raise HTTPException(413, "File too large")
    return s3.upload_url(f"scans/{user.id}/{uuid4()}", size=body.size, sha256=body.sha256)

The client sends the returned headers as they are: Content-Length and x-amz-checksum-sha256 are signed, so S3 (MinIO, R2) refuses any other length (403), and bytes whose checksum isn't the one given (400).

docs.title: Checking what was uploaded
docs.text:
Neither the form nor the URL say what the file is. check_uploaded reads it back from the bucket, runs FastAPIUploads's checks on it, its malware scanner too, and moves it to a key the clients never get a URL for, or deletes it when it fails them (pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[uploads]"):

from fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.direct import check_uploaded


@app.post("/scans/{scan_id}/done")
async def scan_done(scan_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    checked = await check_uploaded(  # 413, 415, 422: and deleted
        uploads, s3, f"incoming/scans/{scan_id}", move_to=f"scans/{scan_id}"
    )
    await checked.file.close()
    return {"type": checked.content_type}
  • Why it's moved: a presigned URL or form works until it expires, as many times as the client likes. Checked where it was uploaded, the object could be replaced by another the next second, of the same size, and the app would serve what it never checked. So check_uploaded copies it to move_to only if it's still the object it read (x-amz-copy-source-if-match with its ETag), and deletes it from where it was. Replaced in between: deleted, and a 409. Give clients URLs under one prefix (incoming/) and serve another.
  • Under the type it is: the copy's Content-Type is the one found in its bytes, not the one the uploader sent: a PNG uploaded as text/html is served as image/png.
  • At most max_size + 1 bytes are read: a larger object is "too large" without reading the rest.
  • Refused (413, 415, 422): deleted from the bucket with a signed DELETE, and the HTTPException goes on. Not scanned (503, the scanner down): kept where it was, to check later. No such object: 404; the service failing: 502.
  • The returned CheckedFile holds the bytes read (in memory up to 1 MiB, then on disk): close it when done.
  • Not yet: multipart (resumable) uploads.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
@app.get("/invoices/{invoice_id}")
async def invoice(invoice_id: int, user: CurrentUser) -> RedirectResponse:
    invoice = await db.invoices.get(invoice_id, owner=user.id)  # yours to authorize
    url = s3.download_url(f"invoices/{invoice.id}.pdf", filename="invoice.pdf", expires=60)
    return RedirectResponse(url, status_code=303)

With filename, browsers download the object as that file (Content-Disposition: attachment) rather than show it, so an uploaded HTML or SVG never runs on the bucket's origin. content_type overrides the type it's served with.
