docs.title: Keys and services
docs.text:
• Object keys are 1 to 1024 bytes, without a leading /, an empty, . or .. segment, or control characters: a key made from user input can't escape its prefix.
  • Other services: endpoint is their URL (https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, http://localhost:9000 for MinIO), and the bucket goes in the path: what most of them want. With AWS, the bucket is in the host (path_style=False). Plain http is only for localhost.
  • Temporary credentials (STS, an instance's role): session_token is signed into each URL. The URLs stop working when the credentials expire, whatever their expires.

docs.title: Second factor
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

The codes of an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, 1Password, Authy, Bitwarden…) after the password, recovery codes for a lost phone, and a recent code for sensitive actions: FastAPITOTP, with the crypto extra, which seals the secrets.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPITOTP

totp = FastAPITOTP(issuer="Example", secret=settings.totp_secret, audit=audit)

docs.title: Adding the app
docs.text:
@app.post("/totp/enroll")
async def enroll(request: Request, user: CurrentUser) -> dict[str, str]:
    enrollment = totp.enroll(user.id, label=user.email)
    request.session["enrolling"] = enrollment.sealed  # until a code of it is confirmed
    return {"uri": enrollment.uri, "secret": enrollment.secret.get_secret_value()}


@app.post("/totp/confirm")
async def confirm(request: Request, form: Code, user: CurrentUser) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    sealed = request.session["enrolling"]
    if not await totp.verify(user.id, sealed, form.code, request=request):
        raise HTTPException(400, "Wrong code: try the next one")
    recovery = totp.recovery_codes(user.id)
    await db.users.update(user.id, totp=sealed, recovery=recovery.digests)
    return {"recovery_codes": recovery.codes}  # shown once
  • The secret: 160 random bits (RFC 4226). uri is the otpauth:// URI to show as a QR code (with a library such as segno or qrcode, in your page); secret, the same in base32, for those who type it.
  • Sealed, never in clear: sealed is the secret encrypted with AES-256-GCM, bound to its user: store it, not the secret. It doesn't open for another user, nor without secret, so a copy of the database, or a sealed secret moved to another account, gives nobody codes. A list rotates secret: the first one seals, all of them open.
  • Confirmed first: turn the second factor on once the user has typed a code of the new app, so that a QR code scanned wrong doesn't lock them out.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
@app.post("/login/totp")
async def login_totp(request: Request, form: Code) -> dict[str, str]:
    user = await db.users.get(request.session["pending"])  # set by the password step
    if not await totp.verify(user.id, user.totp, form.code, request=request):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Wrong code")
    log_in(request, user)
    totp.mark(request, user.id)  # the second factor is recent: step-up
    ...
  • The codes: RFC 6238's, SHA1, 6 digits every 30 seconds, as every app does (digits=8, algorithm="SHA256", period=60 for those that support it). The current one is accepted, and window=1 step before and after, for clocks out of step.
  • Each code once: a code accepted is refused afterwards (RFC 6238, 5.2), in every process: someone who saw it over the user's shoulder, or a phishing page that relays it, gets nothing. Of two requests with the same code, one wins.
  • Guesses: after max_attempts (5) wrong codes, recovery codes included, the user's codes are refused for lockout (15 minutes) from the first of them, the right one too. A right code forgives the wrong ones before it. The other users aren't affected.
  • Halfway in: between the password and the code, keep in the session who's logging in, not that they're logged in: the routes for logged-in users don't take them yet.
  • When the backend fails, nothing is accepted: no code is checked for replay, nor guesses counted. The backend must hold locks, which mark each code used: every backend shipped with fastapi-alcazaba does, and one of your own without them is refused.

docs.title: Recovery codes
docs.text:
used = await totp.use_recovery_code(user.id, form.code, user.recovery, request=request)
if used is None:
    raise HTTPException(401, "Wrong code")
await db.users.update(user.id, recovery=[d for d in user.recovery if d != used])
  • Ten codes, XXXXX-XXXXX of letters and digits that can't be mistaken for each other (about 50 bits each), typed in any case, with or without the dash. Shown once; the database keeps their digests (HMAC-SHA256 with secret, bound to the user).
  • Each once: use_recovery_code returns the digest used, to delete; until it's deleted, another request with the same code is refused. Wrong ones count as guesses.
  • New ones replace the old ones: recovery_codes(user.id) again, and store its digests instead.

docs.title: Step-up
docs.text:
@app.delete(
    "/account",
    dependencies=[Depends(totp.require_recent(current_user_id, max_age=300))],
)
async def delete_account(...) -> None: ...
  • A recent code: require_recent lets through the users who gave their second factor in this session in the last max_age seconds; the others get a 403 (Second factor required), to ask for a code, and requests without a user a 401. totp.mark(request, user.id) notes it, after verify or use_recovery_code, and gives the session a new id: it holds more privileges now.
  • Bound to the user: the mark says whose it is; another user who logs in in the same browser session doesn't inherit it.
  • Sessions: with ServerSessionMiddleware (or Starlette's SessionMiddleware).
  • Shared with passkeys: a login with a verified passkey marks the session the same way (webauthn.mark), and either require_recent takes a code or a passkey; both are fastapi_alcazaba.auth.stepup's.

docs.title: By factor, and for tokens
docs.text:
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.stepup import require_recent

passkey_only = require_recent(current_user_id, max_age=300, methods={"passkey"}, audit=audit)

# API clients with the provider's tokens: its auth_time, amr and acr decide.
claims = auth.authenticate("oidc_tokens")  # returns the token's claims
recent_mfa = require_recent(
    current_user_id, max_age=600, claims=claims, methods={"hwk", "otp"}, acr_values={"urn:mfa"}
)
  • Which factor: methods lists those that count: the method the session was marked with ("passkey", "totp", or yours: stepup.mark(request, user_id, "password")), or for tokens their amr values (RFC 8176: "hwk" a hardware key, "otp", "mfa"…). stepup.verified_with(request, user_id) says which one the session holds.
  • The front end knows what to do: a session that falls short gets a 403 problem (type: "urn:fastapi-alcazaba:problem:step-up", with max_age and methods; install FastAPIProblemDetails to get it as application/problem+json).
  • Tokens: with claims= (a dependency that returns the token's claims when there's one), the token must be the user's: its sub is what current_user_id returns (subject= reads another claim), so a fresh token of an attacker's own, sent with a stolen session, steps nobody up. Its auth_time must be within max_age, an amr among methods, and its acr among acr_values. Otherwise a 401 with RFC 9470's challenge: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_user_authentication", ..., max_age="600", acr_values="urn:mfa", for the client to send the user back to the provider with those.
  • Audited: with audit=, each check is an auth.stepup event: the user, the method, how old, and the reason when it's refused (none, too_old, wrong_method, no_auth_time, wrong_acr, other_subject).

docs.title: In the audit trail
docs.text: With audit=, each code checked is an auth.mfa event and each recovery code tried an auth.recovery_code one, with the user, the outcome (the reason when it failed: wrong, replayed, malformed, locked, unchecked), and the request's route and client. Never the code. Counted in fastapi_alcazaba.totp.verifications and fastapi_alcazaba.totp.recovery, by outcome: a burst of wrong or locked is someone guessing.

docs.title: Checking uploads
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

The name and the Content-Type of an upload are whatever the client chose: an HTML page sent as cat.png would be served back as HTML. FastAPIUploads checks the file itself, with nothing but the standard library:

from fastapi_alcazaba.uploads import IMAGES, CheckedFile, FastAPIUploads

uploads = FastAPIUploads(types=IMAGES, max_size=5 * 1024 * 1024, max_pixels=25_000_000)


@app.post("/avatars")
async def avatar(upload: Annotated[CheckedFile, Depends(uploads)]) -> dict[str, str]:
    name = f"{uuid4()}{upload.extension}"  # never the client's name
    await storage.save(name, upload.file.file, content_type=upload.content_type)
    return {"name": name}

As a dependency it reads the form field file; for other fields or several files, call await uploads.check(file). It returns a CheckedFile: the UploadFile read back to its start, the content_type found in its bytes, its size, its width and height (images) and a safe filename.

  • The real type (sniff(data)): PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, PDF, ZIP, GZIP, MP4 and QuickTime from their signatures; Word, Excel and PowerPoint documents from the content types their [Content_Types].xml declares (as Office reads them), with the macro-enabled ones (.docm, .xlsm, .pptm) told apart, and anything ambiguous reported as a plain ZIP; UTF-8 text without control characters (text/plain: CSV is text, it can't be told apart). Text that starts with a tag is HTML, SVG or XML, never plain text, and SVG is never an image: all three can carry scripts. types must come from KNOWN_TYPES (IMAGES, OFFICE_DOCUMENTS...), so a typo like image/jpg fails at start-up. Store and serve files with the detected type, never the client's, plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (SecurityHeadersMiddleware).
  • Size: counted while the file is read in chunks, whatever UploadFile.size says; 413 beyond max_size, 415 for a type that isn't allowed, 422 for an empty file. By the time an endpoint runs the multipart parser has stored the whole request already, so limit it with BodySizeLimitMiddleware on the route as well.
  • Decompression bombs: the width and height of PNG, JPEG (however much metadata comes before the frame), GIF and WebP images are read from their headers (image_size(data)) without decoding them; more than max_pixels (40 million by default) gets a 413, and an image whose dimensions can't be read a 415.
  • Safe names (safe_filename(name)): NFKC-normalised, only the last path component, without control or invisible characters (such as the right-to-left override that shows exe.txt as txt.exe), <>:"|?* replaced, without leading dots or dashes, _ in front of the names Windows reserves (CON, NUL, COM1...), and at most 255 bytes, keeping the extension. For display and Content-Disposition; store files under names of your own (CheckedFile.extension).
  • What it doesn't do by itself: look inside the files. A PDF can carry scripts, Office documents macros, archives may expand to far more than their size, and the frames of a GIF aren't counted. Allow HTML, SVG or XML only to serve them as attachments from another domain. A malware scanner looks inside them: see below.

docs.title: Scanning for malware
docs.text:
from fastapi_alcazaba.uploads import ClamAVScanner, FastAPIUploads

scanner = ClamAVScanner("tcp://clamav:3310")  # or "unix:///run/clamav/clamd.ctl"
uploads = FastAPIUploads(
    types=OFFICE_DOCUMENTS,
    scanner=scanner,
    on_infected=quarantine,  # optional: (file, result) -> None, before the 422
)
app.include_router(health_router({"clamav": HealthCheck(scanner.ping, critical=False)}))

pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[clamav]": nothing more is installed, ClamAVScanner speaks clamd's protocol itself.

  • After the other checks: only a file of an accepted type, size and pixels is scanned: the scanner never gets a 2 GB upload or an unknown type.
  • ClamAV: the file goes to clamd (ClamAV's daemon) with its INSTREAM command, in chunks over TCP or a Unix socket, never through a shared disk; ping() is a health check. Run clamd next to the app (the clamav/clamav image), with freshclam keeping its signatures up to date; give it about 1 GB of memory, and raise its StreamMaxLength (25 MB by default) above max_size, or larger files can't be scanned.
  • Infected: a 422 File rejected, which doesn't say what was found; the threat's name is logged, and counted (fastapi_alcazaba.uploads, outcome infected). on_infected(file, result), sync or async, runs before: to keep the file in quarantine, or alert someone.
  • Fails closed: when the scanner doesn't answer within scan_timeout (30 s) or can't scan the file, the upload gets a 503 (scan_failed). scan_fail_open=True accepts it unscanned instead (unscanned, logged).
  • Your own scanner: anything with async scan(file) -> ScanResult (a commercial engine, a sandbox service); the file comes at its start.
  • What it can't do: a scanner knows the malware it has signatures for. A script in a PDF or a macro written for you goes through: keep the other precautions (attachments, another domain).

Files uploaded straight to S3 get the same checks with check_uploaded.

docs.title: Webhooks and outbound calls
docs.text:
Webhooks verified (Standard Webhooks, GitHub, Stripe, Slack), signed and sent the Standard Webhooks way, and calls to other services with a deadline, a circuit breaker and SSRF protection.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Signed webhooks
docs.text:
FastAPIWebhooks accepts only webhooks signed with your secret, and each delivery once. WebhookSigner signs the ones you send. Both follow Standard Webhooks, the format of Svix, Supabase, Clerk, Resend, OpenAI and others: webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature: v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256 of "id.timestamp.body">, with whsec_... secrets.

from fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks import FastAPIWebhooks, WebhookMessage, WebhookSigner

webhooks = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.webhook_secret)  # "whsec_..."


@app.post("/webhooks/payments")
async def payment_event(message: Annotated[WebhookMessage, Depends(webhooks)]) -> None:
    event = message.json()
    ...  # idempotent on message.id: retries of a message keep its id


# Sending them: sign the exact bytes you send.
signer = WebhookSigner(settings.webhook_secret)  # WebhookSigner.generate_secret() makes one
body = json.dumps(event).encode()
await client.post(url, content=body, headers=signer.sign(body))
  • Raw body, still readable: the signature is checked over the body exactly as it arrived, read up to max_body_size bytes (1 MiB; a 413 beyond, and a Content-Length over it is refused before reading). It stays in the request, for message.json() or await request.json(). Validate it with your model there (Event.model_validate_json(message.body)) rather than with a pydantic body parameter: FastAPI reads and validates those before any dependency runs, so the body would be read without the limit, and an unsigned malformed one would get a 422 before its signature is checked. Not a form parameter either, which consumes the body first.
  • Freshness: a timestamp more than tolerance seconds (300) away from the server's clock, in the past or the future, is refused.
  • Constant time, one answer: every signature in the header is compared in constant time against each secret. A wrong signature, a stale timestamp and a replay all get the same 401 ("Invalid webhook"); only missing or malformed headers get a 400.
  • Replays: each accepted delivery (its id and timestamp, as a SHA-256 digest under Cache.state_key) is counted in the cache's backend until its timestamp can't be accepted anymore, so a captured request sent again is refused by every process. Only accepted deliveries are counted: a forged copy can't burn the id of the real one. A retry of the sender has a new timestamp and signature and goes through, as it must after a failed attempt: make the endpoint idempotent on message.id (a unique constraint) if a message must not be processed twice. The backend must support counters, as every built-in backend does.
  • Backend down: a 503 with Retry-After (fail closed): senders retry later, while a replay would run its effects again. fail_open=True accepts correctly signed webhooks without the replay check instead.
  • Rotation: FastAPIWebhooks([new, old]) accepts a signature by either secret; WebhookSigner([new, old]) signs every message with both, so receivers with either secret accept it.
  • Without a dependency: webhooks.verify(headers, body) checks the signature and the timestamp (not replays), for queues and scripts.

docs.title: Ed25519 signatures (v1a)
docs.text:
Standard Webhooks also signs with Ed25519 (webhook-signature: v1a,<base64>): receivers verify with the sender's public key alone, so no shared secret leaks from a receiver. With the crypto extra:

private, public = WebhookSigner.generate_key_pair()  # "whsk_...", "whpk_..."
signer = WebhookSigner(private)  # or [hmac_secret, private]: v1 and v1a in one header
webhooks = FastAPIWebhooks(public)  # the receiver's: verifies, can't sign

A whsk_ key is the base64 of the 32-byte seed (or libsodium's 64 bytes, seed and public key).

docs.title: GitHub, Stripe and Slack
docs.text:
scheme= verifies the webhooks of these senders with the same checks: the raw body and its size limit, constant time, the tolerance on timestamps, replay marks, rotation with a list of secrets, and one 401 for every failure.

github = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.github_webhook_secret, scheme="github")
stripe = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.stripe_webhook_secret, scheme="stripe")  # "whsec_..." as given
slack = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.slack_signing_secret, scheme="slack")
Scheme What's checked message.id message.timestamp github X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<HMAC of the body> X-GitHub-Delivery None stripe Stripe-Signature: t=<time>,v1=<HMAC of "time.body"> (any of its v1) a digest of what's signed t slack X-Slack-Signature: v0=<HMAC of "v0:time:body">, X-Slack-Request-Timestamp a digest of what's signed the header
  • GitHub signs no time: a delivery is refused again only within the replay window (twice tolerance, plus a minute); a capture sent later goes through. Keep the endpoint idempotent on message.id, the delivery id, which redeliveries keep.
  • Stripe's secret is used as the string it gives you, whsec_ included (not decoded as Standard Webhooks' are); its event id is in the body (message.json()["id"]).
  • Slack sends slash commands and interactions as forms: take the body with await request.form() after the dependency (it keeps the body), not as form parameters.
  • Their secrets are at least 16 characters.

docs.title: Sending webhooks
docs.text:
WebhookSender delivers webhooks to the URLs your users register, through the task queue: signed the Standard Webhooks way, through the SSRF guard, retried with backoff until the receiver takes them, at least once. With the webhooks extra.

from fastapi_alcazaba.background.outbox import OutboxMessage, OutboxRelay
from fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks import WebhookEndpoint, WebhookSender


async def endpoint(endpoint_id: str) -> WebhookEndpoint | None:
    row = await endpoints_table.get(endpoint_id)  # yours: the URL and the secret the user got
    return WebhookEndpoint(row.url, row.secret) if row is not None else None


sender = WebhookSender(queue, endpoint)  # before the queue starts: it registers its task


# The webhook is written with the change, in its transaction, and sent once it's committed.
@app.post("/orders/{order_id}/pay")
async def pay(order_id: int) -> None:
    async with async_session() as session, session.begin():
        ...  # the change
        for endpoint_id in await subscribed(session, "order.paid"):
            event = {"type": "order.paid", "data": {"order_id": order_id}}
            await outbox.add(session, "webhook", {"endpoint": endpoint_id, "event": event})


async def deliver(message: OutboxMessage) -> None:
    payload = message.payload
    await sender.send(payload["endpoint"], payload["event"], message_id=message.id)


relay = OutboxRelay(outbox, deliver)
  • At least once, one id: each (endpoint, message) is one task of the queue, enqueued once while it's pending (unique_key): a message the outbox relays twice is delivered once, and every attempt carries the same webhook-id, for the receiver to deduplicate on. The body is serialised once, at send(); each attempt is signed afresh.
  • Retries: a 2xx is delivered; any other status or a transport error is tried again, retries times (8) with exponential backoff and jitter from backoff (5 s) up to max_backoff (6 h). Then the task goes to the queue's dead letters, where requeue_dead_letters() or fastapi-alcazaba tasks ... requeue sends it again.
  • Safe destinations: its own client refuses URLs that resolve to private, loopback or metadata addresses (SSRFGuardTransport; allow= for an internal receiver), doesn't follow redirects, gives each attempt timeout seconds (10) and reads at most 64 KiB of the answer, only for its status. client= gives yours instead, and the guard is then yours to add.
  • Endpoints that keep failing: after disable_after (20) failed attempts in a row, or at once when the receiver answers 410 Gone, the endpoint is disabled: its deliveries are skipped, not retried. health(endpoint_id) says how many failures in a row and whether it's disabled; enable() turns it back on (send the skipped messages again), disable() turns it off.
  • Records: delivery(endpoint_id, message_id) gives its state as of its last attempt (retrying, succeeded, failed, skipped), the attempts, the last status code and error type, and when; never the body nor the secret. Kept record_ttl (7 days).
  • Secrets stay with you: the queue carries the endpoint's id, the message's id and the body; endpoints() is asked for the URL and the secret at each attempt, so a rotated secret or a changed URL is used at once, and an endpoint deleted skips its deliveries.
  • One sender per queue; await sender.aclose() at shutdown closes its client.

docs.title: Outbound calls
docs.text:
ResilientTransport is an httpx transport for the calls your app makes to other services: a deadline for each call and a circuit breaker for each origin. It needs httpx2 (or httpx):

import httpx2 as httpx

from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import CircuitOpenError, ResilientTransport


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    transport = ResilientTransport(timeout=5, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="https://api.example.com") as client:
        app.state.partner_api = client
        yield


@app.get("/quote")
async def quote(request: Request) -> Quote:
    try:
        response = await request.app.state.partner_api.get("/quote")
    except CircuitOpenError:  # the service keeps failing: don't wait for it
        raise HTTPException(503, "Quotes are unavailable, try again later")
    return Quote.model_validate(response.json())
  • Deadline: timeout bounds the whole call, from sending the request to the last byte of the response. httpx's own timeouts are per phase, and its read timeout restarts with every byte, so a server that trickles a byte every few seconds would keep the request open forever. Past the deadline, httpx.TimeoutException. It applies to each request the transport sends: with follow_redirects=True, every hop gets a deadline of its own.
  • Response size: responses are read whole before they're returned, so don't stream large downloads through it. max_response_size caps the bytes read (as received, before decompression); past it, ResponseTooLargeError, an httpx.RequestError.
  • Circuit breaker: each origin (scheme, host and port) has its own. After failure_threshold consecutive failures, calls to that origin fail at once with CircuitOpenError for reset_timeout seconds, without reaching the server; then a single trial call decides whether it's back. CircuitOpenError is an httpx.TransportError, so code that already handles httpx errors handles it too. transport.state(url) says "closed", "open" or "half-open", handy in a health check. failure_threshold=None turns it off.
  • What counts as a failure: the origin's transport errors (connection and protocol errors, timeouts, yours and httpx's) and responses whose status is in failure_statuses (500, 502, 503 and 504 by default), which are still returned to you. Any other response, 4xx included, is a success. Your own errors are neither: an illegal header value (httpx.LocalProtocolError), a URL scheme httpx can't send (httpx.UnsupportedProtocol), an exception from your request body, ResponseTooLargeError. Otherwise anyone who can put a string in an outbound header could switch the integration off for everybody.
  • Your own transport settings: ResilientTransport(httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(verify=..., limits=..., proxy=...)).

docs.title: URLs your users give: SSRF
docs.text:
Calling a URL that a user typed (a webhook endpoint, a link preview, an avatar by URL) lets them make your server call its own network: http://169.254.169.254/ (the cloud's metadata service and its credentials), http://localhost:6379/, an admin panel on 10.0.0.0/8. SSRFGuardTransport only calls the public internet:

from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import (
    BlockedDestinationError,
    ResilientTransport,
    SSRFGuardTransport,
)

client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    transport=ResilientTransport(SSRFGuardTransport(ports=(443,)), timeout=10),
    follow_redirects=True,
)

try:
    await client.post(subscription.url, content=body, headers=signer.sign(body))
except BlockedDestinationError:
    ...  # tell the user the URL isn't allowed
  • What's refused: a host with any address that isn't public: private, loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16 and its metadata services, fe80::/10), carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10), multicast, reserved, documentation and benchmarking ranges, unique-local IPv6 (fc00::/7, AWS's fd00:ec2::254), and the IPv6 forms of those IPv4 addresses (::ffff:127.0.0.1, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4, Teredo). Literal addresses in URLs are checked without DNS; anything else goes to DNS, so numeric spellings (http://2130706433/, http://0x7f.1/) and localhost are refused for what they resolve to. Also refused: schemes other than http and https and, with ports, other ports. BlockedDestinationError says which host, never the address it resolved to (that's logged instead).
  • Pinned against DNS rebinding: the transport resolves the host itself and connects to the address it checked: the URL is rewritten to it, the Host header keeps the name, and TLS gets the name for SNI and the certificate check. A DNS server that answers a public address to the check and a private one to the connection gets nowhere. If the first address can't be reached, one of the other family (IPv4/IPv6) is tried.
  • Redirects: with follow_redirects=True, every hop goes through the transport and is checked like the first one.
  • Checking a URL when it's given: await guard.check(url) checks it as a request would be (scheme, port, every address its host resolves to) without sending anything, so a webhook's endpoint can be refused when a user registers it. Each request is checked again all the same: DNS answers change.
  • Allowed internal destinations: allow=["billing.internal", "*.svc.cluster.local", "10.1.2.0/24"] lets those names (exact, or subdomains) and networks through although they aren't public; they're still pinned.
  • With ResilientTransport: wrap the guard in it (not the other way round): the deadline then covers the DNS lookup and each breaker is per host name. BlockedDestinationError is an httpx.RequestError but not a TransportError, so it doesn't count against the origin's breaker or trigger retry policies.
  • Connections: each host name gets an httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport of its own (sharing one SSL context), at most max_hosts (100) kept open: pinned connections are pooled by address, and two names on one address (a CDN) must not share a connection whose certificate was checked for the other. Pass a factory for your own settings, SSRFGuardTransport(lambda: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(http2=True)), or a transport instance (a mock in tests), which then carries every request.
  • Proxies: a proxy connects on its own, so pinning can't work through it: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(proxy=...) as the inner transport is refused. Don't pass proxy= or mounts= to the client either: those requests would bypass the transport. (The client ignores the HTTP_PROXY variables when it's given a transport.) An egress proxy that filters destinations itself, such as Smokescreen, is the alternative.

docs.title: Authentication strategies
docs.text:
Who makes a request, told by strategies: JWTs, bearer tokens, sessions, logins with GitHub or any OAuth2 provider, logins with an OpenID Connect provider whose ID token is verified, single sign-on with a SAML identity provider, API keys kept by Unkey, or your own.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
FastAPIAuth tells who makes a request by strategies: each strategy knows one way (a JWT, a session, a login with GitHub…), and a dependency tries those of a route in order. The first one that finds a user gives it to the route; when none does, a 401. Each strategy has its extra:

pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-jwt]"          # JWTStrategy, with PyJWT
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oauth2]"       # OAuth2Strategy, with httpx2
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oidc]"         # OIDCStrategy, with httpx2 and PyJWT
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-saml]"         # SAMLStrategy, with signxml
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-http-bearer]"  # HTTPBearerStrategy: nothing more
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-unkey]"        # UnkeyStrategy, with httpx2

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import FastAPIAuth, SessionStrategy
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt import JWTStrategy
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.oauth2 import OAuth2Strategy

auth = FastAPIAuth()
github = auth.use(
    OAuth2Strategy(
        name="github",
        authorization_url="https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize",
        token_url="https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token",
        userinfo_url="https://api.github.com/user",
        client_id=settings.github_client_id,
        client_secret=settings.github_client_secret,
        redirect_uri="https://example.com/auth/github/callback",
        verify=find_or_create_user,  # (tokens, profile) -> your user
    )
)
sessions = auth.use(SessionStrategy(load_user))  # load_user(user_id) -> your user
tokens = auth.use(JWTStrategy(settings.jwt_secret, verify=lambda c: load_user(c["sub"])))

CurrentUser = Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("session", "jwt"))]
GitHubUser = Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("github"))]


@app.get("/me")
async def me(user: CurrentUser) -> User:  # a browser's session, or a script's token
    return user


@app.get("/login/github")
async def login() -> RedirectResponse:
    return github.redirect()  # to GitHub, which sends the user back to the callback


@app.get("/auth/github/callback")
async def callback(request: Request, user: GitHubUser) -> RedirectResponse:
    sessions.login(request, user.id)
    return RedirectResponse("/me", status_code=303)

The strategies of a dependency are tried in order. Each returns the user; None when the request doesn't carry its credentials; or raises AuthenticationFailed when they're there but wrong (logged, never sent). Either way the next one is tried. When none finds a user, a 401 with the WWW-Authenticate challenges of those tried, a WebSocket is closed with 1008, and optional=True gives None. Any other error is a 500, never a request let through. Without a dependency: await auth.user(connection). The verify and load_user functions that turn credentials into your user can be async or not, and return None to refuse them. A request is authenticated once: the dependencies of a route that ask for the same strategies get the user the first one found, so a token is decoded, and an API key verified, once.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
Routes that need scopes ask for them the FastAPI way, with Security, and the OpenAPI schema shows them:

from fastapi import Security

Writer = Annotated[User, Security(auth.authenticate("jwt"), scopes=["orders:write"])]


@app.post("/orders")
async def place_order(order: Order, user: Writer) -> Order: ...


@app.delete("/orders/{order_id}", dependencies=[Depends(auth.authenticate(scopes=["admin"]))])
async def delete_order(order_id: int) -> None: ...
  • Granted by the strategy that found the user: JWTStrategy grants the token's scope (a string separated by spaces, RFC 9068) and scp (a list: Entra ID, Okta); scope_claims= names others (Auth0's permissions). HTTPBearerStrategy grants what scopes_of(user) gives. Your own strategy calls self.grant(connection, scopes). Sessions and logins grant none: a route that needs scopes refuses them. granted_scopes(request) tells a route what was granted.
  • A missing scope is a 403 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="orders:write" (RFC 6750) for Bearer strategies; a WebSocket is closed with 1008.
  • API keys of FastAPIAPIKeys have scopes of their own: keys.require("orders:read"). Unkey's have their permissions, which UnkeyStrategy(permissions=...) asks Unkey about.

docs.title: In the audit trail
docs.text:
FastAPIAuth(audit=audit) sends a FastAPIAudit what security reviews ask for, with the request's route, client and ID:

  • auth.failure: credentials there but wrong, with the strategy; never the reason's text, which may carry what the client sent.
  • auth.login: a login by OAuth2, OpenID Connect or SAML, with who logged in.
  • auth.scope: a request without a scope it needed, with the scopes missing.

Each request authenticated isn't recorded, nor those without credentials: they'd bury the rest. actor= tells who a user is (its ID); by default the user itself when it's an ID, else its sub or id.

Each strategy has its page:

  • JWTStrategy: JWTs, the app's own or an identity provider's.
  • OAuth2Strategy: logins with GitHub or any OAuth2 provider.
  • OIDCStrategy: logins with an OpenID Connect provider (Google, Entra ID, Keycloak, Okta…), its ID token verified.
  • SessionStrategy: the user kept in the session at login.
  • HTTPBearerStrategy: opaque bearer tokens that your function looks up.
  • SAMLStrategy: single sign-on with a SAML identity provider.
  • UnkeyStrategy: API keys that Unkey keeps, with their permissions, credits and rate limits.
  • Your own strategy: an API key, a client certificate, a signed request…

docs.title: HTTPBearerStrategy
docs.text:
Opaque bearer tokens that your function looks up: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-http-bearer]", which installs nothing more.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

HTTPBearerStrategy takes opaque tokens of Authorization: Bearer, which your verify(token) looks up (in a database, at the provider's introspection endpoint). It needs no other library.

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import HTTPBearerStrategy


async def find_token(token: str) -> User | None:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()  # store digests, not tokens
    return await db.user_by_token_digest(digest)


bearer = auth.use(HTTPBearerStrategy(find_token))

A token that isn't RFC 6750's syntax, or longer than 4 KiB, fails without reaching verify. scopes_of(user) gives the scopes it grants (its row's, the introspection's scope), for the routes that need some: Scopes. Keep digests of the tokens, not the tokens. Behind a JWTStrategy, JWTs go to that one and opaque tokens to this one.

docs.title: JWTStrategy
docs.text:
JWTs, the app's own or an identity provider's: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-jwt]".

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

JWTStrategy reads the token of Authorization: Bearer (or of the cookie named by cookie=) and verifies it with PyJWT: the signature, exp, nbf and the required claims (exp, sub), and aud and iss when given; a token with an aud is refused when no audience is set, as it's meant for another service. alg: none never, and each key verifies with its own algorithm only: a public key taken for an HMAC secret would let anyone sign.

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import TokenBlocklist
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt import JWTStrategy

# The app's own tokens, signed with the first secret; the second one still verifies.
tokens = auth.use(
    JWTStrategy(
        [settings.jwt_secret, settings.previous_jwt_secret],
        verify=lambda claims: load_user(claims["sub"]),
        blocklist=TokenBlocklist(),
    )
)
token = tokens.issue(str(user.id), expires_in=900)

# An identity provider's tokens, with its public keys.
idp = auth.use(
    JWTStrategy(
        jwks_url="https://idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
        algorithms=["RS256"],
        audience="https://api.example.com",
        issuer="https://idp.example.com/",
        name="idp",
    )
)
  • Keys: HMAC secrets have at least 32 bytes and rotate with a list; keys of any type rotate with keys= (see "Rotating keys"); an identity provider's keys come from its JWKS (jwks_url=, see "An identity provider's keys"), with the audience and issuer it requires: a provider signs the tokens of every app it serves with the same keys.
  • Revoked tokens: blocklist= refuses the tokens revoked in a TokenBlocklist (see "Revoked tokens and one-time codes").
  • Issuing: issue(subject, expires_in=900) signs one, with iat, exp, a random jti, and its key's kid in the header.
  • Scopes: the token grants those of its scope (a string separated by spaces) and scp (a list) claims, for the routes that need some (Scopes); scope_claims= names others. A claim that isn't scopes refuses the token.
  • OpenAPI: it shows in the schema, for the docs' Authorize button.

docs.title: Rotating keys
docs.text:
Asymmetric keys (RS256, PS256, ES256, EdDSA) let other services verify the app's tokens with the public key alone. keys= takes JWTKeys, each pinned to one algorithm: the first one signs, all of them verify.

from datetime import UTC, datetime

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt import JWTKey, JWTStrategy

tokens = auth.use(
    JWTStrategy(
        keys=[
            JWTKey(settings.jwt_private_key, algorithm="ES256"),  # the new one: it signs
            JWTKey(
                settings.previous_jwt_private_key,
                algorithm="RS256",
                until=datetime(2026, 12, 1, tzinfo=UTC),  # the rotation + the tokens' lifetime
            ),
        ],
        blocklist=TokenBlocklist(),
    )
)
  • One deploy rotates: put the new key first and give the old one an until. Tokens it signed keep working until then, and are refused after; remove it from the list whenever you like.
  • Key ids: each token names its key in its header (kid), and is verified with that key only. A kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of a public key by default, or an HMAC of a constant for a secret, which reveals nothing of it; JWTKey(..., kid="2026-11") gives one. Tokens without a kid, or with one no key has (another issuer's own ids), are tried with the keys whose kid wasn't given.
  • Private or public: a private key signs, and its public part verifies; a public key only verifies (can_issue is then False): a service that checks another's tokens.
  • From HS256 to RS256: HMAC and asymmetric keys can be in one list, since each verifies with its own algorithm: [JWTKey(private_key, algorithm="RS256"), JWTKey(secret, algorithm="HS256", until=...)].
  • Publishing the public keys: jwks() gives them as a JWKS, with their kids, the retiring ones included and the HMAC secrets never:
@app.get("/.well-known/jwks.json", include_in_schema=False)
async def jwks() -> dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    return tokens.jwks()

key= and algorithms= are the short form for one key (or a list of HMAC secrets).

docs.title: An identity provider's keys
docs.text:
With jwks_url=, the provider's public keys are fetched from its JWKS (HTTPS, or http://localhost in development) and each token is verified with the one its kid names:

  • Kept: for jwks_lifespan seconds (300); then fetched again.
  • A kid it doesn't have (the provider rotated its keys) makes it fetched again, at most every 30 seconds: made-up kids don't make the app call the provider on every request. A token with a kid the provider doesn't have is a 401.
  • Never in the way: fetched asynchronously, within jwks_timeout (3 s) for the whole fetch, with a circuit breaker for the provider (ResilientTransport); requests that need the keys while they're fetched wait for that one fetch.
  • The provider down: the keys fetched before are still used for jwks_stale seconds (an hour) past their lifespan, retried every 30 seconds. Then the requests get a 503 (Retry-After: 30; WebSockets close with 1013): never let through, nor told to log in again. Each fetch is counted in fastapi_alcazaba.auth.jwks, by outcome (fetched, failed).
  • Which keys: signing keys only (no use: enc), never HMAC ones (oct), with their alg when they say one; algorithms are the provider's (RS256, ES256, PS256 and EdDSA by default).
  • Shutting down: await strategy.aclose() in the lifespan closes the client it made; jwks_client= gives one of your own (a proxy, your TLS settings).

docs.title: Refresh tokens
docs.text:
Access tokens should be short (15 minutes), but users shouldn't log in every 15 minutes. RefreshTokens gives each login a refresh token as well, which gets a new pair when the access token expires:

from fastapi import HTTPException

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import RefreshRefused, RefreshTokens, TokenBlocklist, TokenPair
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt import JWTStrategy

tokens = auth.use(JWTStrategy(settings.jwt_secret, blocklist=TokenBlocklist()))
refresh_tokens = RefreshTokens(tokens, secret=settings.refresh_secret)


@app.post("/token")
async def log_in(form: Login) -> TokenPair:
    user = await check_password(form)
    return await refresh_tokens.issue(user.id, scope="read write")


@app.post("/token/refresh")
async def refresh(body: Refresh) -> TokenPair:
    try:
        return await refresh_tokens.exchange(body.refresh_token)
    except RefreshRefused:
        raise HTTPException(401, "Log in again") from None  # never say why


@app.delete("/token", status_code=204)
async def log_out(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(auth.authenticate("jwt"))]) -> None:
    await refresh_tokens.revoke_session(claims["sid"])
  • Rotation: each exchange gives a new pair and uses the refresh token up. A login (a family) has an id, the access tokens' sid claim; its claims (scope above) go into every access token it gets.
  • A copied token ends the login: a refresh token already exchanged that comes back was copied, by a thief or from the user. Whoever comes second, the login ends: its refresh token and its access tokens are refused, and it's logged, counted (fastapi_alcazaba.refresh, outcome reused) and audited. The user logs in again; the thief is out.
  • Grace: within grace seconds (10) of an exchange, the token just exchanged gets the newest refresh token again, with a new access token: tabs or requests that refresh at once all end up with one token. After that, it's a copy.
  • Lifetimes: a login lasts lifetime (30 days) from the password, and idle (7 days) without a refresh; access_ttl (900 s) is the access tokens'.
  • Clients: issue(..., client="ios") binds the login to a client; an exchange must give the same client=, and a token presented by another one ends the login.
  • Logging out: revoke(refresh_token) with the refresh token, revoke_session(sid) with an access token's sid (a list of the user's devices, an operator), revoke_subject(user_id) everywhere (after a password change; the login started during that second stays, for the session that changed it). The strategy's TokenBlocklist refuses the access tokens until they expire, so it must have one.
  • Nothing stored makes a token: a refresh token is r1.<family>.<generation>.<MAC>, the MAC made with secret. The backend keeps one record per login, with a random salt, never a token: whoever reads it can't make one. Every generation can be checked, so a forged token naming a real family (its id is in every access token) is refused without ending anything. secret is a list to rotate it, as the strategy's key.
  • One exchange at a time: each login's exchanges hold its lock, so the backend must hold locks (every shipped backend does). If the backend fails, nothing is issued: BackendUnavailable.
  • Where clients keep it: a refresh token is a password for 30 days. Browsers: an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to the refresh route, not JavaScript's storage; apps: the keychain. That's up to the app; nothing here enforces it.
  • RefreshRefused has a reason (malformed, unknown, forged, expired, revoked, reused, wrong_client) for your logs, never for the client.

docs.title: OAuth2Strategy
docs.text:
Logins with GitHub or any OAuth2 provider: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oauth2]". For an OpenID Connect provider (Google, Entra ID, Keycloak…), OIDCStrategy verifies its ID token too.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried, and the code of a login with GitHub: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

OAuth2Strategy logs people in with the authorization code flow and PKCE, for any OAuth2 provider (GitHub, GitLab…). It doesn't verify an id_token the provider may send: don't rely on its claims, and use OIDCStrategy, which does, for OpenID Connect providers.

  • The login: redirect() sends the browser to the provider with a random state; the state and the PKCE verifier wait in a cookie for 10 minutes (__Host-, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax).
  • The callback: the strategy checks the state, so that nobody can log a user in with their own account (login CSRF); exchanges the code, with the app's credentials by HTTP Basic (client_auth="post" in the form); reads userinfo_url; and calls verify(tokens, profile). It only goes on the callback route: elsewhere it finds nobody.
  • The provider: its URLs are HTTPS (or http://localhost); a provider that doesn't answer is a 502.

docs.title: OIDCStrategy
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

Logins with an OpenID Connect provider (Google, Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, Zitadel…), whose ID token is verified before your code sees its claims: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oidc]", which installs httpx2 and PyJWT.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

OIDCStrategy is OAuth2Strategy's login (the authorization code flow, PKCE and a state in a __Host- cookie), plus what OpenID Connect adds: a nonce, the provider's endpoints and keys from its issuer, and the ID token verified as OpenID Connect Core says.

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.oidc import OIDCStrategy


def find_or_create_user(claims: dict[str, Any], userinfo: dict[str, Any] | None) -> User | None:
    user_id = f"{claims['iss']}#{claims['sub']}"  # unique and stable; an e-mail address isn't
    return db.users.get(user_id) or db.users.create(user_id, email=claims.get("email"))


google = auth.use(
    OIDCStrategy(
        name="google",
        issuer="https://accounts.google.com",
        client_id=settings.google_client_id,
        client_secret=settings.google_client_secret,
        redirect_uri="https://example.com/auth/google/callback",
        verify=find_or_create_user,
    )
)


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    await google.discover()  # its endpoints and keys: the app doesn't start without them
    yield
  • Discovery: await discover() reads the issuer's /.well-known/openid-configuration, whose issuer must be issuer exactly: a document of another issuer would have its tokens accepted as this one's. Its endpoints are HTTPS (or http://localhost); those given to the strategy (token_url=, a proxy…) win, and with authorization_url, token_url and jwks_url there's nothing to discover.
  • The ID token: refused unless it's signed by a key of the provider's JWKS with one of algorithms (RS256, ES256, PS256, EdDSA; never none, nor HS256 with the client secret, which the provider knows too); its iss is the issuer; its aud has client_id, and its azp is it when there are several audiences or an azp; exp hasn't passed and iat isn't in the future (leeway, 60 s); it carries the nonce of this login, kept in the state cookie; its at_hash, when it has one, is the access token's; and with max_age=600, its auth_time is at most 10 minutes old. A provider that sends no ID token is refused.
  • The keys: fetched from jwks_uri and kept for jwks_lifespan (an hour). A token whose kid isn't among them makes them fetched again, the provider having rotated its keys, but at most every 30 seconds: made-up kids don't make the app fetch them on every request. Keys for encryption (use: enc) don't verify signatures.
  • Userinfo: with userinfo=True, the userinfo endpoint is read too, for claims the ID token doesn't carry, and refused when its sub isn't the ID token's.
  • The user: verify(claims, userinfo) gets the verified claims, and returns your user or None to refuse the login; by default the user is the claims. Key users by iss and sub, never by e-mail address, and refuse email_verified: false when you use the address.
  • Failures: each check that fails refuses the login with a 401, the reason in the log (at INFO, by FastAPIAuth); a provider that doesn't answer is a 502.

OAuth2Strategy doesn't verify the id_token it may get: for an OpenID Connect provider, use this one.

docs.title: Logging out
docs.text:
Ending the app's session doesn't end the provider's: the next login there goes through without a password. Two ways to end both, from either side.

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import UserSessions

user_sessions = UserSessions()  # given to ServerSessionMiddleware(users=user_sessions)
keycloak = auth.use(
    OIDCStrategy(
        ...,
        post_logout_redirect_uris=["https://app.example.com/logged-out"],
    )
)


@app.get("/auth/callback")
async def callback(request: Request, user: Annotated[dict, Depends(auth.authenticate("keycloak"))]):
    sessions.login(request, user["sub"])
    request.session["oidc_sid"] = user.get("sid")  # which login: for back-channel logout
    request.session["id_token"] = request.state.id_token  # for logout_url's hint
    ...


@app.post("/logout")
async def logout(request: Request) -> RedirectResponse:
    id_token = request.session.get("id_token")
    clear_session(request)
    url = keycloak.logout_url(
        id_token_hint=id_token, post_logout_redirect_uri="https://app.example.com/logged-out"
    )
    return RedirectResponse(url, status_code=303)


# The provider tells the app when the user logged out there (or an admin ended the session).
app.post("/auth/backchannel-logout")(keycloak.backchannel_logout_endpoint(user_sessions))
  • From the app (RP-Initiated Logout): logout_url() is the provider's end_session_endpoint (from discovery, or end_session_url=) with the app's client_id, the login's ID token as id_token_hint (the provider ends that session without asking), and a post_logout_redirect_uri, which must be one of post_logout_redirect_uris, as registered there: never one from the request, which would be an open redirect. state comes back with it. The raw ID token is in request.state.id_token once the callback is authenticated.
  • From the provider (Back-Channel Logout): register the endpoint's URL at the provider. It takes the provider's logout token, verifies it (signed by the provider's keys with one of algorithms, its iss, its aud, issued in the last 5 minutes, a jti, the logout event, a sub or a sid, no nonce), takes it once (its jti, in the cache's backend), and ends the app's sessions of that login: those whose oidc_sid is the token's sid, or, with a sub only, every session of the user (user_id= maps the provider's sub to yours). It answers 200, or 400 invalid_request with the reason in the log, never in the answer.
  • Without a client secret: client_auth="private_key_jwt" with client_key=JWTKey(private_key, algorithm="ES256", kid="app-1") authenticates to the token endpoint with a JWT signed by the app's key (RFC 7523): give the provider the public key (the JWKS of a JWTStrategy(keys=[...]), jwks()), and no secret is shared.
  • Not yet: front-channel logout (an iframe per app), PAR and DPoP.

docs.title: SAMLStrategy
docs.text:
Single sign-on with a SAML identity provider: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-saml]".

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

SAMLStrategy is SAML 2.0 single sign-on with an identity provider (Okta, Entra ID, ADFS, Keycloak…):

  • The login: redirect() sends the browser to the IdP with an AuthnRequest; the IdP posts its answer to the ACS route.
  • The answer: the strategy verifies its XML signature with the IdP's certificate (signxml, SHA-2 only, no DTDs). Then, on what the signature covers and nothing else (signature wrapping), it checks the issuer, the audience (entity_id), the recipient (acs_url), the request it answers and when it's valid.
  • Once: each assertion works once: it's kept in the cache's backend until it expires, and logins are refused when the backend fails.
  • Metadata: metadata() is the app's metadata, for the IdP.
  • Not supported: logins the IdP starts, encrypted assertions, signed requests, single logout.

The SAML request's id waits in a SameSite=None cookie, because the IdP posts the answer from its own site; for the same reason CSRFMiddleware must let the ACS through:

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.saml import SAMLStrategy

saml = auth.use(
    SAMLStrategy(
        entity_id="https://example.com/saml/metadata",  # this app, at the IdP
        acs_url="https://example.com/saml/acs",
        idp_entity_id=settings.idp_entity_id,
        idp_sso_url=settings.idp_sso_url,
        idp_certificate=settings.idp_certificate,  # PEM; a list while it rotates
        verify=find_or_create_user,  # (SAMLProfile) -> your user
    )
)
SAMLUser = Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("saml"))]
app.add_middleware(CSRFMiddleware, exempt_paths=["/saml/acs"])  # the IdP posts it


@app.get("/saml/login")
async def saml_login() -> RedirectResponse:
    return saml.redirect()


@app.post("/saml/acs")
async def saml_acs(request: Request, user: SAMLUser) -> RedirectResponse:
    sessions.login(request, user.id)
    return RedirectResponse("/me", status_code=303)


@app.get("/saml/metadata")
async def saml_metadata() -> Response:
    return Response(saml.metadata(), media_type="application/samlmetadata+xml")

docs.title: SessionStrategy
docs.text:
The user kept in the session at login, for the browsers of an app's users.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried, and the code of a login that starts a session: Strategies. The sessions themselves: Sessions, CSRF and security headers. Every argument: the API reference.

SessionStrategy finds the user id that sessions.login(request, user_id) kept in the session, and loads the user with load_user. With ServerSessionMiddleware the session gets a new id at login (no session fixation), and sessions.logout(request) deletes it from the backend. A session whose user doesn't exist any more fails.

docs.title: UnkeyStrategy
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

API keys that Unkey keeps and verifies, with their permissions, credits and rate limits: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-unkey]", which installs httpx2.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

UnkeyStrategy reads the key of Authorization: Bearer (or of a header, header="X-API-Key") and asks Unkey's API to verify it (keys.verifyKey, v2) on every request. UnkeyKeys issues and deletes them, for the page where your users make theirs.

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import FastAPIAuth
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies import UnkeyStrategy
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.unkey import UnkeyClient, UnkeyKey, UnkeyKeys

# A root key for each use, with only the permissions it needs.
verifier = UnkeyClient(settings.unkey_verify_key)  # may only verify keys
keys = UnkeyKeys(UnkeyClient(settings.unkey_admin_key), api_id=settings.unkey_api_id)


async def load_user(key: UnkeyKey) -> User | None:
    return await db.users.get(key.external_id)  # the ID given when the key was made


auth = FastAPIAuth(
    UnkeyStrategy(verifier, load_user, permissions="documents.read"),
    UnkeyStrategy(verifier, load_user, name="unkey-write", permissions="documents.write", cost=5),
)


@app.post("/documents", dependencies=[Depends(auth.authenticate("unkey-write"))])
async def write_document(document: Document) -> Document: ...
  • What Unkey answers: VALID gives the user, verify(key) with an UnkeyKey (its id, external_id, meta, credits left, permissions, roles, rate limits), or the UnkeyKey itself without verify. A key that doesn't exist, is disabled or expired fails, a 401, or the next strategy is tried. One without the permissions (permissions=, Unkey's query syntax: "a AND (b OR c)") gets a 403; one over its rate limit, a 429 with Retry-After; one out of credits, a 429, or a 402 with credits_status=402. A code this version doesn't know fails, with a warning: nothing but VALID lets a request through.
  • Each route its permissions: a strategy has one query and one cost; a route that needs others has a strategy of its own, with another name and the same client.
  • Credits and rate limits: each verification spends cost credits (1 by default, 0 for none) of keys that have a limit, and counts in the key's rate limits; ratelimits=["tokens"] applies others by name. Nothing is cached: a key deleted or disabled is refused at once (Unkey takes up to 30 seconds to spread a deletion), and the credits are right.
  • Fails closed: each call has a deadline (timeout, 2 seconds) and Unkey a circuit breaker (ResilientTransport). Unkey down, slow or limiting the workspace (its 429) is a 503 for the request (1013 for a WebSocket), never let through. A root key that may not verify raises UnkeyError: a 500, a mistake to fix.
  • Not sent: a key that isn't a token (spaces, non-ASCII, longer than 512 characters) fails without reaching Unkey, and no key is ever logged.
  • Counted: each verification in fastapi_alcazaba.auth.unkey, by strategy and Unkey's code, and unavailable when it didn't answer.

docs.title: Issuing and deleting keys
docs.text:
created = await keys.create(
    external_id=user.id,
    name="Ana's laptop",
    credits_left=1_000,
    refill=CreditRefill(1_000, day=1),  # back to 1,000 on the 1st of each month
    ratelimits=[KeyRatelimit("requests", 100, timedelta(minutes=1))],
    permissions=["documents.read"],
    expires=datetime(2027, 1, 1, tzinfo=UTC),
)
show_once(created.key.get_secret_value())  # Unkey keeps only its hash
await db.keys.add(user.id, created.key_id)

await keys.delete(created.key_id)  # its verifications fail within 30 seconds
  • Shown once: created.key is a SecretStr, kept out of logs and reprs: show it to its owner and forget it. Keep key_id, to delete it later, and check that a key belongs to the user who asks to delete it.
  • Two root keys: give UnkeyStrategy a root key that may only verify, and UnkeyKeys another that may create and delete: a leak of the first can't make keys.
  • Close them: await client.aclose() in the lifespan, at shutdown, for the clients UnkeyClient made.

docs.title: Your own strategy
docs.text:
An API key, a client certificate, a signed request…: any way to tell who makes a request.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

Your own strategy (an API key, a client certificate, a signed request…) is a Strategy whose authenticate() returns the user, None, or raises AuthenticationFailed; challenge and openapi_scheme() are optional:

from fastapi import HTTPException
from starlette.requests import HTTPConnection

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import AuthenticationFailed, FastAPIAPIKeys, Strategy


class APIKeyStrategy(Strategy):
    challenge = "APIKey"

    def __init__(self, keys: FastAPIAPIKeys[Any]) -> None:
        super().__init__("api-key")
        self.keys = keys

    async def authenticate(self, connection: HTTPConnection) -> Any:
        key = connection.headers.get("x-api-key")
        if key is None:
            return None  # not this strategy's: the next one is tried
        try:
            return await self.keys.authenticate(key)
        except HTTPException as exc:  # FastAPIAPIKeys' 401
            raise AuthenticationFailed("invalid API key") from exc


auth.use(APIKeyStrategy(keys))
# For routes that need scopes, grant those of the key: self.grant(connection, record.scopes)

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Who may do what to which resource, decided by a policy per route or for every request, instead of checks spread over the routes.

In an app: the examples. Every class and function: the API reference.

FastAPIAuthz is a dependency that lets a request through only when the policy allows it, and AuthzMiddleware checks every request. Neither is tied to an engine: they take an enforcer, anything with enforce(subject, *values) -> bool, or async def enforce for an engine that answers through the network, which they await.

  • In process: the engine runs in your app, with the policy in memory: no network, a few microseconds per check.
    • Casbin: a model and a policy (ACL, RBAC, RBAC with domains, ABAC), its enforcers as they are. The casbin extra.
    • Cedar: policies in Cedar's language, validated against a schema, with entities and their attributes; a forbid beats every permit. The cedar extra.
  • As a separate service: a policy decision point that the app asks over the network, shared by every service; when it doesn't answer, a 503.
    • Open Policy Agent: policies in Rego, queried through its REST API. The opa extra.
from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import FastAPIAuthz

authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_username)  # your dependency: who's asking

# (user, path, method): may ana PUT /articles/7?
api = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(authz)])


# (user, *values): your own objects and actions. Both dependencies return the user.
@app.post("/articles/{article_id}/publish")
async def publish(
    article_id: int,
    editor: Annotated[str, Depends(authz.require("articles", "publish"))],
) -> Article: ...


# {name} takes a path parameter: (user, "projects/7", "archive").
archive = authz.require("projects/{project_id}", "archive")


@app.post("/projects/{project_id}/archive", dependencies=[Depends(archive)])
async def archive_project(project_id: int) -> None: ...
  • Who: subject is a FastAPI dependency that returns who makes the request: a user name, an id, or what the engine reads attributes from (an object for Casbin's ABAC matchers, an entity for Cedar); None when nobody is logged in. Its own dependencies (a bearer token, a session) appear in the OpenAPI schema, for the docs' Authorize button. Without one, the user of Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware (its identity).
  • What: Depends(authz) checks the path the app routes (without the root_path a proxy or a mount adds in front) and the method: GET for HEAD, which runs the GET route, and WEBSOCKET for WebSockets, so a policy for GET doesn't open them. authz.require(...) checks your own values instead, {name} filled from the path parameters.
  • Answers: a request without a subject gets a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer (challenge=), without asking the policy; anonymous="*anonymous" has the policy check it as that subject instead, for routes open to everybody: a name no user can have, or whoever signs up as it gets its rules. A subject that the policy refuses gets a 403. WebSockets are closed with 1008 (policy violation). A path with control characters (/users/%0A) gets a 400 without asking the policy: Starlette routes it to /users/, while the policy would read the newline. With FastAPIProblemDetails, the errors are problem details.
  • In a route: await authz.enforce(user, "drafts", "read") returns a bool, for what depends on the data: the items of a list, the owner of an object.
  • Counted: every decision in the fastapi_alcazaba.authz metric, by outcome (allowed, denied, unauthenticated, unavailable): a burst of denied is someone probing.
  • In the audit trail: with audit= (a FastAPIAudit), each request the policy refuses is an authz.denied event (the 403s, and the 400s of paths with control characters), and each one the engine couldn't decide an authz.unavailable, with who asked (actor=, subject_id by default: an ID, a Cedar entity's id, a sub, id or name), what (the path, or the values of require), the route and the client. Not the 401s of requests without a subject, nor enforce()'s checks in a route.

AuthzMiddleware checks every request instead, as (user, path, method) with the user of Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware, and refuses requests without one. Add it before AuthenticationMiddleware, so that it runs after it. With anonymous="*anonymous", those are checked as that subject, and the policy opens the public routes (/docs, /login…) to it:

from starlette.middleware.authentication import AuthenticationMiddleware

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import AuthzMiddleware

app.add_middleware(AuthzMiddleware, enforcer=enforcer, anonymous="*anonymous")
app.add_middleware(AuthenticationMiddleware, backend=JWTBackend())

Refusals get a 403 with {"detail": "Forbidden"}, like FastAPI's errors, or a 401 with WWW-Authenticate when there's no user (or anonymous is refused), and a 400 for paths with control characters; WebSockets are closed with 1008. OPTIONS requests are checked like the others: add CORSMiddleware after AuthzMiddleware (outside it), to answer the preflights.

docs.title: Casbin
docs.text:
Who may do what, in a Casbin model and policy (ACL, RBAC, RBAC with domains, ABAC…), checked in the process by FastAPIAuthz and AuthzMiddleware.

In an app: the example. How the dependency and the middleware work: Authorization. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Casbin policies
docs.text:
The casbin extra installs PyCasbin, and its enforcers go to FastAPIAuthz as they are.

A Casbin model says what a request is and how it matches the policy; the policy, who may do what. Here a request is (user, object, action), and users get permissions through roles:

model.conf
[request_definition]
r = sub, obj, act

[policy_definition]
p = sub, obj, act

[role_definition]
g = _, _

[policy_effect]
e = some(where (p.eft == allow))

[matchers]
m = g(r.sub, p.sub) && keyMatch2(r.obj, p.obj) && r.act == p.act
policy.csv
p, reader, /articles/:id, GET
p, editor, /articles/:id, PUT
p, editor, articles, publish
g, editor, reader
g, ana, editor

import casbin

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import FastAPIAuthz

enforcer = casbin.Enforcer("model.conf", "policy.csv")
authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_username)  # your dependency: who's asking

# (user, path, method): may ana PUT /articles/7?
api = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(authz)])


# (user, *values): your own objects and actions. Both dependencies return the user.
@app.post("/articles/{article_id}/publish")
async def publish(
    article_id: int,
    editor: Annotated[str, Depends(authz.require("articles", "publish"))],
) -> Article: ...


# {name} takes a path parameter: (user, "projects/7", "archive").
archive = authz.require("projects/{project_id}", "archive")


@app.post("/projects/{project_id}/archive", dependencies=[Depends(archive)])
async def archive_project(project_id: int) -> None: ...
  • Names in keyMatch2: :name is a parameter, so name objects without colons (projects/7, not project:7), or the rule for project:7 lets project:8 through.
  • Visitors: with anonymous="*anonymous", p, *anonymous, /catalog, GET opens a route to everybody.
  • Fails closed: a broken model, or a request that doesn't fit it (invalid request size), raises: a 500, never a request let through. A disabled enforcer (enforcer.enable_enforce(False)) lets everything through, as Casbin does.
  • Enforcers: any of Casbin's: Enforcer, SyncedEnforcer, FastEnforcer, AsyncEnforcer (for async adapters; await enforcer.load_policy() in the lifespan). The checks run in the event loop, like an AsyncEnforcer's changes: a request never sees half a change. Casbin tries the rules one by one, a few microseconds each (about 2.5 ms per request with 1,000 rules on a laptop): give permissions to roles rather than users, and roles to users.
  • Several processes: each one has its copy of the policy. A change made in one (await enforcer.add_role_for_user(...)) reaches the database through the adapter, and the other processes when they load the policy again: a Casbin watcher (casbin-redis-watcher…) tells them.

docs.title: Cedar
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

Who may do what, in Cedar's policy language, evaluated in the process by CedarEnforcer for FastAPIAuthz and AuthzMiddleware. The cedar extra installs cedarpy, the bindings of Cedar's engine.

In an app: the example. How the dependency and the middleware work: Authorization. Every class and function: the API reference.

A Cedar policy permits or forbids a principal an action on a resource, with conditions on their attributes; what no policy permits is denied, and a forbid beats every permit:

policies.cedar
// The members of a document's team read it.
permit (principal, action == Action::"read", resource)
when { principal.team == resource.team };

// Its owner reads and edits it.
permit (principal, action in [Action::"read", Action::"edit"], resource)
when { resource.owner == principal };

// Admins delete documents.
permit (principal in Role::"admin", action == Action::"delete", resource == Resource::"documents");

// Contractors never see a confidential document, whatever else allows it.
forbid (principal, action, resource)
when { principal.contractor && resource is Document && resource.confidential };

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import FastAPIAuthz
from fastapi_alcazaba.authz.cedar import CedarEnforcer

enforcer = CedarEnforcer(
    Path("policies.cedar").read_text(),
    entities=[{"uid": {"type": "Role", "id": "admin"}, "attrs": {}, "parents": []}],
    schema=Path("schema.cedarschema").read_text(),  # the policies are validated against it
)
authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_user)  # returns the user's entity


@app.get("/documents/{document_id}")
async def read_document(document_id: int, user: SignedIn) -> Document:
    document = await load_document(document_id)
    if document is None or not await authz.enforce(user, document_entity(document), "read"):
        raise HTTPException(404, "No such document")
    return document
  • The requests: FastAPIAuthz's (subject, object, action) become Cedar's (principal, action, resource). A name is an entity of principal_type (User), action_type (Action) or resource_type (Resource): Depends(authz) asks whether User::"ana" may Action::"PUT" the resource Resource::"/articles/7", and authz.require("documents", "delete") about Resource::"documents". Each resource named so gets an id attribute, its name, so that a policy matches paths: when { resource.id like "/articles/*" }.
  • Entities: what the policies read about the principal and the resource. entities= are those of every request (roles and their hierarchy, resources with their attributes). enforce also takes a whole entity instead of a name ({"uid": ..., "attrs": ..., "parents": [...]}): the user your authentication loaded, with its roles as parents, and the row the route just read. entities_of(subject) adds others for each request: a plain function for what's at hand, an async def for what it reads from the database. An entity given twice (in entities= and by the route) must be the same both times, or enforce raises ValueError, a 500: neither copy wins, as a forbid would depend on which.
  • context: await authz.enforce(user, resource, "deploy", {"hour": now.hour}) gives the policies context.hour.
  • A schema (schema=, in Cedar's language or JSON) validates the policies when the enforcer is made: a misspelled attribute or an action that doesn't apply to a type raises ValueError at start, not a wrong answer later. The entities are checked against it too. Invalid policies raise too.
  • Fails closed: a policy that can't be evaluated (an attribute an entity doesn't have, an entity that doesn't exist) refuses the request, with a warning that says why. Cedar on its own skips such a policy, and a forbid that fails would let the request through.
  • Several processes: each one evaluates its own copy of the policies, made at start: to change them, deploy them, or make a new CedarEnforcer when they change.

docs.title: Open Policy Agent
docs.text:
Experimental

New in 0.6: its API may still change in any release, as its use shows what's missing. Scope and stability lists the tools that are settled.

Who may do what, in Open Policy Agent's policy language, Rego, decided by an OPA that runs as a service of its own: OPAEnforcer asks it through its REST API for FastAPIAuthz and AuthzMiddleware. The opa extra installs httpx2, which it asks with.

In an app: the example. What changes from an engine in the process: As a separate service. Every class and function: the API reference.

A Rego rule is true when every condition in one of its bodies is; default gives it a value when none is:

shop.rego
package shop

# Nothing is allowed unless a rule below says so.
default allow := false

# Everybody reads the catalogue, signed in or not.
allow if {
    input.action == "GET"
    input.resource == "/products"
}

# The support staff refund up to 100 euros; above that, a manager does.
allow if {
    input.action == "refund"
    "support" in input.subject.roles
    input.resource.total <= 100
}

allow if {
    input.action == "refund"
    "manager" in input.subject.roles
}

$ docker run -p 8181:8181 -v "$PWD:/policies:ro" openpolicyagent/opa:1.21.4 \
    run --server --addr 0.0.0.0:8181 /policies/shop.rego

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import FastAPIAuthz
from fastapi_alcazaba.authz.opa import OPAEnforcer

enforcer = OPAEnforcer(settings.opa_url, rule="shop.allow", token=settings.opa_token)
authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_user)  # returns the user, with its roles


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    yield
    await enforcer.aclose()


@app.post("/orders/{order_id}/refund")
async def refund_order(order_id: int, user: SignedIn) -> Order:
    order = await load_order(order_id)
    if not await authz.enforce(user, order.model_dump(), "refund"):
        raise HTTPException(403, "Refunds are for the support staff, and a manager above 100 euros")
    ...
  • The query: each check asks for rule (shop.allow, the rule allow of package shop) with the input {"subject": ..., "resource": ..., "action": ..., "context": {...}}: POST /v1/data/shop/allow. Depends(authz) sends the path and the method ("/products", "GET"), authz.require("orders", "export") its values, and authz.enforce(user, order, "refund") whatever you give it, dicts with attributes too. Every value goes as JSON.
  • Only true allows: false refuses, and so does a rule that is undefined for the input, with a warning: give it a default, default allow := false. A result that isn't a boolean (a rule that names a package, a rule that gives an object) raises RuntimeError, a 500.
  • Fails closed: an OPA that doesn't answer within timeout (1 second), or answers with a 5xx, raises PolicyUnavailable, and the request gets a 503. The enforcer's own client has a circuit breaker (ResilientTransport): after 5 failures in a row, requests are refused at once for 30 seconds instead of each waiting for OPA. A query OPA refuses (a 4xx: a wrong token) raises RuntimeError, a 500: a mistake to fix, not a refusal.
  • Where it runs: next to the app, as a sidecar on localhost, so that each check stays under a millisecond. client= takes an httpx2 client of your own, for TLS to an OPA farther away or a transport of your own; aclose() only closes the enforcer's own.
  • A token: with opa run --authentication=token, OPA asks for a bearer token: token= (a SecretStr from your settings). An empty one raises ValueError at start.
  • Changing the policy: OPA loads it from files, bundles or its API, and every app that asks it sees the change at once, without a deploy of theirs.

docs.title: As a separate service
docs.text:
A policy decision point that runs apart from the app: every service of a company asks the same one, over the network, and the policies are deployed and audited in one place.

How the dependency and the middleware work: Authorization. The engines that run in the process, with no network: Casbin and Cedar.

Service Model For Open Policy Agent Policies in Rego, any model One policy language for the whole infrastructure (Kubernetes, gateways, services) OpenFGA, SpiceDB Relationships, as Google's Zanzibar Permissions that follow relationships: shared documents, organisations, teams Cerbos Policies in YAML, RBAC and ABAC Readable policies with tests of their own

What changes from an engine in the process:

  • Latency: each check is a request over the network, a fraction of a millisecond next to the service, against a few microseconds in the process. Ask once per request, not once per item of a list.
  • Failures: when the service doesn't answer, the request is refused, never let through. An enforcer raises PolicyUnavailable, and the request gets a 503 (Authorization unavailable), a WebSocket 1013 (try again later), counted as unavailable in the fastapi_alcazaba.authz metric. Each call has a deadline, and a circuit breaker stops asking a service that is down, so that requests don't each wait for it.
  • Async: a call over the network can't block the event loop. FastAPIAuthz and AuthzMiddleware await an enforce that is a coroutine function.

Open Policy Agent has an enforcer of its own, OPAEnforcer. For another service, an enforcer is a class with an async enforce, which raises PolicyUnavailable when the service doesn't answer:

import httpx2 as httpx

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import FastAPIAuthz, PolicyUnavailable
from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import ResilientTransport


class PolicyService:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        # A deadline for each call, and a circuit breaker for the service.
        self.client = httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=url, transport=ResilientTransport(timeout=0.5))

    async def enforce(self, subject: str, resource: str, action: str) -> bool:
        try:
