            response = await self.client.post(
                "/check", json={"subject": subject, "resource": resource, "action": action}
            )
        except httpx.TransportError as exc:
            raise PolicyUnavailable(f"the policy service didn't answer: {exc!r}") from exc
        if response.status_code >= 500:
            raise PolicyUnavailable(f"the policy service answered {response.status_code}")
        response.raise_for_status()  # a 4xx is a mistake to fix: a 500
        return response.json()["allowed"] is True  # only true allows


enforcer = PolicyService("http://policy-service:8080")  # enforcer.client.aclose() at shutdown
authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_username)

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: In an app: the examples. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
Seven strategies, with nothing but FastAPI and pydantic. Each is configured once and used as a dependency, which reads and checks its query parameters; the endpoint gets them as an argument, so @cache keeps each page under a key of its own:

Strategy Query parameters For PaginationPageNumber page, page_size Numbered pages, with the total PaginationOffset offset, limit Slices, with the total or without counting the list PaginationRange start, end Ranges of items, with Content-Range PaginationCursor cursor, limit Opaque, signed cursors, both ways, bound to the query: feeds, infinite scroll PaginationKeyset after, limit The key of the last item in plain sight (an id, a time, several values): syncing, public APIs PaginationScroll scroll_id, batch_size A snapshot kept in the backend, read in batches PaginationStreaming none Every item as it comes, as NDJSON

Which one: numbered pages for people who jump to page 7, PaginationOffset for slices of a list that doesn't change much (without its total when counting it is slow), PaginationCursor for feeds and lists that change while they're read, PaginationKeyset when clients sync or write their own starting point (?after=2026-10-29T10:00:00Z), and a scroll or a stream to read everything: exports, reindexing.

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.page_number import (
    PageNumberPage,
    PageNumberParams,
    PaginationPageNumber,
)

pages = PaginationPageNumber(default_page_size=20, max_page_size=100)


@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["products"])
async def products(
    params: Annotated[PageNumberParams, Depends(pages)],
) -> PageNumberPage[Product]:
    return pages.paginate(await load_products(), params)
  • By position or by key: page numbers, offsets and ranges count items, so a row added or deleted meanwhile shifts the pages (an item skipped or seen twice), and a database walks past every row before the page. Cursors and keysets point at the last item instead: the pages don't shift, and an index finds any of them as fast as the first.
  • Links: the response links to the pages around it in the Link header (RFC 8288), as GitHub's API does: </products?page=3&page_size=20>; rel="next". The links keep the request's other query parameters and leave out the host, so they don't depend on the Host header nor on a proxy in front. Pages served from the cache get them too, made for the request they answer.
  • From a database: paginate takes the whole list and finds the page in it, or the rows the database returned for the page: with their total for the strategies that count, or queried=True for the others, which fetch one row more (params.fetch) to tell whether there's a next page.
  • Limits: each strategy has its own maximum (100 items by default), so that nobody asks for a million rows at once: anything beyond, or malformed, is a 422 before the endpoint runs. They're in the OpenAPI schema too.
  • Cached: every page, size and filter is one entry: tag them (tags=["products"]) to drop them all when the data changes. For short lists, caching the whole list with get_or_set and slicing every page from it keeps a single entry. The pagination example does it three ways, with the database session left out of the key (exclude_params).

Each strategy has its page:

  • PaginationPageNumber: numbered pages, with the total: ?page=2&page_size=20.
  • PaginationOffset: slices, with the total or without it: ?offset=40&limit=20.
  • PaginationRange: ranges of items, with Content-Range: ?start=0&end=24.
  • PaginationCursor: opaque, signed cursors, both ways: ?cursor=...&limit=20.
  • PaginationKeyset: the key of the last item, readable: ?after=42&limit=20.
  • PaginationScroll: a snapshot kept in the backend, read in batches: ?scroll_id=....
  • PaginationStreaming: every item as it comes, as NDJSON, without pages.

And for the queries: With SQLAlchemy, page_query and count_query from the parameters of any strategy.

docs.title: PaginationCursor
docs.text:
Opaque, signed cursors, both ways, bound to the query: ?cursor=...&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

A cursor points at the item at the edge of a page by its sort key, not by its position: rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages (no item skipped or seen twice), and a database finds any page through an index, from either side, as fast as the first. Cursors are the way to the next and previous pages and nothing else: opaque, signed, bound to the query they were issued for and, with a ttl, short-lived. For feeds, infinite scroll, lists with "Previous" and "Next", and public APIs whose pagination may change behind the cursor without breaking anybody:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.cursor import CursorPage, CursorParams, PaginationCursor

cursors = PaginationCursor(settings.cursor_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/events")
@cache(expire=60)
async def events(
    params: Annotated[CursorParams, Depends(cursors)],
    kind: Kind | None = None,
) -> CursorPage[Event]:
    key = tuple_(Event.created_at, Event.id)
    if params.before is not None:  # the page before: the nearest rows first
        query = select(Event).where(key < params.before)
        query = query.order_by(Event.created_at.desc(), Event.id.desc())
    else:
        query = select(Event).order_by(Event.created_at, Event.id)
        if params.after is not None:
            query = query.where(key > params.after)
    if kind is not None:
        query = query.where(Event.kind == kind)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query.limit(params.fetch))).all()
    return cursors.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda e: (e.created_at, e.id), queried=True)

GET /events?kind=login&limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "prev_cursor": null, "next_cursor": "WyJhIixb..."}, and ?kind=login&cursor=<next_cursor> the next page: next_cursor is null on the last page, prev_cursor on the first. The Link header has the first page and, when there's one, the previous and the next.

  • The sort key (key) must be unique: (created_at, id), not created_at alone, which two items may share. Its values can be strings, integers (up to 64 bits), floats, booleans, datetimes, dates, UUIDs and decimals, and params.after and params.before have them back as such: one of them is set, by the cursor's direction, neither on the first page.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those the database returned, up to params.fetch (the limit and one more, which tells whether there's another page that way): past params.after in order, or with params.before, before it in the reverse order, nearest first, which paginate puts back in order. The other way there's always a page, the one the cursor came from. Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole sorted list. descending=True for newest first, where after reads key < :after and before key > :before ORDER BY key.
  • What a cursor holds: its direction, the sort key, a digest of the request's other query parameters (all but cursor and limit, in any order) and, with a ttl, when it was issued, signed with HMAC-SHA256 (secret is required; a list rotates secrets). A cursor that a client made or changed, that comes with other query parameters than its own (the next page of kind=login asked with kind=logout), or older than ttl is a 400 before the endpoint runs; one longer than 1024 characters or malformed is a 422. Cursors are base64, not encrypted: clients can read the sort key, so sort by what they may see.
  • Cached apart: the query's digest is part of CursorParams, so @cache keeps the pages of each query apart, even for parameters the endpoint doesn't read. With a ttl, a page served from the cache hands out the cursors issued when it was stored: keep expire well under ttl.
  • Links of your own: cursors.encode(position, before=False, query=[...]) makes the cursor of the page after (or before) any position, such as the events after a date.
  • Its limits: no total and no page numbers, only the first, previous and next pages. Going back from a page that didn't start where the first page's walk would have, the first page can be shorter than the limit. For a key clients read and write themselves, use PaginationKeyset.

docs.title: PaginationKeyset
docs.text:
The key of the last item, in plain sight: ?after=42&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

The items after the sort key of the last one seen: GET /messages?after=42&limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "after": "62", "has_more": true}, and ?after=62 the next page. The key travels as it is, neither encoded nor signed: clients read it, keep it, and may write their own to start anywhere (the events since a date). Each page is a query through an index, as fast as the first, and rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages. For syncing, chats, exports and public APIs where clients drive the position:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.keyset import KeysetPage, KeysetParams, PaginationKeyset

messages = PaginationKeyset(sort=int, default_limit=20, max_limit=100)  # by id: ?after=42


@app.get("/messages")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["messages"])
async def list_messages(
    params: Annotated[KeysetParams, Depends(messages)],
) -> KeysetPage[Message]:
    query = select(Message).order_by(Message.id).limit(params.fetch)
    if params.after is not None:
        query = query.where(Message.id > params.after)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return messages.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda m: m.id, queried=True)

A key of several values, such as a time and the id that breaks its ties, goes as a JSON array:

events = PaginationKeyset(sort=(datetime, int))  # ?after=["2026-10-29T10:00:00Z",42]


@app.get("/events")
async def list_events(params: Annotated[KeysetParams, Depends(events)]) -> KeysetPage[Event]:
    query = select(Event).order_by(Event.at, Event.id).limit(params.fetch)
    if params.after is not None:  # (at, id) of the last event seen
        query = query.where(tuple_(Event.at, Event.id) > params.after)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return events.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda e: (e.at, e.id), queried=True)
  • Declared types: sort is the type of the key, or the types of its values in order: int, float, str, bool, datetime (with a time zone), date, UUID and Decimal. params.after has the key converted (a tuple for several values), and the page gives it as after takes it: a value as text (42, 2026-10-29T10:00:00Z), several as a JSON array with datetimes and dates in ISO 8601, UUIDs and decimals as strings. A value of another type, another number of them or JSON that doesn't parse is a 400, and more than 1024 characters a 422, before the endpoint runs.
  • The key must be unique: m.id, or (e.at, e.id), not the time alone. A key that isn't of the types of sort is a TypeError.
  • after and has_more: after is the key of the page's last item, null when it's empty (a client that has caught up keeps its own); has_more says whether there's a next page. A client that syncs keeps after from the last page and asks with it later for what came since. The Link header has the first page and, while has_more, the next one.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those of the page, queried past params.after up to params.fetch (the limit and one more: it tells whether there's a next page). Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole sorted list. descending=True for newest first: the next page holds the keys smaller than after (WHERE id < :after ORDER BY id DESC).
  • Readable and writable: nothing stops a client from asking for any position, so sort by what they may see. For keys they can't change or reuse with other filters, and pages in both directions, use PaginationCursor.

docs.title: PaginationOffset
docs.text:
Slices, with the total or without counting the list: ?offset=40&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

GET /products?offset=40&limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "offset": 40, "limit": 20, "has_more": true, "total": 245}: the same as page numbers for clients that count in items rather than pages, and can ask for any slice. When counting the list is slow (big tables, searches, joins) or outdated as soon as it's made, leave the total out: the database is asked for one row more than the page (params.fetch), which isn't returned but tells whether there's a next one, and total is null.

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.offset import OffsetPage, OffsetParams, PaginationOffset

offsets = PaginationOffset(default_limit=20, max_limit=100)


@app.get("/products")
async def products(params: Annotated[OffsetParams, Depends(offsets)]) -> OffsetPage[Product]:
    rows = await session.scalars(select(Product).limit(params.limit).offset(params.offset))
    return offsets.paginate(rows.all(), params, total=await count_products())


@app.get("/logs")
@cache(expire=10)
async def logs(params: Annotated[OffsetParams, Depends(offsets)]) -> OffsetPage[Line]:
    query = select(Line).order_by(Line.id.desc()).limit(params.fetch).offset(params.offset)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return offsets.paginate(rows, params, queried=True)  # no count
  • Three ways to call paginate: with total=, the rows are the page (LIMIT params.limit OFFSET params.offset); with queried=True, they're those of LIMIT params.fetch OFFSET params.offset, one more than limit when there's a next page; with neither, paginate slices the page from the whole list, and counts it.
  • Links: first, previous and, while has_more, next; with the total, the last page too. First, previous and last are on the grid of limit from 0, where clients that start at the first page walk.
  • By position: a row added or deleted before the page shifts it, so an item may be skipped or seen twice, and a database still walks past every row before the offset: deep pages get slower. For lists that grow while they're read, page by key (PaginationCursor, PaginationKeyset).
  • Limits: limit up to max_limit and offset from 0, a 422 otherwise.

docs.title: PaginationPageNumber
docs.text:
Numbered pages, with the total: ?page=2&page_size=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Numbered pages, with the total: GET /products?page=2&page_size=20 answers {"items": [...], "total": 245, "page": 2, "page_size": 20, "pages": 13}. For lists that people browse page by page, jump through, and want to know the size of.

  • From a database: query only the page, with params.offset and params.limit, and count: pages.paginate(rows, params, total=count). Without total, paginate slices the page from the whole list.
  • Links: first, previous, next and last.
  • Its cost: counting the whole list on every page, and the shifting of pages by position.

docs.title: PaginationRange
docs.text:
Ranges of items, with Content-Range: ?start=0&end=24.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Ranges of items by the indexes of the first and the last, from 0 and both included: GET /contacts?start=0&end=24 answers {"items": [...], "start": 0, "end": 24, "total": 319, "limit": 25} with Content-Range: items 0-24/319. For data grids and tables that ask for the rows they show, and read from the header which ones they got and how many there are:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.ranges import PaginationRange, RangePage, RangeParams

ranges = PaginationRange(default_items=25, max_items=100)


@app.get("/contacts")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["contacts"])
async def contacts(params: Annotated[RangeParams, Depends(ranges)]) -> RangePage[Contact]:
    query = select(Contact).order_by(Contact.name).limit(params.limit).offset(params.offset)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return ranges.paginate(rows, params, total=await count_contacts())
  • The range returned: end is the index of the last item in the response, which is short of the one asked for at the end of the list; null, and Content-Range: items */319, when there are none. limit is the size asked for, which the links keep.
  • From a database: query the range with params.offset and params.limit, and count: ranges.paginate(rows, params, total=count). Without total, paginate slices the range from the whole list.
  • Errors: without end, a range holds default_items. One whose end is before its start, or that holds more than max_items items, is a 400 before the endpoint runs; one that starts past the last item of a list that isn't empty, a 416 with Content-Range: items */<total>.
  • Links: first, previous, next and last ranges of the same size, the first and last on the grid of that size from 0. Pages served from the cache get their Content-Range too.
  • Its cost: like page numbers, a count on every range, and pages that shift when rows are added or deleted before them.

docs.title: PaginationScroll
docs.text:
A snapshot kept in the backend, read in batches: ?scroll_id=....

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

A scroll runs the query once and keeps what it found as a snapshot in the cache's backend, which the client reads in batches: what was there when the scroll started, whatever is written meanwhile. For exports, reports and jobs that read a whole result set while it changes, and for queries too costly to run once per page:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.scroll import PaginationScroll, ScrollPage, ScrollParams

scroll = PaginationScroll(Order, secret=settings.scroll_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/orders/export")
async def export(params: Annotated[ScrollParams, Depends(scroll)]) -> ScrollPage[Order]:
    if params.scroll_id is None:  # a new scroll: query once, one row more than it keeps
        query = select(Order).where(Order.status == "paid").order_by(Order.id)
        rows = await session.scalars(query.limit(scroll.max_items + 1))
        return await scroll.start(rows.all(), params)
    return await scroll.next(params)


@app.delete("/orders/export", status_code=204)
async def stop(scroll_id: str) -> None:
    await scroll.clear(scroll_id)

GET /orders/export?batch_size=100 answers the first batch, {"items": [...], "scroll_id": "WyJsR3Nq...", "total": 2450}, and ?scroll_id=<scroll_id> the next one; scroll_id is null after the last. The Link header has the next batch.

  • A snapshot: start writes the items into one entry of the backend, as JSON through their type (PaginationScroll(Order, ...)), and next reads them back as such. Rows added, changed or deleted meanwhile don't show, and no item is skipped or seen twice.
  • Kept alive while it's read: the snapshot lasts keep_alive seconds (60 by default) after each batch; a scroll_id whose snapshot has expired is a 404, and the client starts again. clear deletes it as soon as the client is done. The cache's own clear() leaves snapshots alone, and with a TieredBackend they're in the shared tier only.
  • Retries are safe: a scroll_id holds the snapshot's id and where the next batch starts, signed with HMAC-SHA256: the same request gets the same batch, and one made up or changed is a 400 before the endpoint runs. Each request may ask for its own batch_size, up to max_batch_size (1000 by default; a 422 beyond).
  • Who may read it: a scroll_id reads the rest of the snapshot without the endpoint's query running again, so whoever has one gets the results it was given for. When they depend on who asks, pass owner=str(user.id) to start, next and clear: a scroll_id is then only good for that user.
  • Sealed: the snapshot is sealed with the cache's signing_key, or encryption_key when it holds personal data, and one that someone planted in the backend is ignored.
  • Its limits: each batch reads the whole snapshot from the backend and writes it back to keep it alive, and each start keeps a new one, so start refuses more than max_items items (10,000 by default; query one more than that and it raises ValueError) and a rate limit on the endpoint keeps clients from starting scrolls without end. The snapshot is one entry: mind the backend's limit on the size of an entry (1 MB in Memcached, 400 KB in DynamoDB). A backend that fails is a 503, and the client retries. Don't put @cache on a scroll: each start must keep a snapshot of its own. To read a big table without keeping it anywhere, PaginationStreaming sends every row as it comes.

docs.title: With SQLAlchemy
docs.text:
The queries of the strategies, written for SQLAlchemy 2: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[sqlalchemy]".

How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

The JSON of a page is the easy part; the query is where pagination goes wrong: a sort key that isn't unique skips rows, a comparison column by column instead of as a row value walks past the index, a previous page read in the wrong order comes back reversed, a forgotten extra row loses has_more. page_query writes it from the parameters the dependency gave:

from sqlalchemy import select

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.cursor import CursorPage, CursorParams, PaginationCursor
from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.sqlalchemy import count_query, page_query, sort_key

cursors = PaginationCursor(settings.cursor_secret)
BY = (Event.created_at, Event.id)  # unique as a whole


@app.get("/events")
async def events(
    params: Annotated[CursorParams, Depends(cursors)],
    session: SessionDep,
    kind: Kind | None = None,
) -> CursorPage[EventOut]:
    statement = select(Event)
    if kind is not None:
        statement = statement.where(Event.kind == kind)
    query = page_query(statement, params, by=BY, descending=True)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return cursors.paginate(rows, params, key=sort_key(*BY), descending=True, queried=True)

By position, with the total:

@app.get("/products")
async def products(
    params: Annotated[PageNumberParams, Depends(pages)],
    session: SessionDep,
) -> PageNumberPage[ProductOut]:
    statement = select(Product).where(Product.active)
    total = await session.scalar(count_query(statement))
    rows = (await session.scalars(page_query(statement, params, by=(Product.id,)))).all()
    return pages.paginate(rows, params, total=total)
  • By key (CursorParams, KeysetParams): by is the sort key, and the statement has no ORDER BY of its own. page_query adds WHERE (created_at, id) > (:a, :b) (< newest first), the order of by, and LIMIT one more than the page. For the page before a cursor, it reads the other way, nearest first, as paginate(..., queried=True) expects. The comparison is a row value, which PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, MariaDB and SQLite 3.15+ answer from an index on the columns of by, in that order.
  • By position (PageNumberParams, OffsetParams, RangeParams): OFFSET and LIMIT, in the statement's order or that of by. With OffsetParams it fetches one row more, for queried=True; with total= the extra row is left out of the page.
  • count_query(statement): SELECT count(*) of the statement, without its order, limit or offset.
  • sort_key(*columns): the key of paginate for those columns, read from each row by name: (event.created_at, event.id), or the value alone for one column.
  • Positions that don't fit: a cursor whose key has another number of values than by (one of another endpoint signed with the same secret) is a 400, like any invalid cursor.

docs.title: PaginationStreaming
docs.text:
Every item as it comes, as NDJSON, without pages.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Every item in one response, as they come, without pages: NDJSON (application/x-ndjson), one JSON value per line, which a client reads while the rest is still being queried. For exports, for syncing everything to another system, and for scripts that would otherwise walk hundreds of pages. It isn't a dependency: it makes the response.

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.streaming import PaginationStreaming

stream = PaginationStreaming(batch_size=100)


@app.get("/events")
async def events() -> StreamingResponse:
    async def fetch(after: int | None, limit: int) -> list[Event]:
        query = select(Event).order_by(Event.id).limit(limit)
        if after is not None:
            query = query.where(Event.id > after)
        return list((await session.scalars(query)).all())

    return stream.response(stream.batches(fetch, key=lambda e: e.id))

GET /events answers one event per line, {"id":1,...}, {"id":2,...}..., each hundred sent as soon as it's read, before the next hundred are queried, until the last event.

  • response(items) takes a list, a generator or an async iterable, and sends it in chunks of batch_size lines, models serialised with pydantic as FastAPI would. A synchronous generator is read in the thread pool, batch_size items at a time, so a blocking driver doesn't stop the event loop.
  • batches(fetch, key=...) reads a big table without loading it: fetch(None, batch_size), then fetch(key(last row), batch_size), until a batch comes back shorter than batch_size. Each query finds its batch through an index, as fast as the first. fetch can be sync or async, and key must be unique ((e.created_at, e.id) rather than e.created_at). It yields the rows one by one, ready for response().
  • max_items ends the response there, whatever is left (None, the default, for no end). The source is closed then, or at its end: a generator's finally runs.
  • A client that disconnects stops the stream: nothing more is read from the source, and no more queries are made.
  • Not cached: @cache doesn't keep streams, so each request reads the database again; don't put it on these endpoints.
  • Its limits: the status and headers go out before the first item, so an error halfway through can only cut the stream short; clients should check that they got what they expected (a count in another endpoint, or the last id). There's no resuming in the middle: a client that needs it pages by cursor instead.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
Here is how to learn Alcazaba: a tutorial that starts with a quick start and takes each tool in turn, how to set it up for production, and complete example apps. Read the tutorial in order the first time; come back to a tool's page when you need it.

  • Tutorial - User Guide

    A first app in three steps, a cache, a rate limit and authorization, then a page per tool.

  • Production setup

    The configuration from the environment, and the state in Redis, shared by every process.

  • Examples

    Small, complete apps, each with a tool at work as it's meant to be used in production.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Here's the reference, or code API: every public class and function, by tool, with its parameters and what it raises. The Tutorial - User Guide tells how to use them, and the examples show them in complete apps.

  • Response cache

    Cache, FastAPICache, the @cache decorator, key builders and coders. In fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache.

  • Backends

    Where entries and state live: in memory, Redis, Valkey, GLIDE, memcached, DynamoDB, two levels. In fastapi_alcazaba.backends.

  • Pagination

    The seven strategies, with their parameters and pages. In fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.

  • Rate and concurrency limits

    Requests per window and requests at a time, per client or shared, across processes. In fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit.

  • Idempotency keys

    The middleware that replays the first response to a retried request. In fastapi_alcazaba.idempotency.

  • Authentication strategies

    FastAPIAuth, Strategy, and the JWT, bearer, OAuth2, SAML and session strategies. In fastapi_alcazaba.auth.

  • API keys, tokens and codes

    Passwords, API keys stored as digests, revoked tokens, one-time codes, the second factor (TOTP) and passkeys (WebAuthn). In fastapi_alcazaba.auth.

  • Authorization

    A Casbin, Cedar or Open Policy Agent policy per route or for every request: FastAPIAuthz, AuthzMiddleware, CedarEnforcer and OPAEnforcer. In fastapi_alcazaba.authz.

  • Sessions, CSRF and security headers

    What a cookie-based app needs: server-side sessions, CSRF protection, headers and body limits. In fastapi_alcazaba.security.

  • Accounting

    FastAPIAccounting, its quotas, usage reports and records, and their sinks. In fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.

  • Audit trail

    FastAPIAudit, its entries and events, sinks, and the trail's verification. In fastapi_alcazaba.audit.

  • Checking uploads

    The type of a file from its bytes, its size and pixels, safe file names, and signed URLs for object storage. In fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.

  • E-mail

    FastAPIMail, which builds messages nothing can add headers to, with their attachments; SMTPSender and SESSender. In fastapi_alcazaba.mail.

  • Webhooks and outbound calls

    Standard Webhooks in and out, and httpx transports with deadlines, breakers and SSRF checks. In fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks and fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.

  • Errors and observability

    Problem details, request IDs, request deadlines, health checks and logs as JSON. In fastapi_alcazaba.observability.

  • Background work

    Scheduled jobs, the task queue, leader election and locks shared by every process, broadcast and the outbox. In fastapi_alcazaba.background.

  • Operations

    Circuit breakers, maintenance mode and feature flags, switched at runtime. In fastapi_alcazaba.operations.

  • Integrity, resilience and errors

    What signs and encrypts entries, RFC 8785 canonical JSON, the backends' circuit breaker, and the exceptions. In fastapi_alcazaba.core.

docs.title: Accounting
docs.text:
FastAPIAccounting, its quotas, usage reports and records, and their sinks. In fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.

In the guide: Accounting. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.FastAPIAccounting
docs.text:
FastAPIAccounting(*, subject: Subject, quotas: Iterable[Quota] = (), period: Period = 'month', sinks: Iterable[UsageSink] | None = None, cache: Cache | None = None, fail_open: bool = True, challenge: str = 'Bearer', headers: bool = True, timeout: float = 5.0, metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Meters what each subject uses, per period, and holds it to its quotas.

meter(name) is a dependency that charges each request: 1 unit by default, checked against the quota and counted in one atomic operation, so concurrent requests never go past it. A request over its quota gets a 429 with Retry-After (when the period ends), or a 402, and isn't counted. meter(name, amount=None) gives the endpoint a Metering to add what it uses as it goes (tokens, bytes, seconds), charged when it ends; the quota is checked when it starts, so the requests already running may together go past it.

Responses carry the RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers of the IETF draft, the quota's name being the meter's, for clients to see what they have left.

What's charged: a request that gets a client error (a 4xx, a validation error) was served and stays charged; one that fails on the server (an exception, a 5xx) or whose client went away is refunded, and has no record. What an endpoint added to its Metering is charged whatever happens next: it was used.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default subject Subject

a dependency that returns who uses it: a user's, an API key's or a tenant's ID, None when nobody is authenticated (a 401, WWW-Authenticate: <challenge>).

required quotas Iterable[Quota]

a Quota per meter at most. Meters without one are counted, not bounded.

() period Period

the period of the meters without a quota.

'month' sinks Iterable[UsageSink] | None

where the usage records go; a LoggingUsageSink by default, () for none.

None cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the counters; the app's (get_cache) by default.

None fail_open bool

when the backend fails, let requests through uncounted (the default: the records still have them) or refuse them with a 503.

True challenge str

the WWW-Authenticate of the 401s.

'Bearer' headers bool

send the RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers.

True timeout float

seconds each sink has to write a record.

5.0 metrics Metrics | None

where to count the requests (fastapi_alcazaba.accounting), the units (fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.usage) and the records not written (fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.undelivered); the cache's by default.

None

docs.title: meter
docs.text:
meter(meter: str, *, amount: int | None = 1) -> Callable[..., AsyncIterator[Any]]

A dependency that charges amount units of meter to the request's subject before the endpoint runs, within its quota, and returns the subject's ID. With amount=None it returns a Metering, to which the endpoint adds what it uses; the total is charged when it ends.

docs.title: record async
docs.text:
record(subject: str | int | UUID, meter: str, amount: int, *, request: HTTPConnection | None = None) -> UsageRecord

Charges amount units of meter to subject without checking its quota (it's been used already): for what happens outside a metered request, such as a job or a webhook. Counted in the backend (when it answers) and sent to the sinks; returns the record.

docs.title: usage async
docs.text:
usage(subject: str | int | UUID, meter: str, *, at: datetime | None = None, request: HTTPConnection | None = None) -> UsageReport

What subject has used of meter in the period that holds at (now by default), and what its quota leaves. The counters keep the current period and the one before; the records have the older ones. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.Quota dataclass
docs.text:
Quota(meter: str, limit: Limit, period: Period = 'month', status: int = HTTP_429_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS)

How much of meter a subject may use per period.

Quota("requests", limit=10_000)  # a month, the same for everybody
Quota("tokens", limit=tokens_of_plan, period="day")  # each subject's plan says

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default meter str

what it bounds, as FastAPIAccounting.meter() names it.

required limit Limit

the units allowed per period, 0 for none; or limit(subject), a function (or a coroutine function) of the subject's ID that gives them, None for no limit.

required period Period

a calendar hour, day or month, in UTC: the counter starts again at 0 when it ends.

'month' status int

what a request over the quota gets: 429 (Too Many Requests, with Retry-After: when the period ends) or 402 (Payment Required: a plan to upgrade).

HTTP_429_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS

What meter(name, amount=None) gives the endpoint: it adds what it uses as it goes (add(tokens)), and the total is charged when it ends.

A charge, as the sinks get it; to_dict() and to_json() give its JSON form.

random, unique: billing counts each record once, should a sink deliver it twice.

when it was charged (UTC).

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.UsageSink
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Where usage records go. write gets each one when it's charged, within the FastAPIAccounting's timeout: queue it if writing takes longer. What it raises is logged, with the record.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.LoggingUsageSink
docs.text:
LoggingUsageSink(log: str | Logger = 'fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.usage', level: int = logging.INFO)

Writes each record as one line of JSON to the logger log (a name or a Logger), at level, for the log pipeline to keep and add up; handlers that format their own JSON find the record in the log record's usage attribute too. When the logger outputs nothing at that level (no handler, or a higher level), it says so once, as a warning.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.accounting.period_of

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.audit.FastAPIAudit
docs.text:
FastAPIAudit(sinks: Iterable[AuditSink] | None = None, *, signing_key: AuditKeys | None = None, redact: Collection[str] = (), timeout: float = 5.0, metrics: Metrics | None = None, checkpoint_interval: float | None = None, cache: Cache | None = None, name: str = 'default')

An audit trail: action() records what endpoints do, record() and log() the rest.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sinks Iterable[AuditSink] | None

where the events go; a LoggingAuditSink by default.

None signing_key AuditKeys | None

signs and chains the events (see verify_audit_trail): an Ed25519 private key (PEM, or cryptography's object; generate_audit_key_pair()), whose public key verifies and can't sign; or an HMAC secret of at least 32 bytes. Several rotate them: the first signs, the others are kept for nothing else (verification takes the old keys). The same in every process.

None checkpoint_interval float | None

seconds between two checkpoints (an audit.checkpoint event listing the newest event of every process's stream, through the cache's backend), written with the next event after that long. Needs a signing_key.

None cache Cache | None

whose backend shares the heads of the streams for the checkpoints; FastAPICache's by default. Without one (or when it fails), a checkpoint lists its own stream only.

None name str

trails of different names keep their checkpoints apart.

'default' redact Collection[str]

words that mark secrets in the keys of details, besides SENSITIVE_WORDS.

() timeout float

seconds each sink has to write an event.

5.0 metrics Metrics | None

where to count the events (fastapi_alcazaba.audit) and those not written (fastapi_alcazaba.audit.undelivered); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.audit.verify_audit_trail
docs.text:
verify_audit_trail(events: Iterable[AuditEvent | Mapping[str, Any]], keys: AuditKeys) -> list[str]

What's wrong with a trail: an empty list when nothing is. keys verify it: the public keys of Ed25519 signing keys, or the HMAC secrets, of every rotation the events span (each signature names its key). events are AuditEvents or their to_dict() (the JSON lines read back), of one stream or several, in any order; the same event given twice counts once.

Each stream's chain is checked from its oldest event given, since older ones may have been rotated out of the logs. Each checkpoint's heads must be there: a stream whose newest events were removed ends before the head a later checkpoint saw. Events after the last checkpoint can still be removed unnoticed: last_checkpoint() says when that was.

docs.title: API keys, tokens and codes

Passwords, API keys stored as digests, revoked tokens, one-time codes, the second factor (TOTP), passkeys (WebAuthn) and step-up. In fastapi_alcazaba.auth.

In the guide: Passwords, API keys, Revoked tokens and one-time codes, Second factor, Passkeys. In an app: the example, the second factor's.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.FastAPIPasswords
docs.text:
FastAPIPasswords(*, parameters: ScryptParameters | None = None, pepper: str | SecretStr | None = None, min_length: int = 15, max_attempts: int = 10, lockout: int = 900, reset_ttl: int = 3600, pwned: PwnedPasswords | None = None, cache: Cache | None = None, namespace: str = 'passwords', audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None)

Passwords, from sign-up to reset.

  • Hashes: scrypt with a random salt each, in a thread (it takes a fifth of a second on purpose); with a pepper, the password is first an HMAC of it, so that a stolen database without the pepper gives nothing to guess against.
  • Guesses: after max_attempts wrong passwords for an account, its logins are refused for lockout seconds, the right password too; the attempts of other accounts aren't affected. Put a rate limit per client on the login route too, for one client trying many accounts.
  • Unknown accounts take as long as known ones: verify hashes against a made-up hash.
  • Leaked passwords: with pwned (PwnedPasswords), check says when a password is among those leaked, which attackers try first.
  • Resets: reset_token makes a random token, kept as a digest for reset_ttl seconds, that use_reset_token turns into its user once; a new one replaces the user's last.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default parameters ScryptParameters | None

scrypt's cost.

None pepper str | SecretStr | None

a secret of 32 bytes or more, kept out of the database (your settings). It can't be rotated without the passwords: keep it.

None min_length int

characters a new password needs (NIST SP 800-63B: 15 when the password is the only factor, 8 with another).

15 max_attempts int

wrong passwords per account before the lockout.

10 lockout int

seconds an account's logins are refused after them.

900 reset_ttl int

seconds a reset token lasts.

3600 pwned PwnedPasswords | None

checks the passwords against those leaked; None for no check.

None cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the attempts and the reset tokens; FastAPICache's by default.

None namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'passwords' audit FastAPIAudit | None

the audit trail that records each password checked (auth.password) and each reset (auth.password_reset), with their outcome.

None

docs.text:

No rule on its characters: length is what makes it strong. An empty list when it's fine.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.FastAPIAPIKeys
docs.text:
FastAPIAPIKeys(lookup: Lookup[R], *, header: str = 'X-API-Key', prefix: str = 'ak', bearer: bool = False, pepper: Secrets | None = None, cache_ttl: float = 0.0, cache_size: int = 1024, scheme_name: str = 'APIKey', metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Bases: Generic[R]

FastAPI dependency that authenticates a request by its API key and returns its record.

keys = FastAPIAPIKeys(load_key, pepper=settings.api_key_pepper)

@app.get("/me")
async def me(key: Annotated[StoredKey, Depends(keys)]) -> ...

@app.delete("/orders/{id}", dependencies=[Depends(keys.require("orders:write"))])

The key comes in the header (X-API-Key by default) or, with bearer=True, as Authorization: Bearer <key>; both appear in the OpenAPI schema, for the docs' Authorize button. A missing, malformed, unknown, wrong or expired key gets the same 401 (with WWW-Authenticate); a valid key without a scope that require asks for gets a 403. Keys and secrets are never logged; put a FastAPIRateLimiter in front, since each request with a well-formed key costs a lookup.

Revoking a key: delete its record, or set its expires_at to the past. With cache_ttl, records are kept in each process for that many seconds, so a revocation takes up to that long to reach every process.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lookup Lookup[R]

lookup(key_id): the stored record of that id, or None. Async, or a plain function, which runs in a thread like FastAPI's sync dependencies.

required header str

the request header holding the key.

'X-API-Key' prefix str

the start of every key (ak_...): letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. Secret scanners (GitHub's, GitLab's) can be taught to spot it, and to check its checksum.

'ak' bearer bool

also accept the key as Authorization: Bearer <key>.

False pepper Secrets | None

a server secret (at least 32 bytes) mixed into every digest, kept out of the database (an environment variable, a secret manager). A list rotates it: the first one is used for new keys, all of them are accepted; old peppers must stay as long as keys made with them do. Changing it without keeping the old one invalidates every key.

None cache_ttl float

seconds each process keeps a record it looked up; 0 looks up every request.

0.0 cache_size int

records kept at most per process (the least recently used are dropped).

1024 scheme_name str

name of the scheme in the OpenAPI schema.

'APIKey' metrics Metrics | None

where to count the outcomes (fastapi_alcazaba.api_keys); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.TokenBlocklist
docs.text:
TokenBlocklist(cache: Cache | None = None, *, namespace: str = 'revoked', fail_open: bool = False, leeway: int = 60)

Revoked tokens (by their jti), sessions (by their sid: every token of one login, see RefreshTokens) and subjects logged out everywhere (revoke_subject).

blocklist = TokenBlocklist()

async def current_user(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(decode_jwt)]) -> str:
    sub, iat = claims["sub"], claims["iat"]
    if await blocklist.is_revoked(claims["jti"], subject=sub, issued_at=iat):
        raise HTTPException(401)
    return sub

Each mark lasts while the token could still be accepted, leeway included, and then the backend drops it. When the cache has a signing_key or encryption_key, the marks are sealed with it and planted ones are ignored; but whoever can delete keys in the backend can still un-revoke tokens, so keep it out of reach.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the marks; FastAPICache's by default, resolved at each call (so the blocklist can be created before FastAPICache.init).

None namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'revoked' fail_open bool

when the backend fails, is_revoked answers False (tokens are accepted) instead of True (refused, the default).

False leeway int

seconds your JWT library still accepts a token after its exp (PyJWT's leeway): marks are kept that much longer.

60

docs.title: revoke async
docs.text:
revoke(token_id: str, *, expires_at: Moment | None = None, ttl: int | None = None) -> None

Refuse the token token_id (its jti) until it would have expired anyway: give its exp as expires_at, or the seconds it has left as ttl. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails: the token isn't revoked then.

docs.title: revoke_subject async
docs.text:
revoke_subject(subject: str, *, ttl: int) -> None

Refuse every token of subject issued before the current second: log out everywhere, e.g. after a password change. ttl is the longest lifetime of your tokens. iat has whole seconds, so the tokens issued during this second stay valid, among them the one you issue right after for the current session. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails.

docs.title: revoke_session async
docs.text:
revoke_session(session: str, *, ttl: int) -> None

Refuse every token whose sid is session (one login, on one device), for ttl seconds: the longest lifetime of its tokens. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails.

docs.title: is_revoked async
docs.text:
is_revoked(token_id: str, *, subject: str | None = None, issued_at: Moment | None = None, session: str | None = None) -> bool

Whether the token is refused: its jti was revoked, its session (sid, give it as session) was, or its subject was logged out everywhere after it was issued (give its sub and iat). When the backend fails, not fail_open.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.OneTimeCodes
docs.text:
OneTimeCodes(secret: Secrets, cache: Cache | None = None, *, digits: int = 6, ttl: int = 300, max_attempts: int = 5, namespace: str = 'otp')

Codes of digits digits, sent by e-mail or SMS, that prove who someone is: each lasts ttl seconds, works once, and subject has max_attempts guesses for each ttl seconds, whatever the number of codes issued.

codes = OneTimeCodes(secret=settings.otp_secret)

code = await codes.issue(user.email, purpose="login")  # send it to the user
...
if not await codes.verify(form.email, form.code, purpose="login"):
    raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid or expired code")

The backend holds an HMAC of each code with secret, never the code: a plain digest of a 6-digit code is brute-forced in milliseconds by whoever reads the backend. Issuing a code replaces the previous one, but doesn't give the guesses back: asking for code after code doesn't add up to more than max_attempts guesses each ttl seconds. Once they're used, the subject waits for the window to end (up to ttl seconds), new codes included; the right code starts the count again. Still put a FastAPIRateLimiter on the route that issues them: each code sent costs an e-mail or an SMS.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default secret Secrets

at least 32 bytes (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)), from the environment or a secret manager. A list rotates them: the first one is used, all of them are accepted.

required cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the codes; FastAPICache's by default, resolved at each call.

None digits int

length of the codes, 4 to 10.

6 ttl int

seconds each code lasts.

300 max_attempts int

guesses allowed for each subject and purpose in ttl seconds, right or wrong, across the codes issued.

5 namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'otp'

A new code for subject (an e-mail address, a user id...) and purpose ("login", "reset-password"...), replacing the previous one; the guesses already made still count. Raises BackendUnavailable when the backend fails.

docs.text:
verify(subject: str, code: str, purpose: str = '') -> bool

Whether code is the current code of subject for purpose; it's used up then. Of several requests with the right code at the same time, only one gets True. False when the backend fails.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.FastAPITOTP
docs.text:
FastAPITOTP(*, issuer: str, secret: Secrets, cache: Cache | None = None, digits: int = 6, period: int = 30, window: int = 1, algorithm: Algorithm = 'SHA1', max_attempts: int = 5, lockout: int = 900, namespace: str = 'totp', audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None)

The codes of authenticator apps as a second factor (RFC 6238), recovery codes, and step-up for the routes that need a recent one.

  • The secrets are sealed with AES-256-GCM, each for its user: store sealed, never the secret. A sealed secret copied to another user doesn't open, nor without secret.
  • A code is accepted within window steps of period seconds before or after now, for clocks out of step; each one once (RFC 6238, 5.2): another request with the same code, from someone who looked over the user's shoulder, is refused.
  • Guesses: after max_attempts wrong codes (recovery codes included), the user's codes are refused for lockout seconds, whatever they are: a 6-digit code isn't guessed.
  • When the backend fails, nothing is accepted: no code is checked for replay, nor guesses counted.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default issuer str

the name the authenticator app shows for the account ("Example").

required secret Secrets

at least 32 bytes (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)), from your settings: it seals the TOTP secrets and makes the recovery codes' digests. A list rotates it: the first one seals, all of them open.

required cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the codes used and the guesses; FastAPICache's by default, resolved at each call. Its backend must hold locks (not memcached).

None digits int

of each code, 6 or 8.

6 period int

seconds each code lasts.

30 window int

steps accepted before and after the current one.

1 algorithm Algorithm

SHA1, which every app supports, SHA256 or SHA512.

'SHA1' max_attempts int

wrong codes before the lockout.

5 lockout int

seconds the codes are refused after max_attempts wrong ones, counted from the first of them.

900 namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'totp' audit FastAPIAudit | None

the audit trail that records each second factor checked (auth.mfa) and each recovery code tried (auth.recovery_code), with their outcome.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.FastAPIWebAuthn
docs.text:
FastAPIWebAuthn(*, rp_id: str, rp_name: str, origins: Collection[str], user_verification: UserVerification = 'required', algorithms: Sequence[int] = (ES256, EDDSA, RS256), timeout: int = 300, cache: Cache | None = None, namespace: str = 'webauthn', audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None)

Passkeys and security keys: registering them (registration_options, verify_registration) and logging in with them (authentication_options, verify_authentication), as WebAuthn Level 2 says.

  • The challenges are random (32 bytes), kept in the cache's backend for timeout seconds, bound to the ceremony and to the user they were made for, and used once: of two answers to the same challenge, one is checked.
  • The origin of the answer must be one of origins, never in a cross-origin iframe, and the authenticator's data must be for rp_id: a phishing site's origin is refused, and so is its RP ID, which the browser wouldn't sign for another site.
  • The user must be present (a touch), and verified (a PIN, a fingerprint, the phone's lock) with user_verification="required", the default: a passkey is then both factors.
  • The counter: a credential whose counter goes back (or doesn't move, for those that count) was cloned: refused. Synced passkeys count 0, and aren't checked.
  • When the backend fails, no answer is checked: the challenges can't be used once.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rp_id str

the relying party's ID: the site's domain, or one it's under (example.com for https://login.example.com). The credentials only work there.

required rp_name str

the name the authenticator shows ("Example").

required origins Collection[str]

the origins the answers come from, https://example.com (or http://localhost:8000, in development); each on rp_id or under it.

required user_verification UserVerification

required, preferred or discouraged.

'required' algorithms Sequence[int]

the COSE algorithms accepted, in order of preference.

(ES256, EDDSA, RS256) timeout int

seconds a challenge lasts, and the browser waits for the user.

300 cache Cache | None

the Cache whose backend keeps the challenges; FastAPICache's by default.

None namespace str

part of the keys, after the cache's prefix (see Cache.state_key).

'webauthn' audit FastAPIAudit | None

the audit trail that records each passkey registered (auth.passkey.register) and each login with one (auth.passkey), with their outcome.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.stepup.require_recent
docs.text:
require_recent(user_id: Callable[..., Any], max_age: int = 300, *, methods: Collection[str] | None = None, claims: Callable[..., Any] | None = None, acr_values: Collection[str] | None = None, subject: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Any] | None = None, audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None) -> Callable[..., Any]

A dependency that lets through the users who authenticated in the last max_age seconds, with one of methods when given, and returns their ID; requests without a user get a 401.

  • Sessions: the session's mark (mark) must be this user's, recent, and of one of methods ("passkey", "totp"...). Otherwise a 403 problem (PROBLEM_TYPE, "Second factor required") with max_age and methods, for the front end to ask for one and mark it.
  • Tokens: when claims (a dependency) gives the request's token claims (a dict), they decide instead: the token must be the user's (its sub is user_id's), with auth_time within max_age, an amr among methods (RFC 8176's names: "hwk", "otp", "mfa"...), an acr among acr_values. Otherwise a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_user_authentication" and the max_age and acr_values to ask the provider for (RFC 9470), as a problem too.
  • Audited: with audit, each check is an auth.stepup event with the method and the age (and the reason when it's refused).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default user_id Callable[..., Any]

a dependency that returns the request's user ID, or None.

required claims Callable[..., Any] | None

a dependency that returns the token's claims when the request came with one (auth.authenticate("jwt", optional=True)), None for a session.

None subject Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Any] | None

the user ID a token's claims belong to, compared with user_id's; the sub claim by default. A token of someone else (a fresh one of the attacker's own, sent with a stolen session) never steps anybody up.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.FastAPIAuth
docs.text:
FastAPIAuth(*strategies: Strategy, metrics: Metrics | None = None, audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None, actor: Actor | None = None)

The strategies of an app, and the dependencies that authenticate with them.

auth = FastAPIAuth(JWTStrategy(...), SessionStrategy(...))

@app.get("/me")
async def me(user: Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("jwt", "session"))]): ...

None actor Actor | None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt.JWTStrategy
docs.text:
JWTStrategy(key: Secrets | None = None, *, keys: Sequence[JWTKey] | None = None, jwks_url: str | None = None, algorithms: Sequence[str] | None = None, audience: str | None = None, issuer: str | None = None, leeway: float = 0, required: Sequence[str] = ('exp', 'sub'), verify: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Any] | None = None, blocklist: TokenBlocklist | None = None, cookie: str | None = None, jwks_lifespan: float = 300, jwks_stale: float = 3600, jwks_timeout: float = 3.0, jwks_client: Any = None, token_type: str | None = None, scope_claims: Sequence[str] = ('scope', 'scp'), name: str = 'jwt')

Bases: Strategy

Authenticates by a JWT in Authorization: Bearer <token> (or a cookie), verified with the app's keys or the provider's JWKS. The signature, exp, nbf and the claims of required are always checked, aud and iss when given; a token with an aud is refused when no audience is, as it's meant for some other service. alg: none is never accepted, and each key verifies with its own algorithm only.

Only access tokens: the provider signs its ID tokens and logout tokens with the same keys, often for the same aud, and those travel through less guarded places (a logout URL, the browser). A token with a header typ other than JWT or at+jwt (logout+jwt...), with a nonce (an ID token) or events (a logout token, a security event), or whose typ claim is Keycloak's ID, Logout or Refresh, is refused.

Give one of keys, key and jwks_url.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key Secrets | None

what verifies the tokens: a secret of at least 32 bytes for HS256, HS384 and HS512 (a list rotates them: the first one signs, all of them verify), or a public key (PEM) for RS256, ES256, EdDSA... keys does this for keys of any type.

None keys Sequence[JWTKey] | None

JWTKeys, each with its algorithm: the first one signs (when it can) and doesn't retire, all of them verify, until their until. HMAC and asymmetric keys may be mixed (from HS256 to RS256). A token is verified with the key its kid names; one without a kid, or with one no key has (another issuer's own ids), with the keys whose kid wasn't given.

None jwks_url str | None

the provider's JWKS (HTTPS) instead of keys: its keys are fetched, by the kid of each token, and kept for jwks_lifespan seconds; a kid it doesn't have makes it fetched again, at most every 30 seconds. Needs audience and issuer: the provider signs the tokens of every app it serves with the same keys.

None algorithms Sequence[str] | None

those accepted. With key, the first one signs (HS256 by default); with jwks_url, asymmetric ones (RS256, ES256, PS256 and EdDSA by default). Not with keys.

None audience str | None

the aud the tokens must have.

None issuer str | None

the iss the tokens must have.

None leeway float

seconds of tolerance on exp and nbf, for clocks out of step; the blocklist's leeway must be at least as long.

0 required Sequence[str]

claims a token must have.

('exp', 'sub') verify Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Any] | None

verify(claims): the user, or None to refuse the token. Async, or a plain function, which runs in a thread. By default the user is the claims themselves.

None blocklist TokenBlocklist | None

refuses the tokens revoked there (by jti, by sid for one login, and by sub and iat for "log out everywhere"); tokens then need a jti and an iat.

None cookie str | None

also reads the token from this cookie, for browsers.

None jwks_lifespan float

seconds the provider's keys are kept before they're fetched again.

300 jwks_stale float

seconds more they're used while the JWKS can't be fetched; then the requests get a 503 until it can.

3600 jwks_timeout float

seconds for the whole fetch of the JWKS.

3.0 jwks_client Any

the httpx2 client to fetch the JWKS with; one of its own by default, with a deadline and a circuit breaker (ResilientTransport), closed by aclose().

None token_type str | None

the header typ every token must have ("at+jwt", RFC 9068's), for a provider that sets it; any of JWT, at+jwt or none by default.

None scope_claims Sequence[str]

the claims whose scopes the token grants, for the routes that need some (Security(..., scopes=[...])): RFC 9068's scope, a string of them separated by spaces, and scp, a list (Entra ID, Okta); permissions for Auth0's.

('scope', 'scp') name str

what FastAPIAuth.authenticate calls it by.

'jwt'

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.oauth2.OAuth2Strategy
docs.text:
OAuth2Strategy(*, name: str, authorization_url: str, token_url: str, client_id: str, client_secret: str | SecretStr, redirect_uri: str, scopes: Sequence[str] = (), userinfo_url: str | None = None, verify: Callable[[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any] | None], Any] | None = None, client_auth: Literal['basic', 'post'] = 'basic', params: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, secure: bool = True, timeout: float = 10.0, client: Any = None)

Bases: AuthorizationCodeFlow

Authenticates the requests that come back from the provider's login page (the callback): checks their state, exchanges their code for tokens, reads the user's profile, and returns the user that verify makes of them. Other requests carry nothing for it (None): it only goes on the callback route.

redirect() starts the login: it sends the browser to the provider with a random state and a PKCE challenge, whose verifier waits in a short-lived cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, __Host- when Secure). A callback without that cookie or with another state is refused: nobody can log a user in with their own account (login CSRF) nor use a stolen code.

For OpenID Connect providers, OIDCStrategy also verifies the ID token they send.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

what FastAPIAuth.authenticate calls it by, and the cookie's name.

required authorization_url str

the provider's login page.

required token_url str

where codes are exchanged for tokens.

required client_id str

the app's id at the provider.

required client_secret str | SecretStr

the app's secret at the provider.

required redirect_uri str

the callback's absolute URL, as registered at the provider.

required scopes Sequence[str]

what to ask the provider for.

() userinfo_url str | None

where to read the user's profile with the access token; None for none.

None verify Callable[[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any] | None], Any] | None

verify(tokens, profile): your user, or None to refuse the login. tokens is the token endpoint's answer (access_token, refresh_token...), profile the JSON of userinfo_url (None without it). An id_token among them isn't verified: use OIDCStrategy to rely on its claims. Async, or a plain function, which runs in a thread. By default the user is the profile (or the tokens without it).

None client_auth Literal['basic', 'post']

how the app authenticates to the token endpoint: basic (HTTP Basic, RFC 6749's default) or post (in the form).

'basic' params Mapping[str, str] | None

more parameters for the login page (prompt, access_type...).

None secure bool

the cookie is Secure (browsers accept it from http://localhost too).

True timeout float

seconds for each call to the provider.

10.0 client Any

the httpx2 client to call the provider with; one of its own by default.

None

OIDCStrategy(*, name: str, issuer: str, client_id: str, client_secret: str | SecretStr | None = None, redirect_uri: str, scopes: Sequence[str] = ('openid', 'email', 'profile'), verify: Callable[[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any] | None], Any] | None = None, userinfo: bool = False, max_age: int | None = None, algorithms: Sequence[str] = ('RS256', 'ES256', 'PS256', 'EdDSA'), leeway: float = 60, authorization_url: str | None = None, token_url: str | None = None, userinfo_url: str | None = None, jwks_url: str | None = None, jwks_lifespan: float = 3600, jwks_stale: float = 3600, client_auth: Literal['basic', 'post', 'private_key_jwt'] = 'basic', client_key: JWTKey | None = None, post_logout_redirect_uris: Sequence[str] = (), end_session_url: str | None = None, params: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, secure: bool = True, timeout: float = 10.0, client: Any = None)

Bases: AuthorizationCodeFlow

Authenticates the callback of an OpenID Connect login: exchanges its code for tokens, verifies the ID token, and returns the user that verify makes of its claims.

The ID token is refused unless it's signed with one of algorithms by a key of the provider's JWKS (never none, never with the client secret), comes from issuer, is meant for this app (aud has client_id, and azp is it when there are several audiences or an azp), hasn't expired (exp) nor was issued in the future (iat), carries the nonce the login sent, the at_hash of the access token when it has one, and an auth_time within max_age when it's set. A provider that sends no ID token is refused.

Its endpoints and keys come from the issuer's discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration), read by await discover() in the lifespan; whose issuer must be issuer exactly. Endpoints given here aren't read from it, and with all of them (authorization_url, token_url, jwks_url) there's nothing to discover.

The raw ID token of a login is in request.state.id_token once the callback is authenticated: keep it in the session for logout_url(id_token_hint=...). The claims have the provider's session id (sid): keep it as oidc_sid in the session for back-channel logout to find it (UserSessions).

what to ask for; openid is required.

('openid', 'email', 'profile') verify Callable[[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any] | None], Any] | None

verify(claims, userinfo): your user, or None to refuse the login. claims are the ID token's, verified; userinfo the userinfo endpoint's (with userinfo=True; None otherwise), whose sub is the ID token's. Async, or a plain function, which runs in a thread. By default the user is the claims, with the userinfo's added.

None userinfo bool

also read the userinfo endpoint, for claims the ID token doesn't carry.

False max_age int | None

the signature algorithms accepted.

docs.title: verify_logout_token async
docs.text:
verify_logout_token(logout_token: str) -> LogoutToken

The logout token's claims, verified as Back-Channel Logout 1.0 (2.6) says: signed by a key of the provider's JWKS with one of algorithms, from issuer, for this app, issued in the last LOGOUT_TOKEN_LIFETIME seconds, with a jti, the logout event, a sub or a sid, and no nonce. Raises AuthenticationFailed otherwise. Replays aren't checked here: backchannel_logout_endpoint does.

docs.title: backchannel_logout_endpoint
docs.text:
backchannel_logout_endpoint(sessions: UserSessions, *, user_id: Callable[[str], Awaitable[Any] | Any] | None = None, cache: Cache | None = None) -> Callable[[Request], Awaitable[Response]]

The endpoint the provider POSTs logout tokens to (Back-Channel Logout 1.0), to mount at the URL registered there: app.post("/auth/backchannel-logout")(endpoint).

A valid token ends the app's sessions of that login: those whose oidc_sid is its sid (UserSessions.end_sid: keep the ID token's sid there at login), or, for a token with a sub and no sid, every session of the user (end_all). user_id(sub) (sync or async) gives the app's user id of the provider's sub (the sub itself by default; None: nothing to end). Each token is taken once (its jti, kept in cache's backend, the app's or FastAPICache's, for LOGOUT_TOKEN_LIFETIME seconds). Answers 200, or 400 with invalid_request (the reason is logged, not sent), with Cache-Control: no-store.

Bases: Strategy

The authorization code flow with PKCE, which OAuth2Strategy and OIDCStrategy share: redirect() sends the browser to the provider, and the callback's request is authenticated by its code. Subclasses set the endpoints and implement _finish.

redirect() starts the login: it sends the browser to the provider with a random state and a PKCE challenge, whose verifier waits in a short-lived cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, __Host- when Secure). A callback without that cookie or with another state is refused: nobody can log a user in with their own account (login CSRF) nor use a stolen code.

SAMLStrategy(*, entity_id: str, acs_url: str, idp_entity_id: str, idp_sso_url: str, idp_certificate: str | Sequence[str], verify: Callable[[SAMLProfile], Any] | None = None, name_id_format: str | None = None, clock_skew: float = 60, cache: Cache | None = None, name: str = 'saml')

Bases: Strategy

Authenticates the requests the IdP posts to the Assertion Consumer Service (the ACS): checks the signature of their response with the IdP's certificate, and that it answers the login this browser started; the user is what verify makes of the profile. Other requests carry nothing for it (None): it only goes on the ACS route.

redirect() starts the login (SP-initiated: logins the IdP starts by itself aren't accepted). The id of its request waits in a short-lived cookie (__Host-, HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=None: the IdP posts to the ACS from its own site), and the answer must carry it.

Checked on what the signature covers: the issuer, the audience (entity_id), the recipient (acs_url), the request it answers, when it's valid (with clock_skew), and that it's a bearer assertion. Each assertion works once: its id is kept in the cache's backend until it expires, so a copy is refused by every process. Not supported: encrypted assertions, signed requests, single logout.

the NameID format to ask for (urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid- format:emailAddress...); the IdP's default without one.

docs.text:
UnkeyStrategy(unkey: UnkeyClient, verify: Callable[[UnkeyKey], Any] | None = None, *, permissions: str | None = None, cost: int = 1, ratelimits: Sequence[str] = (), keyspaces: Sequence[str] = (), tags: Sequence[str] = (), header: str | None = None, credits_status: int = HTTP_429_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, name: str = 'unkey', metrics: Metrics | None = None)

Bases: Strategy

Authenticates by an API key that Unkey verifies: Authorization: Bearer <key> by default, or the header header. Each request is one verification, which spends the key's credits and counts in its rate limits: nothing is cached, so a key deleted or disabled is refused at once (Unkey takes up to 30 seconds to spread a deletion).

What Unkey answers:

  • VALID: the user is verify(key) (an UnkeyKey), the key itself without verify.
  • NOT_FOUND, DISABLED, EXPIRED: authentication fails (a 401, or the next strategy).
  • INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS, FORBIDDEN: a 403; the key is valid, it may not do this.
  • RATE_LIMITED: a 429 with Retry-After; USAGE_EXCEEDED (no credits left): a 429, or a 402 with credits_status=402.
  • Unkey down, slow (timeout) or limiting the workspace: a 503. A root key without the verify permission: UnkeyError, a 500.

A route that needs other permissions or costs more credits has a strategy of its own, with another name and the same client: UnkeyStrategy(verifier, name="unkey-admin", permissions="admin.*").

the client, with a root key that may verify keys.

credits each verification spends (0 for none); a key without a credit limit spends nothing.

the keyspaces (APIs) the key must belong to; any by default.

the header the key comes in (X-API-Key), instead of Authorization: Bearer.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
A policy per route (FastAPIAuthz) or for every request (AuthzMiddleware), held by Casbin, Cedar (CedarEnforcer) or Open Policy Agent (OPAEnforcer). In fastapi_alcazaba.authz.

In the guide: Authorization. In an app: the examples.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.authz.FastAPIAuthz
docs.text:
FastAPIAuthz(enforcer: Enforcer, *, subject: Subject | None = None, anonymous: str | None = None, challenge: str = 'Bearer', metrics: Metrics | None = None, audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None, actor: Actor | None = None)

FastAPI dependency that lets a request through only when the policy allows it.

authz = FastAPIAuthz(enforcer, subject=current_username)

# (subject, path, method): the path the app routes, and the HTTP method.
router = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(authz)])

# (subject, *values): your own objects and actions; {id} takes the path parameter.
archive = authz.require("projects/{id}", "archive")
@app.post("/projects/{id}/archive", dependencies=[Depends(archive)])

A request without a subject gets a 401 (with WWW-Authenticate: <challenge>), unless anonymous names the subject the policy knows them by; one that the policy refuses, a 403; one the engine couldn't answer (PolicyUnavailable), a 503. Paths with control characters (%0A...) get a 400 without asking the policy, as the app could route them elsewhere than the policy reads them. On WebSocket routes, the connection is closed with 1008 (policy violation) instead, 1013 (try again later) for the 503. Both dependencies return the subject (None for anonymous requests let through).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default enforcer Enforcer

a Casbin enforcer, a CedarEnforcer, or anything with enforce (a plain function or a coroutine function), with its policy loaded (await enforcer.load_policy() in the lifespan for an AsyncEnforcer). PolicyUnavailable refuses the request with a 503; any other exception it raises, with a 500: never the route.

required subject Subject | None

a dependency returning who makes the request (a user name, an id, an object for ABAC matchers), or None when nobody is authenticated. By default the user of Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware (starlette_user).

None anonymous str | None

the subject of requests without one, for policies that open some routes to everybody (p, anonymous, /catalog, GET); None refuses them without asking the policy. A name no user can have (*anonymous), or a user who takes it gets its rules, and every anonymous request that user's.

None challenge str

the WWW-Authenticate of the 401s: the scheme your users log in with.

'Bearer' metrics Metrics | None

where to count the decisions (fastapi_alcazaba.authz); FastAPICache's by default.

None audit FastAPIAudit | None

the audit trail that records the requests the policy refuses (authz.denied: the 403s, and the 400s of paths with control characters) and those the engine couldn't decide (authz.unavailable), with what was asked, the route and the client. Not the 401s of requests without a subject, which authentication tells, nor enforce()'s checks in a route, whose answer the route decides what to do with.

None actor Actor | None

who the subject is, in those events: actor(subject), an ID; subject_id by default.

None

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.authz.AuthzMiddleware
docs.text:
AuthzMiddleware(app: ASGIApp, enforcer: Enforcer, *, anonymous: str | None = None, challenge: str = 'Bearer', metrics: Metrics | None = None, audit: FastAPIAudit | None = None, actor: Actor | None = None)

Checks every request against the policy, with the user of Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware. Add it before AuthenticationMiddleware, so that it runs after it:

app.add_middleware(AuthzMiddleware, enforcer=enforcer)
app.add_middleware(AuthenticationMiddleware, backend=BasicAuth())

Each request is checked as (user, path, method): the user's identity (anonymous when it isn't authenticated), the path the app routes (without the root_path a proxy or a mount adds in front) and the method, GET for HEAD and WEBSOCKET for WebSockets. Refused requests get a 403, or a 401 (with WWW-Authenticate: <challenge>) when they have no user, and a 503 when the engine didn't answer (PolicyUnavailable); WebSockets are closed with 1008 (policy violation), or 1013 (try again later). Paths with control characters (%0A...) get a 400 without asking the policy, as the app could route them elsewhere than the policy reads them. Every request is checked, OPTIONS too: add CORSMiddleware after this one (outside it), and it answers the preflights before they get here.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default enforcer Enforcer

a Casbin enforcer, a CedarEnforcer, or anything with enforce (a plain function or a coroutine function), with its policy loaded.

required anonymous str | None

the subject of requests without a user, a name no user can have (*anonymous); None refuses them without asking the policy.

None challenge str

the WWW-Authenticate of the 401s.

'Bearer' metrics Metrics | None

where to count the decisions (fastapi_alcazaba.authz); FastAPICache's by default.

None audit FastAPIAudit | None

the audit trail that records the refusals, as FastAPIAuthz's audit says.

None actor Actor | None

who the subject is, in those events; subject_id by default.

None

CedarEnforcer(policies: str, *, entities: Sequence[Entity] = (), entities_of: Callable[[Any], Sequence[Entity] | Awaitable[Sequence[Entity]]] | None = None, schema: str | Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, principal_type: str = 'User', action_type: str = 'Action', resource_type: str = 'Resource')

An enforcer of Cedar policies, for FastAPIAuthz(enforcer) and AuthzMiddleware.

await enforce(subject, resource, action, context=None) asks Cedar whether subject may do action on resource. Cedar denies what no policy permits, and a forbid beats every permit. the entity type of subjects given as strings.

the entity type of actions.

'Action' resource_type str

the entity type of resources given as strings, paths too.

Whether the policies let subject do action on resource.

subject and resource are each a name (of principal_type or resource_type), an entity uid ({"type": "Team", "id": "core"}), or a whole entity with its attributes ({"uid": ..., "attrs": {"owner": ...}, "parents": [...]}), which this request sees: the user your authentication loaded, the document the route just read. action is a name of action_type or a uid. context is Cedar's context.
